Earshot's macOS build uses the shared, Core ML-capable sherpa-onnx / ONNX Runtime libraries. The previous static runtime explicitly disabled Core ML. Earshot is a desktop and web app for live-production crews, built by RVLT. One computer, the host, listens to many intercom ("comms") channels at once, turns the speech into text on that same computer, and shows the transcript on any phone, tablet or laptop on the show network. It can also send show-control cues (OSC, MIDI, web requests) when it hears a phrase you chose. This manual is for the people who run the show: stage managers, sound and lighting operators, and production managers. New to Earshot? Get started with the desktop app. Install it, follow the setup assistant, check your first transcript and connect the crew. The Feed, showing the app's built-in mock show. Every picture in this manual uses made-up lines. None is from a real show.

It listens to many comms channels at once (party lines, talkbacks, radios) through the audio inputs of one computer. It turns speech into text on that computer. The speech model runs locally. It shows the text as a live transcript on the host and in any browser on the show network. Each person can read it in their own language. It keeps every session. You can search it and export it, and replay the audio behind a line if you chose to save it. It can correct names and gear the recogniser gets wrong, with a glossary. It can show who is talking when several people share one channel, if it has learned their voices. It can show channels from another Earshot computer on this one. It can send cues when it hears a phrase you chose, with a master Armed/Safe switch, cooldowns, a test bench and an activity log.

Audio stays on the computer unless you turn on cloud speech for a channel. Cloud speech (Deepgram) is off. You choose it for one channel at a time, and Earshot asks you to confirm. Cloud translators (DeepL, Claude) send the text of lines out, and also ask first. Nothing else sends audio or text to a company. The other things that go out are model downloads (when you press Download) and the messages your automations send while the show is Armed. Privacy has the full list. Nothing is sent to a console unless the show is Armed. In Safe, automations only log "would have fired". Speech recognition makes mistakes Treat a phrase automation as a convenience that sits beside your normal cue calling, not instead of it. How Earshot hears numbers explains what Earshot checks before it fires a number, and what it cannot check.

This is work in progress. It runs and is tested on macOS (Apple Silicon). The headless host has passed a demo startup smoke test on Windows and Linux; their installer interfaces and desktop windows have not been tested. It has not been tried against Dante, MADI or other many-input hardware, with a real microphone on real comms, or in a real venue. Limits and known behaviour says exactly what has been tried and what has not. Read it before you trust Earshot on a show.

documents.t: These are planned. They are either not built, or built but not usable from the app. Do not rely on any of them. Feature What you will see "Play a sound" and "Show or hide the window" actions You can add them to an automation, but they do not run. The automation shows a problem saying so. The other actions in the same automation still run. A signed installer Unsigned downloads are published for macOS Apple Silicon, Windows x64 and Linux x86_64. The Mac app is signed ad hoc only and is not notarised. Windows and Linux installer interfaces and desktop windows have not been tested. There is no Intel Mac installer. Turning on https for Earshot's own address Earshot serves plain http. There is no setting to give it a certificate. Encrypted links between Earshot computers The link screen offers "Encrypted (https)", but it has not been proven end to end in this build. Treat links as not encrypted. Choosing the network interface or web port There is no Setup screen for them. The headless program takes --bind and --port. Importing a speech model from a folder (for a venue with no internet) There is no screen for it. Download the model once while you have internet.

Things you press are in bold: Hold to arm, Make safe, Download. Words the app shows you are in "quotes", exactly as they appear. Things you type, addresses and file names are in this type. Setup, Models means: open the Setup view, then the Models section. A red box means something can send a cue or lose part of the show. A yellow box means something is untested or easy to get wrong. Where a feature has only been tried on computer-made voices, or never against the real service, the page says so. Those sentences are there on purpose. Unsure of a word? See Words used in this manual.

This page is the reference for the Then part of the automation editor ("What happens, in this order.") and for the Safety part beneath it. Actions run in order, top to bottom. To add one, choose its kind in the box at the bottom of Then and press Add action. The arrows on an action move it up and down, and the bin removes it. An automation with no actions can be saved, with the note "With no actions this does nothing when it fires." Three actions in order, on the mock show's "Roll video" automation. Mock show, not a real show. Actions really send only while Armed While the show is Safe, every action is a dry run: Earshot logs what it would have done and sends nothing. That includes the actions that stay inside Earshot, such as adding a marker or setting a flag. See Safe and Armed. Most text fields accept {{variables}}, such as {{capture.number}}. Pick one from Insert variable… under the field, or type it. See Variables.

Sends one OSC message to a destination. Field What it is Destination Where it goes. Listed as, for example, Eos (UDP 10.0.1.20:8000). Manage destinations opens the list. Address The OSC address. "Must start with /." Accepts variables. Arguments None by default ("No arguments: a bare message."). Add an argument adds one.

A value put into an address by a variable may not contain / * ? [ ] { } , # or a space. If it does, or if the variable is empty, that action is skipped and the reason is logged. It is never tidied up and sent anyway. This is what stops a mis-heard word from turning /eos/cue/{{capture.number}}/fire into an address that hits every cue. The parts of the address you typed yourself are not restricted.

Each argument has a type and a value. The value accepts variables. Type in the editor Value Example Whole number A whole number that fits 32 bits. 1 or {{capture.number}} Decimal number A decimal number. 0.5 Text Any text. go True / false true, false, 1 or 0. true Nothing (nil) No value. Impulse (bang) No value. Raw bytes Hex bytes. 0A FF 10 If a value cannot be read as its type when the automation fires, the action is skipped and Activity says why. Earshot never substitutes a default. For example, a Whole number argument set to {{capture.number}} is skipped when someone says "cue twelve point five", because 12.5 is not a whole number. Use Decimal number if you expect point cues.

A destination is a device that receives OSC: "a lighting desk, a video server, a QLab machine". Destinations belong to the show, so every automation can use them. OSC destinations. The addresses are made up. Mock show, not a real show. Press Manage destinations, then Add a destination: Field What it is Name What you call it, for example Eos. Host The device's address, for example 192.168.1.20. Port The port the device listens on for OSC. Protocol UDP or TCP. Use what the device expects. The list shows how many automations use each destination. Deleting one that is in use leaves those actions with a problem: "That OSC destination no longer exists. Pick another, or add it again." UDP or TCP matters when you press Safe: A UDP message is gone the moment it is sent. OSC waiting for a TCP destination is discarded when you press Safe. A TCP destination that is down is retried, and the sends skipped meanwhile are logged. Editing one destination reconnects only that destination. Pressing Safe resets all of them.

Field What it is Output port The MIDI output to send to. A port that has gone is listed as "(not found)". Message type Note on, Note off, Control change, Program change or Raw bytes. MIDI channel (1 to 16) For every type except Raw bytes. Note and Velocity Note on. 0 to 127 each. A new action starts at note 60, velocity 100. Note Note off. 0 to 127. Controller and Value Control change. 0 to 127 each. Program Program change. 0 to 127. Raw bytes (hex) "Like 90 3C 7F: status byte, then data bytes." The number fields accept variables, so a MIDI trigger can pass its own note on: {{midi.note}}. The result must be a whole number from 0 to 127, or the action is skipped. A MIDI send is on time or it does not go. If the port is busy for more than 1 second, the send is dropped and Activity says "not sent: the MIDI port was busy for more than 1 s".

Calls a web address: a video server, a show-control system, a chat hook. Field What it is Method GET, POST, PUT or DELETE. URL "Starts with http:// or https://. Variables in the URL are made URL-safe for you." Headers Optional. Add a header adds a name and a value. Body "Optional. Sent as written, with variables filled in (not URL-encoded)." A variable in the URL is percent-encoded, so a ?, & or # in something that was said cannot change the request. A variable in the Body is put in as it is. The request must finish within a few seconds or it counts as failed. At most 5 redirects are followed. Pressing Safe cancels a request in progress, and any redirect is not followed. Earshot does not use a proxy for these requests, even if the computer has one set.

A header value usually holds a key or a token, so Earshot treats every header value as a secret: Once saved, the value is never sent back to any browser. The editor shows •••• (unchanged) with a Replace button. Leave it alone to keep it. Press Replace and type a new value to change it. A duplicated automation does not get the values: "Secrets are not copied. Re-enter 1 header value." An exported show file hides header values and cuts web addresses back to the host name. After an import those automations arrive switched off until you enter them again. Operators and viewers do not see the URL's path, the body or the header values. In Activity everyone sees only the method and the host. See saved secrets.

Runs a command on the host computer, with the rights of the account Earshot runs under. Off unless an admin turns it on Shell commands do nothing unless an admin turns on Setup, Show control, Allow automations to run shell commands. Until then the action is skipped, and the editor says "Shell actions are switched off in Setup, so the engine will skip this one until an admin enables them." Importing a show file never turns the switch on, and every automation with a shell action arrives switched off after an import, whatever this computer's setting. Read what a command does before you switch it on. One field, Command. "Runs on the machine that hosts Earshot, only if an admin has enabled shell actions in Setup. This is not a template." A shell command cannot contain {{…}}. A command with one is refused. Values reach the command as environment variables instead, "so spoken text can never become part of the command itself". The name is the variable's name in capitals, with every other character turned into _, after EARSHOT_: Variable Environment variable {{text}} $EARSHOT_TEXT {{match}} $EARSHOT_MATCH {{capture.number}} $EARSHOT_CAPTURE_NUMBER {{channel.name}} $EARSHOT_CHANNEL_NAME {{osc.args.0}} $EARSHOT_OSC_ARGS_0 {{var.body}} $EARSHOT_VAR_BODY The editor lists the ones your trigger provides under the field. If you paste an old command with {{text}} in it, the button Use environment variables instead rewrites it for you. An example, for a Mac: say "$EARSHOT_TEXT" Always put the variable in double quotes, as above, so a value with spaces stays one value. Things to know: The command gets a nearly empty environment: the EARSHOT_ values, and PATH, HOME and the temporary-folder variables. Nothing else from Earshot's own environment is passed on. Its output is thrown away. Earshot only records whether it ran. A command may run for 5 seconds. After that it is stopped, together with the programs it started. A cue that needs longer must start its own long-running program. Pressing Safe stops a running command and the programs it started. That is untested on Windows. Activity shows "run a shell command", never the command text, because a command line often carries a password.

Puts a large banner across Earshot's screens. Use it for things people must not miss. The mock show's Blackout automation. Not a real show. An alert that stays until someone presses Acknowledge. Mock show, not a real show. Field What it is Alert text "Shown in large type across every screen." Accepts variables. A new action starts as {{text}}, the whole line that was heard. Colour "A hex colour like #ff8800. Empty uses the theme's attention colour." Length of one flash (ms) A new action starts at 3000. Under 400 ms "is shown as a steady banner, not a flash, to avoid strobing". Flashes How many times. A new action starts at 3. With 0, nothing is shown. Stay on screen until someone acknowledges "Operators and admins get an Acknowledge button; it clears on every screen at once." Show to Viewers, Operators, Admins. "Leave all unticked to show it to everyone." "Flashing is slow (at most about 2.5 times a second), and people who ask their device to reduce motion see a steady banner instead."

These two do not run in this build You can add Play a sound and Show or hide the window, but they do nothing. The automation shows a problem saying so ("'Play sound' is not available in this build; the other actions still run."). The other actions in the same automation still run.
documents.s: Play a sound, and Show or hide the window

documents.t: Writes a typed line into a channel, as if someone had typed it. Field What it is Send to A fixed channel or A channel worked out when it runs. Channel For a fixed channel: pick it. Channel name, short name or number For a worked-out channel. "Looked up by name, then short name, then position (1 is the first channel)." Accepts variables. A new one starts as {{channel.slug}}, the channel the trigger came from. Text What to write. Accepts variables. The line appears with the Typed badge, and its author reads "Automation: " followed by the automation's name. A typed line never fires a phrase automation, so this cannot loop. If the channel cannot be found, or the text comes out empty, the action is skipped.

One field, Marker text. "Appears on the timeline in the Archive." Accepts variables. A new action starts as {{text}}. Markers let you jump to a moment later: "Cue 42", "Top of act two". See Archive and markers.

Changes what the Earshot window on the host computer is showing. "Changes the view on the host computer's own Earshot window only. Other devices are not affected." Screen command Extra field Select a channel Channel: "Name, short name or number (1 is the first channel)." Accepts variables. Select the next channel Select the previous channel Scroll up Scroll down Jump to live Mark as read Channel (empty marks every channel read) Larger text Smaller text These are never sent to phones, tablets or other computers. They do nothing while someone at the host is in Setup, Automations, Archive or Activity, so a cue never throws someone out of an editor. The same controls are available by OSC: see the OSC address reference.
Field Choices Channel The channel. Do Pause it or Resume it. A paused channel shows the Paused badge until it is resumed. See status and badges.

One field, Channel: Every channel or one channel. "Clears what is on screen and in this session's live transcript." Clearing also removes saved audio Clearing a transcript makes the saved audio behind those lines unreachable at once, and deletes the files. See Replay a line's audio.

Field What it is Flag name Any name. "Conditions can check it." Set it to Set or Cleared. A flag is an on/off marker that only automations use. One automation sets it; another has an Only if condition, "A flag is set" or "A flag is not set", that checks it. See Triggers and conditions and the interlock in Recipes. Flags start cleared each time Earshot starts. A flag is only really set while the show is Armed: in Safe, this action is a dry run like any other.

One field, Wait (milliseconds). "Actions after this one run later. 1000 is one second." A new action starts at 500. If Safe is pressed during a Wait, the remaining actions do not run. Arming again later does not resume them.

One field, Automation: pick which one. "Runs as part of the same moment. A chain runs each automation at most once, and stops after 32 runs in all." The other automation is handed this one's values, with var. in front of each name. {{capture.number}} here is {{var.capture.number}} there, and {{text}} is {{var.text}}. Its own Only if conditions and cooldown still apply. An automation limited to people cannot be run this way: a chain has no voice. See Automations limited to people. The chain limits, which also break every loop: Limit Value Times one automation can fire in a chain 1 Firings in one chain, in all 32 Depth (one automation running another, running another…) 8 hops Anything past a limit is not run, and Activity says "loop guard: the chain's limit was reached (each automation once per chain, at most 32 firings, 8 hops)". An automation that runs itself gets the warning "This runs itself. An automation fires at most once per chain, so the repeat is skipped."

One action failing does not stop the ones after it. In Activity the automation's row is marked Failed, and opening the row lists which action was not run (for example "action 1 not run") and the reason. Common reasons: The reason given What it means OSC address variable {{capture.number}} = "…" is empty or contains / * ? [ ] { } , # or whitespace A captured value was not safe to put in an OSC address. OSC argument 1: "12.5" is not an int The value does not fit the argument's type. unknown OSC destination … The destination was deleted. no channel matches "…" A worked-out channel name matched nothing. not sent: the show was made Safe Safe was pressed before this action went out. disarmed during run Safe was pressed while the automation was part-way through its actions. The rest did not run. not sent: the MIDI port was busy for more than 1 s See Send MIDI above. shell actions are disabled (an admin must enable allow_shell_actions) The switch in Setup, Show control, is off. See Run a shell command above. shell commands cannot contain {{…}}; use the EARSHOT_* environment variables See Run a shell command above.
Safety. Mock show, not a real show.

"After it fires, it ignores the trigger for this long. 0 means no cooldown. It always fires at most once per utterance." A new automation has 2000 (two seconds). Set it so that a repeated call does not send the cue twice. A caller who says "go… go" a second apart should send one cue, not two. While it is cooling down, Activity says cooling down (N ms left). A firing that Earshot refuses (for example because of the runaway limits) still uses up the cooldown. Spoken phrases are exempt from the runaway stop, so Cooldown is the only limit on how often a spoken cue can fire.

Choice What it does Final text (recommended) Waits for the finished line. A channel that is Behind fires later. Draft text (faster, less safe) Can fire while the person is still speaking, as soon as the draft matches and at least one more word has followed. Draft text can still change, so a mis-hearing that Earshot would have corrected can fire. Either way an automation fires at most once per line. In the list, an automation set to draft text is marked "fires on draft text". "Only spoken phrases use this; other triggers ignore it." Drafts appear only on channels with "Show words as they are spoken" on, and only while Earshot is keeping up. See channel settings.

An automation is a trigger, optional conditions, and a list of actions. This page builds one from start to finish: the "Go cue" automation from the mock show. When the show caller says "go cue forty two", it sends an OSC message with the number 42 to a lighting desk and drops a marker in the Archive. Who can do this Only admins can build and edit automations. Operators see the list, can press Run now and can use the Test bench. Viewers see the list only ("This list is read-only for viewers."). See roles. Read Safe and Armed first. Everything you build here only logs "would have fired" until the show is Armed.

Open Automations. On a phone it is under More. The Automations list. Mock show, not a real show. At the top are two tabs, Automations and Test bench, and a line that says whether the show is Safe or ARMED. Each automation in the list shows: On the row What it is The name, and a Problem badge if something is wrong See When an automation is not running. The Enabled switch, with "On" or "Off" beside it A disabled automation never fires, but keeps its settings. Non-admins see an "Enabled" or "Disabled" badge instead. A summary of the trigger For example Hears "go cue {number}" on Show Caller. "2 actions" Press it to list what the automation does. An automation that fires on draft text also says "fires on draft text". When it last fired "Not fired since you connected", or "Last fired 12:50:04 (dry run: nothing was sent)" or "(sent)". Run now Runs it by hand. See Run now. Operators and admins. Edit, Duplicate, Delete Admins only. A duplicate is made switched off, so it cannot double-fire, and opens in the editor. Delete asks first: "It will stop working straight away and cannot be brought back. Other automations that run it will show a problem." A duplicate does not copy secrets. A web-request trigger gets a fresh address of its own, and HTTP header values are left empty for you to enter again.
Press New automation. The editor opens. It has five parts, in order: Basics, When, Only if, Then and Safety. The editor, open on "Go cue". Mock show, not a real show.

Basics. Mock show, not a real show. Field What to enter Notes Name Go cue What people see in the list and in Activity. Two automations may share a name, but the editor warns that they will be hard to tell apart. Short name go-cue (filled in for you) Used in web addresses and OSC. Lower-case a to z, digits and single hyphens. On a new automation it is a preview: "The engine chooses the final short name, or type your own". Enabled On "A disabled automation never fires, but keeps its settings."

When. Mock show, not a real show. Under This automation starts when it, leave A spoken phrase. Under Match mode, leave Exact phrase. In Phrase 1, type go cue {number}. Under Where to listen, Channels, tick Show Caller. The braces make a capture. {number} stands for exactly one spoken word. When someone says "go cue forty two", Earshot has already turned "forty two" into 42, so the capture is 42. The editor confirms it under the phrase: "Captures you can use in actions: {{capture.number}}". The editor also reminds you: "Automations hear what was said. Glossary corrections change only what you read." Leaving a Where to listen list empty means "listen to everything". Ticking Show Caller means this automation ignores the same words on every other channel. Every trigger and every field is described in Triggers and conditions. How numbers are heard, and what Earshot refuses, is in How Earshot hears numbers.

Only if. Mock show, not a real show. Leave this empty for now. It reads "No extra conditions: it runs whenever the trigger fires." Conditions are optional extra checks, and all of them must be true. To add one, choose its kind in the box and press Add condition. The kinds are listed in Triggers and conditions.
Actions run in order, top to bottom. Then, on a different automation ("Roll video") so you can see three kinds of action. Mock show, not a real show.

A Send OSC action goes to a destination: a lighting desk, a video server, a QLab machine. Make the destination once and every automation can use it. In the box at the bottom of Then, choose Send OSC and press Add action. Press Manage destinations, then Add a destination. Enter Name Eos, Host 10.0.1.20, Port 8000, Protocol UDP. Use your own desk's address and port. Press Add destination, then Done. OSC destinations. The addresses are made up. Mock show, not a real show.

Field What to enter Destination Eos (UDP 10.0.1.20:8000) Address /eos/cue/{{capture.number}}/fire Arguments None. It reads "No arguments: a bare message." {{capture.number}} is a variable. When the automation fires, Earshot puts the captured number in its place, so the desk receives /eos/cue/42/fire. You can type a variable or pick it from Insert variable… under the field. See Variables. Check the address against your desk /eos/cue/…/fire is the receiving product's own OSC address, not Earshot's. Check the exact address in that product's documentation. Earshot has only been tried against stand-ins on one Mac, never against a real console. See Limits and known behaviour.
documents.s: Fill in the Send OSC action

documents.t: Choose Add a marker in the box at the bottom and press Add action. In Marker text, type Cue {{capture.number}}. The marker "appears on the timeline in the Archive", so afterwards you can jump to the moment each cue was called. See Archive and markers. Use the arrows on an action to move it up or down, and the bin to remove it. Every action is described in Actions.

Safety. Mock show, not a real show. Field Leave it at Why Cooldown (milliseconds) 2000 "After it fires, it ignores the trigger for this long. 0 means no cooldown. It always fires at most once per utterance." Two seconds stops a repeated call from sending the cue twice. Fire on Final text (recommended) It waits for the finished line. Draft text (faster, less safe) can fire while the person is still speaking.

Press Save automation. If something is wrong, the editor lists it ("1 thing to fix before saving:") and does not save. Yellow "Check:" notes are warnings: they do not stop you saving. If you try to leave with unsaved changes, Earshot asks "Discard your changes?" with Keep editing and Discard changes.

Open the Test bench tab. Under Phrase to test, type go cue forty two, the way it would be said. Under Channel, choose Show Caller. Press Test phrase. The Test bench after testing "go cue forty two". Mock show, not a real show. The result shows "1 automation would fire.", then a card for Go cue with a Would have fired badge and one line per action, each marked "Would run". The OSC line shows the address with 42 in place of the variable. Nothing is ever sent from the Test bench, whether the show is Safe or Armed. See Testing. Now try the phrases that should not fire. go cue 7 and 8 matches the words but is refused for its number, and the bench does not say why. That reason only appears in Activity when a real line is spoken. See How Earshot hears numbers.
documents.s: Step 8: Try it on the Test bench

documents.t: With the header showing Safe, have the show caller say "go cue forty two" on the real channel. Read the line in the Feed. Check that it was heard the way you expect. Open Activity. Look for a row like Would have fired Go cue: phrase "…" on Show Caller, where the dots are the words that matched, with a Dry run badge. The Activity log. Mock show, not a real show. If there is no such row, or the row says "Go cue" did not fire: …, the reason is on the row. See A cue did not fire.

Only when the dry runs look right: Hold Hold to arm for about 0.7 seconds. The header turns red. Wait a beat. A line fires only if the show was Armed from the moment the words began. Have the caller say the line again. Check Activity for Fired Go cue: … and check the desk. Press Make safe when you are done. Armed really sends While the show is Armed, every enabled automation can fire, not only the one you are testing. Check the list before you arm.
documents.s: Step 10: Arm, and say it again

documents.t: Triggers and conditions: every way an automation can start. Actions: everything an automation can do. Recipes: ten complete automations to copy. Testing: Run now, the Test bench and the Activity log.

A wrong number sends the wrong cue. So when Earshot is not sure it has the whole number, it fires nothing and writes the reason in Activity. A refusal is visible. A wrong cue is not. This page covers what counts as speech for an automation, how a line is tidied before matching, what fires, what is refused, and how to call and write phrases so they work first time.
documents.s: How Earshot hears numbers, and what it refuses

documents.t: Typed lines never fire phrase automations, whoever types them, in any channel, however they get there (the Feed, an OSC message, or another automation). Automations hear what was said, not the glossary-corrected text. The glossary changes only what people read. If a cue depends on a word the recogniser mis-hears, add the mis-hearing to the automation's phrases. Each phrase trigger in the editor says so: "Automations hear what was said. Glossary corrections change only what you read." Translations are never heard by automations. See Read in another language. Lines from another Earshot computer never fire automations here. See linked channels. For example, if you want "alesha go" to fire a cue but the recogniser writes "aleesha go", add aleesha go as another phrase in the automation. The glossary will fix the spelling people read. It will not help the automation.

Before matching, Earshot: makes everything lower case and ignores punctuation; turns spoken numbers into digits: "forty two" becomes 42, "two hundred and five" becomes 205, "four point five" becomes 4.5; turns "Q42" and "Q 7" into "cue 42" and "cue 7"; turns "stand by" into "standby"; drops the filler words um, uh, er, erm, ah and hmm. A lone "one" becomes 1 only straight after a word like cue, scene, song, page, preset, snapshot, channel, mix, track, number, step, look or deck. So "cue one" matches a phrase written cue 1, but "the one on the left" is left alone. Your phrases are tidied the same way, so Go Cue {number} and go cue {number} are the same phrase.
documents.s: How a line is tidied before matching

documents.t: The examples below use the phrase cue {n}. Said Earshot hears Fires with "cue twelve point five" (also "dot" or "decimal") cue 12.5 12.5 "cue twelve point two five" cue 12.25 12.25 "cue four oh five" cue 405 405 "cue twelve oh five" cue 1205 1205 "cue one hundred and five" cue 105 105 "cue forty two" or "Q forty two" or "Q42" cue 42 42 "cue twenty for the reveal" cue 20 for the reveal 20 "cue 7 and video cue 8" 7 (the word after "and" is not a number) "cue twelve point oh" cue 12 point 0 12.0 Careful with "point oh" If a line is cut off right after "point oh", it fires 12.0 even though you meant "point oh five".

When a call is refused, Activity has a row like this: "Lighting" did not fire: the number may be incomplete: "5 6" looks like part of a longer number, so 5 is not fired on its own Said Why nothing fires "cue 7 and 8", "cue seven and eight", "cue 100 and 5" Two numbers joined by "and" could be two cues or one. Earshot will not pick one. "cue seven and a half" Earshot does not read "and a half" as .5. Say "cue seven point five". "cue twenty for" (the line ends there), "cue twenty to five" "for", "to", "too", "fore", "won" and "ate" sound like numbers or joins, so a number followed by one is not trusted. If the line carries on with ordinary words ("cue twenty for the reveal"), it fires. "cue 5 6 7", "cue five six seven" A run of numbers could be one long number or three. "cue four hundred oh five" Earshot reads "four oh five" as 405 but will not guess for "four hundred oh five". It would not be 40005, and it cannot tell what you meant. Say "four oh five". "cue forty um two", "cue twelve point, uh, five" A filler word in the middle of a number, or with commas around it, leaves two separate numbers, and Earshot will not join them. (Earshot drops um, uh, er, erm, ah and hmm before it reads numbers, so "cue twelve point um five" still fires 12.5.) a line that ends "cue 12 point", "cue 12 dot", "cue seven and", "cue one hundred and" The line was cut off. The rest of the number may still be coming. "cue 12 dot com" "dot" and "decimal" count as "point". A number followed by one that does not turn into a decimal number is refused. "cue 5 hundred", "cue 5 oh", "cue zero oh five", "cue four oh five six" Not a clear single number. "cue oh four", "cue point five" The value would be "oh" or "point", not a number. After a refusal, say the call again, more plainly.

Say the cue word, then the number, then stop or say a plain word: "cue forty two, go". Say "point" for decimals: "cue twelve point five". Say digits after "point" one at a time or as one number: "point two five" or "point twenty five". Say "four oh five" for 405, not "four hundred oh five". "One hundred and five" is fine. Do not read a list of cues in one go. One cue per call. Do not leave "um" or a long pause in the middle of a number. Before a number, a word helps ("cue", "scene", "lights"). A phrase that starts with the number, such as {n} go, is refused more often, because "one twenty go" could be the tail of "one twenty". Put this on the caller's desk The short version for whoever calls the show: cue word, number, "go". One cue per call. Say "point" for point cues. No lists, no "um" inside a number.
documents.s: How to phrase a call so it fires first time

documents.t: Put a word between two values: fade {a} to {b}. fade {a} {b} and cue {a} 5 are rejected: the automation shows a problem and never fires. Earshot cannot tell where one number stops and the next starts. fade {a} and {b} and other phrases where only joining words ("and", "point", "oh", "dot", number words) sit between two values are rejected the same way: they could never fire. A phrase containing a filler word (um, uh, er, erm, ah, hmm) is rejected the same way. It would match more than you expect. "to" is allowed between two values because you wrote it into the phrase. A rejected phrase puts a Problem badge on the automation, with a line saying what to change. See When an automation is not running.

Phrase Verdict go cue {number} Good. A word before the number. sound cue {n} go Good. Words on both sides. fade {a} to {b} Good. A word between the two values. {n} go Allowed, but refused more often when called. Put a word in front. fade {a} {b} Rejected. Two values back to back. cue {a} 5 Rejected. A value straight before a number. fade {a} and {b} Rejected. Only a joining word between the values. um go cue {n} Rejected. It contains a filler word.
documents.s: Good and bad phrases at a glance

documents.t: If the recogniser hears a clean, well-formed line that is simply wrong, Earshot cannot know. The example in the notes is "twenty two five" heard as "twenty to five" with the phrase fade {a} to {b}: it looks like a good call and fires 20 and 5. So: Test your phrases on the Test bench. Type them the way they would be said, for example "go cue forty two". Say them in rehearsal on the real comms, with the show Safe, and read Activity. Keep Safe the default until you have. Accuracy in a loud venue is unverified Recognition has been tried only on computer-made voices and a built-in microphone. The recogniser still makes mistakes on clean recordings. Treat every cue as something to confirm. See Limits and known behaviour.

An automation set to Fire on: Draft text (faster, less safe) can fire before the line is finished. Earshot still waits until the number can no longer grow: after a number, a plain word must follow before a draft fires. "cue forty…" does not fire 40 while "two" may still be coming. Draft text can also be corrected a moment later, and a draft-firing automation does not wait for that. For anything with a number in it, leave Fire on at Final text (recommended).

You can limit a phrase automation so that it fires only when a named person says the words. This is experimental. Read this whole page before you use it. The editor's own warning "Experimental. Fires only when Earshot is very sure who spoke. On a noisy comms line that is rare, and someone who sounds very like them can set it off. Do not use this for a cue that must go, or for one that must not go for the wrong person."

There are two places, and they do the same job: In When, under Where to listen, tick names in People. Or in Only if, add a condition of the kind Person is one of and tick names. Both need voice recognition to be working first: The voice model, Voice recognition (CAM++), is installed (Setup, Models). Each person has a learned voice (Setup, People). Separate and recognise voices on this channel is on for the channels the automation listens to (Setup, Channels). See People: recognise voices on a shared channel.

Warning What to do "The voice model is not installed, so this cannot fire. Install it in Setup → Models." Install the voice model. "Priya has no learned voice yet, so this cannot fire for Priya. Learn it in Setup → People." Learn that person's voice. "Voice recognition is off on Show Caller, so this cannot fire. Turn on “Separate and recognise voices on this channel” in Setup → Channels." Switch it on for that channel. (The names are examples. The editor names your own people and channels.)
documents.s: The editor warns when it can never fire

documents.t: In testing with 21 synthetic voices the strict rule named no voice that had not been learned, except within one group of three near-identical voices from the same speech engine. Inside that group it named the wrong one (the closest pair scored 0.92 against a rule that needs 0.90). So: Two people who sound very alike can set off each other's automations. Someone whose voice was never learned can set one off if they sound almost the same as a learned person. No setting removes this. It has not been measured on real voices.
documents.s: It can fire for the wrong person

documents.t: They use one fixed, stricter rule, whatever "Names on lines" says. The Names on lines choice (Cautious, Balanced, Eager) on the People screen changes only the names you read. A name you can read on a line does not mean a people-limited automation will fire for it. The People screen says so: "Automations limited to people always use the most cautious rule, whatever is chosen here." They wait for a confident match. The automation waits up to 1.5 seconds after the final line for Earshot to be sure. Automations with no people limit never wait. If Earshot is not sure, the automation does not fire. It was not sure, the voice was not recognised, the line was too short, or the answer came too late. Activity says why, for example: "Standby sound" did not fire: voice not recognised "Standby sound" did not fire: the voice was Dan, not Priya Safe pressed in between turns a firing into a dry run. Activity says "Safe was pressed before the voice was known".

A people condition never passes when no voice was heard. Run now, a chained automation, an OSC message, MIDI, a web request or a channel-health event has no voice, so a people-limited automation does not fire for any of them. Activity says "no voice was heard for this trigger". You cannot press Run now to fire one. Typed lines never reach it. Lines from another Earshot computer never reach it. The Test bench types a phrase with no voice behind it, so it cannot tell you whether a people-limited automation will fire for a real person. Test these by having that person say the line on the real channel, with the show Safe, and reading Activity.

A line needs about a second of real speech before Earshot can tell who spoke. A "go" or a "copy" on its own usually cannot be told. Limit to people only on phrases long enough to recognise: "standby sound cue", not "go".

On a real host with the show Armed and a local program listening, an automation for the phrase "standby sound cue" on a channel carrying two learned voices fired: Limit Times it fired No people limit 5 Limited to the one person whose voice it was 5 (every one of that person's lines) Limited to the other person 0 That was with clean computer-made voices. In the engine's own test with the real model, the strict rule was confident on only 1 of 4 lines. On a noisy comms line, measured on test voices, it was confident on 0 to 9 in 100 lines. Nothing has been tried on real crew voices. What that means in practice On a real, noisy party line, expect a people-limited automation to stay silent most of the time, even for the right person. It is a filter that errs heavily toward not firing, and it can still fire for a sound-alike. Do not put a cue behind it that the show needs.

Use Verdict A marker in the Archive when the stage manager says "top of act two" Reasonable. If it does not fire, nothing is lost. A reminder alert when one named person says "standby" Reasonable, for the same reason. A lighting cue that must go when the show caller says "go" No. It will often not fire, and "go" is too short to recognise. Stopping a cue from firing when the wrong person says the words No. A sound-alike can set it off. For a cue that should only come from one position, limit by channel instead: put the show caller on their own channel and tick that channel under Where to listen. A channel limit does not depend on recognising a voice. More about where the voice numbers come from is in Limits and known behaviour.

Three different things can keep an automation from doing its job: It is "not running": Earshot has set it aside and says why. See Not running. The runaway stop has stopped it because it fired too fast. See The runaway stop. It is running, but that one call did not fire. See A cue did not fire. A problem on one automation never stops the others.
documents.s: When an automation does not run

documents.t: The Automations list says "1 automation is not running." at the top, with a button: Button What it does Show it (one automation) or Show only these (several) Narrows the list to the automations with a problem. Show all Back to the whole list. One automation that is not running. Mock show, not a real show. The automation itself shows: a red Problem badge beside its name, "Not running" beside its switch, and a line that starts "Not running:" or "Needs fixing:". Read it: it says what to change. "Not running:" comes from the host: it has set the automation aside. "Needs fixing:" comes from the editor's own checks, for example a field left empty. Open the automation with Edit to see the same messages at the top of the editor. Run now on an automation that is not running does nothing. The button says "Run now will do nothing: the host is not running this automation. The reason is listed under it.", and the host answers "this automation cannot run: …".

The line says Why What to do "Will not fire: …" followed by a reason, such as "Put a word between two values, for example fade {a} to {b}" Earshot rejects the phrase: two values back to back, only a joining word between two values, or a filler word in the phrase. Rewrite the phrase. See How Earshot hears numbers. "Needs its webhook address entered again on this computer." The show was imported. A web-request trigger's secret path is never in a show file. Edit it, press Generate new path, copy the new address, save, and switch it on. "Needs its web address entered again on this computer." The show was imported. Web addresses are cut back to the host name in a show file. Edit it, type the full URL again, save, and switch it on. "Needs its header value entered again on this computer." The show was imported. Header values are never in a show file. Edit it, enter the header value, save, and switch it on. "Needs its shell command entered again on this computer." The show was imported. Shell commands are hidden in a show file. Edit it, enter the command, save, and switch it on. "Runs a shell command. Check it, then switch it on." An automation with a shell action always arrives switched off after an import. Read what the command does. Then switch it on. Shell commands also need Setup, Show control, Allow automations to run shell commands. "'Play sound' is not available in this build; the other actions still run." Play a sound does not run in this build. Remove the action, or leave it: the other actions still run. "'Show or hide window' is not available in this build; the other actions still run." Show or hide the window does not run in this build. The same. "Silence triggers do not work on channels from another host." A channel-health trigger is aimed only at a linked channel, which has no audio here. Point it at a local channel. "Stopped after firing 20 times in 10 seconds from OSC or webhooks. Make the show Safe and arm it again, or edit the automation, to restart it." The runaway stop. See below. Find the loop first. Then make the show Safe and arm again, or edit the automation. An automation that arrives emptied after an import is also switched off. Fixing the field is not enough: switch it on again. See show files and saved secrets.

If an automation that was started by OSC or a web request (or by the automations they chain) really fires more than 20 times in 10 seconds, Earshot stops that automation. An alert reads "'Name' fired 20 times in 10 seconds and was stopped" and stays on screen until someone acknowledges it. The automation shows the Problem badge with the "Stopped after firing 20 times…" line. The other automations keep working. To start it again, make the show Safe and then Armed again, or edit the automation. Find the cause before you do, or it will stop again.
It is aimed at loops. The usual one: a console that echoes OSC back into Earshot, so that an automation's own output arrives as its trigger.

Started by Covered by the runaway stop? What limits it instead OSC, or a web request (and the automations they chain) Yes A spoken phrase No Cooldown. Set it on the automation. MIDI No Only the 0.1 second spacing below. Run now, or another manual start No The 0.1 second spacing below. Dry runs are not counted. A loop while the show is Safe sends nothing and trips nothing. Any two firings of one automation from anything other than speech are at least 0.1 seconds apart. A closer one is refused. A firing that Earshot refuses still uses up that automation's cooldown. A MIDI feedback loop is not stopped An automation whose MIDI output comes back in as its own trigger is limited only by the 0.1 second spacing: about ten firings a second, until you make the show Safe. Check that a MIDI device does not echo before you arm.

Go down this list in order. Most answers are on one row of the Activity log, so open that first. The long version, with every other kind of fault, is in Troubleshooting. Is the show Armed? In Safe nothing is sent. A row reading Would have fired Name with Dry run means it matched and Safe held it back. See Safe and Armed. Was the show Armed when the words began? Look for "heard before the show was armed" or "Safe was pressed after this was said". Arm first, then speak. Is the automation on, with no problem? Check the Enabled switch, and look for a Problem badge or "1 automation is not running." above. Did Earshot hear it correctly? Read the line in the Feed. Then use Use last heard line on the Test bench and see whether the automation would fire. It matches whole words, after numbers are turned into digits. Was it refused for a number reason? Look for did not fire: the number may be incomplete: …. See How Earshot hears numbers, and say the number a different way. Cooldown. Activity says cooling down (N ms left). A new automation's cooldown is 2 seconds. A condition. Activity says condition not met: …. Check channel, group, time and flag conditions, and Where to listen. The runaway stop. Look for the alert "fired 20 times in 10 seconds and was stopped". Was the line typed? Typed lines never fire phrase automations. Neither do translations, or lines from another Earshot computer. Is it limited to people? It fires only when Earshot is very sure who spoke, which is rare on a noisy line. See Automations limited to people. Fire on Draft or Final. On Final text it waits for the settled line, and a channel that is Behind is slow. Did it fire, but the destination did not get it? Activity shows the send. A row marked Failed says why when you open it. Check the destination's host, port and protocol (Manage destinations in the editor), and whether the device is on the network. A TCP destination that is down is retried, and the sends skipped meanwhile are logged. If the row says fired and is not marked Failed, Earshot sent it. Look at the receiving device next: its OSC input setting, its port, and the address it expects.

Ten complete automations. Each one lists every field to fill in, in the order the editor shows them, so you can build it exactly as written. Change the names, channels and addresses to suit your show. Read this before you copy anything None of these has been run against a real console, desk or video server. Earshot's show-control path has been exercised only against stand-ins on one Mac. See Limits and known behaviour. The device addresses are not Earshot's. Addresses such as /eos/cue/…/fire and /cue/…/start belong to the receiving product. Check each one against that product's own documentation, and check its OSC port and whether its OSC input is switched on. Every action is a dry run while the show is Safe. That includes alerts, markers, typed text and flags. Nothing in these recipes does anything real until the show is Armed. Rehearse every one with the routine in Testing before you rely on it. The channel, group and destination names below are the mock show's ("Spring Tour at Harbour Hall"): channels Show Caller, Stage Manager, Deck Left and so on, the group Stage, and two OSC destinations.

Several recipes send OSC. Make the destinations first: in any Send OSC action press Manage destinations, then Add a destination. Name Host Port Protocol Eos your lighting desk's address, for example 10.0.1.20 the desk's OSC receive port, for example 8000 UDP QLab your QLab computer's address, for example 10.0.1.30 53000 UDP The two destinations. The addresses are made up. Mock show, not a real show.

The show caller says a cue number, and the lighting desk fires that cue. Part Field Value Basics Name Go cue When This automation starts when it A spoken phrase When Match mode Exact phrase When Phrase 1 go cue {number} When Where to listen: Channels Show Caller Only if (none) Then 1. Send OSC: Destination Eos Then 1. Send OSC: Address /eos/cue/{{capture.number}}/fire Then 1. Send OSC: Arguments (none) Then 2. Add a marker: Marker text Cue {{capture.number}} Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 2000 Safety Fire on Final text (recommended) Said on Show Caller Result "Go cue forty two." Sends /eos/cue/42/fire. Adds the marker "Cue 42". "Go Q 7." Sends /eos/cue/7/fire. "Standby cue forty two." Nothing. The word "go" is not there. "Go cue 7 and 8." Nothing. Activity: "Go cue" did not fire: the number may be incomplete: … "Go cue forty two" on Stage Manager Nothing. Only Show Caller is ticked. Activity shows Fired Go cue: phrase "…" on Show Caller when Armed, or Would have fired Go cue: … with Dry run when Safe. Watch for If your callers say "lighting cue forty two, go", write the phrase that way: lighting cue {number} go. Then "Standby lighting cue forty two" cannot fire it, because no "go" follows the number. In the one full run of the cue path, "Lighting cue 42, go." sent exactly one OSC message with the number 42, and the "Standby…" lines sent nothing. A point cue arrives as 12.5. Check your desk accepts that in an address. Read How Earshot hears numbers for what is refused.

Part Field Value Basics Name Sound go When This automation starts when it A spoken phrase When Match mode Exact phrase When Phrase 1 sound cue {n} go When Where to listen: Channels Show Caller Only if (none) Then 1. Send OSC: Destination QLab Then 1. Send OSC: Address /cue/{{capture.n}}/start Then 1. Send OSC: Arguments (none) Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 2000 Safety Fire on Final text (recommended) Said on Show Caller Result "Sound cue nine, go." Sends /cue/9/start. "Standby sound cue nine." Nothing. "Sound cue nine and ten, go." Nothing. Refused for its number. Activity shows Fired Sound go: phrase "…" on Show Caller. Watch for {n} catches one word, whatever it is. "Sound cue next go" would send /cue/next/start. If your cue numbers are always digits, use recipe 5's pattern style to accept digits only. QLab's cue number is what goes in the address, not its position in the list. Check QLab's documentation for the address and for how to allow OSC control.

Anyone on a stage channel calls a blackout. The desk fires a macro, and every screen shows a red banner until an operator acknowledges it. Part Field Value Basics Name Blackout When This automation starts when it A spoken phrase When Match mode Any of When Words or phrases blackout and kill the lights When Where to listen: Groups Stage Only if (none) Then 1. Send OSC: Destination Eos Then 1. Send OSC: Address /eos/macro/99/fire Then 2. Flash an alert: Alert text BLACKOUT called by {{channel.name}} Then 2. Flash an alert: Colour #ff4639 Then 2. Flash an alert: Length of one flash (ms) 1500 Then 2. Flash an alert: Flashes 3 Then 2. Flash an alert: Stay on screen until someone acknowledges On Then 2. Flash an alert: Show to (none ticked: everyone) Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 5000 Safety Fire on Final text (recommended) The alert, waiting to be acknowledged. Mock show, not a real show. Activity shows Fired Blackout: phrase "…" on Deck Left. Watch for A single word fires wherever it is said. "We go to blackout after the song" on a Stage channel fires this. Matching is on whole words anywhere in the line. For anything that matters, use a longer phrase that nobody says in passing. Operators and admins get the Acknowledge button. It clears the alert on every screen at once. The macro number is an example. Use your own.
documents.s: 3. A blackout call that also alerts everyone

documents.t: Markers make the Archive easy to find your way round afterwards. This one costs nothing if it misfires. Part Field Value Basics Name Act two marker When This automation starts when it A spoken phrase When Match mode Exact phrase When Phrase 1 top of act two When Where to listen: Channels Show Caller Only if (none) Then 1. Add a marker: Marker text Top of act two Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 60000 Safety Fire on Final text (recommended) Activity shows Fired Act two marker: phrase "…" on Show Caller. The marker appears in the Archive. Watch for It also fires on "Standby top of act two, everybody please", because those four words are in that line. For a marker that hardly matters. For a cue it would. The one-minute cooldown stops the "go" a few seconds later from adding a second marker. To mark every cue instead, add an Add a marker action to your cue automations, as recipe 1 does.
documents.s: 4. A marker at "top of act two"

documents.t: "Video four, go" tells a video server to play clip 4 by web request, waits half a second, then starts the matching QLab cue. Part Field Value Basics Name Roll video When This automation starts when it A spoken phrase When Match mode Regular expression When Pattern video (?P<n>\d+) go When Where to listen (all empty: every channel) Only if (none) Then 1. HTTP request: Method POST Then 1. HTTP request: URL http://10.0.1.40:8080/play/{{capture.n}} Then 1. HTTP request: Headers Authorization, with your server's key as the value Then 1. HTTP request: Body (empty) Then 2. Wait: Wait (milliseconds) 500 Then 3. Send OSC: Destination QLab Then 3. Send OSC: Address /cue/{{capture.n}}/start Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 2000 Safety Fire on Final text (recommended) These three actions in the editor. Mock show, not a real show. Said Result "Video four, go." POST to http://10.0.1.40:8080/play/4. Half a second later, /cue/4/start to QLab. "Video playback go." Nothing. \d+ accepts digits only. Activity shows Fired Roll video: phrase "…" on Video, with the web request shown as POST and the host only. Watch for The pattern is matched against tidied text, where spoken numbers are already digits. Write \d+, never "four". The header value is a secret. Once saved it shows as •••• (unchanged). It is not copied when you duplicate the automation and not included in a show file. After an import this automation arrives switched off until you enter the URL and the header value again. If Make safe is pressed during the Wait, the OSC is never sent. If the web request has already arrived at the server, Safe cannot recall it. The web request must answer within a few seconds or it counts as failed. The OSC still goes: one failed action does not stop the next. The URL and port are examples. Use your server's own API.
documents.s: 5. A video server by web request, then a follow-up OSC

documents.t: If an interface is unplugged or stops delivering audio, tell the operators at once. Part Field Value Basics Name Audio device lost When This automation starts when it A channel's health When Channel Any channel When When it Device lost Only if (none) Then 1. Flash an alert: Alert text Audio lost on {{channel.name}} Then 1. Flash an alert: Colour (empty) Then 1. Flash an alert: Length of one flash (ms) 2000 Then 1. Flash an alert: Flashes 2 Then 1. Flash an alert: Stay on screen until someone acknowledges On Then 1. Flash an alert: Show to Operators and Admins Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 2000 Safety Fire on (ignored: only spoken phrases use it) Activity shows Fired Audio device lost: device lost. Watch for The alert only appears while the show is Armed. In Safe this is a dry run like everything else, and you get only a Would have fired row in Activity. The channel's own badge (No input, Offline or Error) shows in any state: see status and badges. It never fires for a channel that comes from another Earshot computer. Make a twin with When it set to Recovered and the text Audio back on {{channel.name}}. Unplugging a USB interface mid-show is untested.
documents.s: 6. An alert when an audio device is lost

documents.t: A button on the lighting desk sends /desk/standby. Earshot writes a line into the Stage Manager channel for everyone to read. Part Field Value Basics Name Desk standby When This automation starts when it An incoming OSC message When OSC address pattern /desk/standby Only if (none) Then 1. Send text to a channel: Send to A fixed channel Then 1. Send text to a channel: Channel Stage Manager Then 1. Send text to a channel: Text Lighting desk: STANDBY Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 1000 Safety Fire on (ignored) Then let the console in, under Setup, Show control: Turn on Controllers may send OSC to Earshot. Under What incoming OSC may do, choose Trigger automations and press Apply. Under Devices allowed to control, add the console's IP address. Point the console at this computer's address and the UDP port shown (4781 unless you changed it). See OSC input. Activity shows an incoming OSC row for /desk/standby, then Fired Desk standby: OSC /desk/standby. The line in the channel has the Typed badge and the author "Automation: Desk standby". Watch for The line it writes is a typed line, so it can never fire a phrase automation. To pass a value, use a capture: the pattern /desk/page/{page} with the text Lighting desk: page {{capture.page}}. An argument on the message is {{osc.args.0}}. The runaway stop applies. A console that sends this more than 20 times in 10 seconds while Armed stops the automation. See Problems and the runaway stop. A UDP sender's address can be forged by anyone on the same network. Use the TCP port for anything that matters. Refused OSC is logged in Activity with the reason, for example "this source is not allowed to trigger". If you only need a line of text and no other action, a console can send /earshot/channel/<channel>/send with the text as its argument, with no automation at all. See the OSC address reference.
documents.s: 7. A console button that sends text into a channel

documents.t: A pad on a MIDI controller runs the "Standby chime" automation, which other triggers can share. First, the automation to be run: Part Field Value Basics Name Standby chime When This automation starts when it Manual only Then 1. Flash an alert: Alert text STANDBY Then 1. Flash an alert: Colour #ffb547 Then 1. Flash an alert: Length of one flash (ms) 1200 Then 1. Flash an alert: Flashes 3 Then 1. Flash an alert: Stay on screen until someone acknowledges Off Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 2000 Then the MIDI trigger: Part Field Value Basics Name Pad 1 standby When This automation starts when it An incoming MIDI message When Input port Any port (or your controller's port) When Message Note on When MIDI channel 1 When Note 60 When Minimum velocity 1 Only if (none) Then 1. Run another automation: Automation Standby chime Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 500 Safety Fire on (ignored) Tick the controller's port under Setup, Show control, MIDI input ports, or Earshot is not listening to it. If you plugged the controller in after Earshot started, press Refresh there first. See MIDI. Activity shows an incoming MIDI row, Fired Pad 1 standby: MIDI … on <port>, then Fired Standby chime: chained (hop 1). Watch for "Standby chime" keeps its own cooldown. Two pads pressed within its 2 seconds flash it once. MIDI is not covered by the runaway stop. A device that echoes MIDI back can fire this about ten times a second until you make the show Safe. A chain runs each automation at most once, at most 32 firings in all, and at most 8 deep. MIDI has been tried only against stand-ins, never on a real controller.
documents.s: 8. A MIDI note that runs another automation

documents.t: A button in another system (a show-control page, a script, a phone shortcut) calls an address, and Earshot drops a marker. Part Field Value Basics Name Show start (web) When This automation starts when it A web request When Path Press Generate new path Only if (none) Then 1. Add a marker: Marker text Show started: {{var.body}} Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 2000 Safety Fire on (ignored) Before you save, press Copy URL. The address is shown only now. Then call it with POST, using the host's address from Setup, Access: curl -X POST http://192.168.1.20:4780/api/v1/webhooks/YOUR-PATH-HERE -d "from the SM desk" That adds the marker "Show started: from the SM desk". With no body, the marker reads "Show started: ". Activity shows Fired Show start (web): webhook. Admins also see the path there; everyone else sees only "webhook". Watch for The address is a password. Whoever has it can fire this automation in any access mode, without signing in. It still obeys Armed and Safe. Called while Safe, it is a dry run and no marker is added. The path cannot be read back after saving. If you lose it, generate a new one. The old address stops working. The runaway stop applies: more than 20 real firings in 10 seconds stops it. After a show-file import it arrives switched off, needing a new path. Web requests have been tried only against stand-ins. See The HTTP API.
documents.s: 9. A web request that marks "show start"

documents.t: You do not want "go cue…" to fire during the half-hour call or a notes session, even if someone has armed the show. A flag makes the cue wait until the stage manager has said "show mode". It takes three automations. A. Turn show mode on Part Field Value Basics Name Show mode on When This automation starts when it A spoken phrase When Match mode Exact phrase When Phrase 1 we are in show mode When Where to listen: Channels Stage Manager Then 1. Set a flag: Flag name show-mode Then 1. Set a flag: Set it to Set Then 2. Flash an alert: Alert text SHOW MODE: cues are live Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 2000 B. Turn show mode off Part Field Value Basics Name Show mode off When This automation starts when it A spoken phrase When Match mode Exact phrase When Phrase 1 we are out of show mode When Where to listen: Channels Stage Manager Then 1. Set a flag: Flag name show-mode Then 1. Set a flag: Set it to Cleared Then 2. Flash an alert: Alert text Show mode off Safety Cooldown (milliseconds) 2000 C. The guarded cue Build recipe 1, and add one condition: Part Field Value Only if Kind of condition A flag is set Only if Flag name show-mode Type the flag's name exactly the same in all three. What happens Result Armed. Caller says "go cue forty two" before show mode. Nothing sent. Activity: "Go cue" did not fire: condition not met: flag show-mode is not set Armed. Stage manager says "we are in show mode". The flag is set. The alert shows. Armed. Caller says "go cue forty two". /eos/cue/42/fire is sent. Stage manager says "we are out of show mode". The flag is cleared. Cues wait again. Watch for A flag is only really set while the show is Armed. In Safe, "Set a flag" is a dry run, so saying "we are in show mode" while Safe does not set it. Arm first, then say it. Flags start cleared every time Earshot starts. After a restart, say "we are in show mode" again. A flag is not a second Safe. It guards only the automations that have the condition. Make safe is still the way to stop everything. The two phrases are deliberately long, so nobody says them in passing. There is no screen that shows a flag's state. The alerts in A and B are how the crew knows. If you are unsure, say the "on" or "off" phrase again.
documents.s: 10. A flag as an interlock: "only in show mode"

documents.t: Different words. Change the phrase, then prove it with the rehearsal routine. If the recogniser keeps mis-hearing a word, add the mis-hearing as another phrase. Several positions. Tick more channels, or a group, under Where to listen. Several things at once. Add more actions. They run in order. Use Wait between them if the order must be spaced out. The same actions from several triggers. Put the actions in one Manual only automation, and have each trigger Run another automation, as recipe 8 does. Remember the second automation sees values as {{var.capture.number}}, not {{capture.number}}: see Variables. Every field used here is described in Triggers and conditions and Actions.

Every automation in Earshot sits behind one switch. In Safe, nothing is sent to a console, a controller or a web address. In Armed, automations that match really send. This page is the one to read twice. Speech recognition makes mistakes Treat a phrase automation as a convenience that sits beside your normal cue calling, not instead of it. Keep Safe as the default until you have tried every phrase on the Test bench and said it out loud on the real comms.

The Armed or Safe control is in the header on every screen. State What it means Safe Automations that match are logged as "would have fired" (marked Dry run in Activity). Nothing is sent. ARMED (red, with a red band across the header and "ARMED" in the browser tab title) Automations that match really send OSC, MIDI and web requests, and run shell commands if you have allowed them. The control while the show is Safe. Mock show, not a real show. The same control while the show is Armed. Mock show, not a real show. The Automations screen repeats the state in a line at the top. In Safe it reads "Safe. Automations that match are logged as “would have fired”, and nothing is sent." In Armed it reads "ARMED. Automations that match will really send OSC, MIDI and HTTP." Earshot starts Safe. The one exception is Start armed (Setup, Show control), which is off by default. See Start armed below.

Who can arm Operators and admins see the control. Everyone else sees a display-only "Safe" or "ARMED". Remember that in Open access mode everyone on the network is an operator. See who can connect. There are two ways to arm, and both are deliberate: Hold "Hold to arm" for about 0.7 seconds. Its tooltip says "Hold for 0.7 seconds to arm". Or press and release it once, and then press Arm now in the box that opens, "Arm automations?". Pressing "Hold to arm" once opens this box. Mock show, not a real show. Once the show is Armed, the header turns red and stays red on every screen, for everyone. The whole screen while Armed. Mock show, not a real show.

Press Make safe. (The same button shows "Safe" while the show is Safe.) Or press Alt+Shift+S from anywhere on the screen. This shortcut can make the show Safe. It can never arm. A console can also make the show Safe by OSC, from any device, as long as OSC input is on. See OSC input. Make sure everyone who may need to press Make safe knows where it is before the show starts.

If the screen loses its connection to the host, the control shows "Safe — connection lost, state unknown" (or Armed). Arming is not possible from that screen, and the arm button's tooltip says "Connection lost: arming is not possible". Press Make safe anyway. It also goes by a second route, so it can get through when the live connection cannot.
documents.s: If the screen has lost the host

documents.t: A red notice says "Could not confirm Safe — the host may still be armed." with a Retry button. Keep pressing until it clears. Do not assume the show is Safe until the header says so.

Arm and Safe are applied in the order the host receives them, and the last one wins. On top of that, Safe is given every advantage: A Safe press cancels a hold in progress, a confirm box that is open, and an Arm that is still on its way. A Safe press blocks arming for one second. An Arm that has not gone through within 2 seconds is dropped, so a Safe never waits behind it. If someone else's Arm reaches the host after your Safe, the screen says "The host is armed. Your Safe was overtaken — press Make safe again." The same order covers the app, the API and OSC together. A Safe from any of them beats an Arm from any of them that was received earlier. Nothing fires while Earshot is shutting down, and the show cannot be armed then.

A line fires a cue only if the show was Armed from the moment the words began, with no Safe in between. Something said while the show is Safe never fires, even if you arm while Earshot is still working out the words. Something said while Armed does not fire if Safe was pressed before the cue went out, even if you armed again in between. Say it again once the show is Armed. Here is one line, "Lighting cue forty two, go", said three ways: When the words began What happened next Result What Activity says Show was Armed Nothing. It stayed Armed until the cue went out. The cue is sent. Fired Go cue: … Show was Safe You armed half a second later, while the person was still talking. Dry run. Nothing is sent. "Go cue" did not fire: heard before the show was armed Show was Armed Someone pressed Make safe, then armed again, before Earshot finished the line. Dry run. Nothing is sent. "Go cue" did not fire: Safe was pressed after this was said The same rule holds for draft lines, for cues limited to people, and for anything waiting in a queue. Pressing Safe and then Arm never releases something from before the Safe. Triggers that are not speech follow the same idea, tied to the moment the host received them. Activity says "the show was Safe when it was received" or "Safe was pressed after it was received". Arm first, then speak Arm, wait a beat, then call the cue. Do not arm in the middle of a call and expect that call to go.
documents.s: Armed from the moment the words began

documents.t: Already in motion What happens A cue in the middle of its action list (for example during a Wait) The remaining actions do not run. Arming again later does not resume it. OSC messages waiting for a TCP destination Unsent data is discarded and the connection is reset, including data waiting in the operating system's send buffer (it is kept small, 8 KiB). The Activity log says what was not sent. A MIDI message Stopped, even while its port is still opening. The message is checked again right before it goes to the driver. A web request in progress Cancelled, and any redirect is not followed. A running shell command Stopped, together with the programs it started. In Activity, an action cut off this way reads "not sent: the show was made Safe". Editing one OSC destination reconnects only that destination. Pressing Safe resets all of them.

Safe stops what Earshot would send next. It cannot reach into your console. Anything that has already left this computer is gone: a UDP message, a MIDI message already handed to the driver, a web request that already arrived, OSC data already delivered. Proven on macOS only A TCP reset is meant to throw away what is still unsent. That has been proven on macOS only, and the other end may not notice the reset at once. Stopping a shell command's child programs when you press Safe is untested on Windows. See Limits and known behaviour.
If the MIDI port is busy for more than 1 second, the send is dropped and Activity says "not sent: the MIDI port was busy for more than 1 s". A MIDI cue is never sent late and then reported as missed.
documents.s: A MIDI send is on time or it does not go

documents.t: Under Setup, Show control, the switch Start armed makes automations able to fire as soon as Earshot starts. It is off by default. Leave it off unless the show runs unattended. With it off, Armed is forgotten whenever the host restarts: the show comes back Safe. See what happens when the host restarts. Two more things always leave the show Safe: Importing a show file never arms. If the show was Armed when you imported, it goes Safe. See show files. Arming by OSC works only over TCP, never UDP, and only at the Full control level. See OSC input.

Do not use the tray to arm In the desktop app, the tray (menu bar) menu has an Armed tick box. It arms with one click, without the hold that the window requires. It has not been tried by hand in this build. Do not use it as your normal way to arm.

These are known gaps. None of them makes Safe unsafe, but they explain a surprise if you meet one. The start of speech is noticed about 30 milliseconds late. A cue word that begins that close before you press Arm can still count as armed. The other way round: right after a channel's audio starts, is paused, changes device or has a gap, a cue that begins within about a third of a second after you press Arm can be treated as "heard before the show was armed". Arm first, then speak. Run now and web hooks are tied to Armed or Safe when the engine receives them, a moment (normally under a thousandth of a second) after the request arrives. A Run now pressed as a test in Safe at the very instant someone else arms could really send. Pressing Safe twice. In a very rare tie between two Arm or Safe commands arriving at the same instant, a Safe can be answered with "conflict". The screen then shows the show's real state. Press Safe again. A line whose beginning Earshot did not catch (it was restarting that channel) never fires. Activity says "the start of this line was missed". A firing that Earshot refuses (for example because of the runaway limits) still uses up that automation's cooldown. A MIDI feedback loop is limited only to about ten firings a second, until you make the show Safe. See the runaway stop. Someone on the network who can forge sender addresses can get a real console's OSC trigger messages rate-limited. They cannot stop its Safe. The full list of what has and has not been tried is in Limits and known behaviour.
documents.s: Small edges you should know about

documents.t: The header shows Safe. Every phrase automation has been tried on the Test bench, and said out loud on the real channel while Safe, then checked in Activity ("would have fired"). Everyone who can press Make safe knows where it is, and knows Alt+Shift+S. The whole list is on the before-show checklist.

Earshot gives you three ways to find out what an automation will do before it matters: Tool What it answers Does it send? Test bench "If someone said this, which automations would fire, and what would each action do?" Never. Always a dry run. Run now "What does this automation do when it runs?" Only while the show is Armed, and it asks first. Activity "What actually happened, and why did that cue not fire?" It is a log. It sends nothing.
documents.s: Testing: Run now, the Test bench and Activity

documents.t: Open Automations, then the Test bench tab. Who can use it Operators and admins. A viewer sees "The test bench needs operator access". The Test bench. Mock show, not a real show. The notice at the top says: "Nothing is ever sent from here. The test bench always runs as a dry run, whether the show is Safe or Armed. It shows what would fire and what each action would do." Under Phrase to test, type the phrase. "Type it the way it would be said, for example “go cue forty two”." It is cleaned up the same way spoken text is. Under Channel, choose the channel it would be heard on, or leave Any channel. "Automations can be limited to certain channels, so pick the one it would be heard on." Press Test phrase. Use last heard line copies the latest spoken line into the box (from the chosen channel, if you chose one). Use it right after someone has said the call for real, to see what Earshot makes of exactly what it heard.

"1 automation would fire." (or more), then one card per automation. Each card has the automation's name, a Would have fired badge, what set it off, and one line per action marked Would run, with its variables filled in. An action that could not run is marked Skipped, with the reason. If nothing matches: "No automation would fire. Check that it is enabled, that the words and channel match, that its conditions hold, and that it is not still cooling down." Under the result, Recent tests lists what you have tried, each marked "1 matched" or "no match". Press one to see it again.

With "Any channel", an automation limited to channels or groups does not match. Pick the channel the line would be heard on. It ignores Cooldown and Fire on. The text is treated as a finished line, and an automation that is cooling down still shows as firing. It does not say why something was refused. A phrase that matches the words but is refused for its number ("go cue 7 and 8") simply shows no automation. For the reason, watch Activity when the real line is spoken. It cannot test a voice. An automation limited to people needs a real voice, and the bench has none. It tests what you typed, not what the recogniser will hear. If the recogniser mis-hears the caller, the bench cannot know. That is what the rehearsal below is for.
documents.s: What the Test bench does not tell you

documents.t: On the Automations list, every automation has a Run now button (operators and admins). It runs that one automation by hand, skipping its trigger. The show is The button reads What happens Safe Run now (dry run) It runs as a dry run and says so: "Dry run — nothing was sent". Armed Run now (live), in red It asks first. See below. Run now on the mock show's Go cue while Safe. With no spoken number to fill in, its OSC action is skipped and says why. Not a real show. Run now while the show is Armed. Mock show, not a real show. While Armed, pressing it shows "Armed: this really sends." with Cancel and Send live. Nothing goes until you press Send live. The result is headed "Fired". After a run, a card under the automation shows what each action did ("Ran") or would have done ("Would run"). If nothing ran it says "Nothing matched — nothing was sent" and "It may be disabled or cooling down, or its conditions did not hold."
