Things to know: Run now still respects the automation's conditions and cooldown. A flag or time-of-day condition that is not met stops it. If you press it twice less than 0.1 seconds apart, the second press is refused. Run now supplies no values. Any {{capture.…}} in the actions is empty, so an OSC address built from one is skipped. To test with a number, use the Test bench. You cannot Run now an automation limited to people: no voice was heard. If an automation is not running (it has a Problem), the button says "Run now will do nothing: the host is not running this automation. The reason is listed under it." A known edge Run now is tied to Armed or Safe at the moment the engine receives it, normally under a thousandth of a second after you press. A Run now pressed as a test in Safe at the very instant someone else arms could really send. See Safe and Armed.

Open Activity (on a phone, under More). Every role can read it. It lists, newest at the bottom, every OSC, MIDI and web message in and out, and every decision an automation made. The Activity log. Mock show, not a real show. When it is empty it says "Nothing yet. OSC, MIDI and HTTP messages and automation decisions appear here as they happen."

Part What it shows Time To the millisecond. Kind OSC, MIDI, HTTP, Automation, Connection or System. Direction In, Out or Internal. Summary What happened, in plain words. Dry run Nothing was sent: the show was Safe, or it was the Test bench. Failed Something did not work. Press the arrow at the end of the row to read why.

Control What it does OSC, MIDI, HTTP, Automation, Connection, System Show only these kinds. Press more than one to combine them. An automation row still shows when the OSC or MIDI it sent matches. Any direction Or Incoming, Outgoing, Internal. OK and failed Or Only OK, Only failed. Search the log Finds text in a row or its details. "12 rows" Or "3 of 12 rows" while filtering, with Clear filters. Pause Holds the list still so you can read it. It becomes Resume (4 new). Clear "Clears the list on this screen only. Nothing is deleted from the engine." If you scroll up to read back, Back to live returns to the newest row.

Row What it means Fired Go cue: phrase "…" on Show Caller It really fired. The show was Armed. Would have fired Go cue: phrase "…" on Show Caller with Dry run It matched, and Safe held it back. This is the row you want to see in rehearsal. Fired Standby chime: manual Run now, the API or OSC ran it by name. "Go cue" did not fire: heard before the show was armed The words began while the show was Safe. "Go cue" did not fire: Safe was pressed after this was said Safe was pressed before the cue went out. "Go cue" did not fire: the start of this line was missed Earshot was restarting that channel when the line began. "Go cue" did not fire: cooling down (1400 ms left) It fired less than its Cooldown ago. "Go cue" did not fire: condition not met: flag show-mode is not set An Only if condition was false. The row names it. "Go cue" did not fire: the number may be incomplete: … Refused for its number. See How Earshot hears numbers. "Go cue" did not fire: voice not recognised A people-limited automation was not sure who spoke. "Go cue" did not fire: no voice was heard for this trigger A people-limited automation was started by something with no voice. "Go cue" did not fire: the automation is disabled or invalid Something tried to run it by name, and it is switched off or has a problem. "Go cue" did not fire: loop guard: the chain's limit was reached (each automation once per chain, at most 32 firings, 8 hops) A chain of automations hit its limit. Inside the brackets is what set it off: phrase "…" on <channel>, OSC <address>, MIDI … on <port>, webhook, manual, chained (hop 1), or a health event such as device lost. A fired row marked Failed means at least one action did not go. Open the row. Typical reasons are "not sent: the show was made Safe", "not sent: the MIDI port was busy for more than 1 s", or an OSC address value that was not safe to send. The full list is in Actions. Refused OSC from a console is logged here too, at most once per sender every 10 seconds, with a count. See OSC input. Viewers and operators see web-request addresses cut back to the host, and never see a web-request trigger's secret path.

Do this for every phrase automation before the first show. It takes a few minutes per cue. Bench. Type the phrase as it will be said, pick the channel, press Test phrase. Check the automation fires and each action has the right address and number. Bench, the other way. Type things that must not fire: the standby call, a different cue word, a list of cues. Check that no automation would fire. Say it in Safe. With the header showing Safe, have the real caller say it on the real channel, at show level, with the room as loud as it will be. Read the Feed. Was it heard the way you expected? If a word keeps coming out wrong, add the mis-hearing to the automation's phrases. Read Activity. Look for Would have fired … with Dry run. If there is a did not fire: row instead, the reason is on it. Say it three more times. One good result is not enough. Also say the standby and the near misses, and check they stay quiet. Check the cooldown. Say the cue twice, a second apart. The second should say cooling down. Arm. Hold Hold to arm. Wait a beat. Say it once. Check Activity for Fired … and check the device received it. Make safe. What rehearsal cannot prove Accuracy in a loud venue is unverified, and Earshot has never been run against a real console. Your rehearsal on your own comms and your own desk is the only evidence there is for your show. See Limits and known behaviour. Then go through the before-show checklist.

This page is the reference for two parts of the automation editor: When (the trigger, "What sets it off.") and Only if (the conditions, "Extra checks. All of them must be true."). For a guided first build, see Building an automation. Whatever the trigger, nothing is sent unless the show is Armed.

Under This automation starts when it, choose one: Trigger The editor says Fires when A spoken phrase "Fires when someone says it on a channel." Someone says it on a channel Earshot is listening to. An incoming OSC message "Fires when a console or controller sends a matching address." A device sends a matching OSC address to Earshot. An incoming MIDI message "Fires on a note, controller or program change." A matching message arrives on a MIDI input you ticked in Setup. A web request "Fires when something calls this automation's URL." Something calls the automation's secret web address. Manual only "Fires from the Run now button, the API, or another automation." Nothing starts it on its own. A channel's health "Fires when a channel's device drops, recovers, or goes quiet." A channel's device is lost, recovers, or has been silent for a set time. Changing the trigger kind replaces the trigger's settings with that kind's defaults.

A spoken-phrase trigger. Mock show, not a real show. The editor says at the top: "Automations hear what was said. Glossary corrections change only what you read." So do not rely on a glossary correction to make a phrase match. If a cue depends on a word the recogniser gets wrong, add the mis-hearing as another phrase. Only real speech fires a phrase automation. Typed lines, translated text and lines from another Earshot computer never do. See How Earshot hears numbers for the full rule.

Match mode The editor says Notes Exact phrase "The words in this order, as whole words. Use {name} to catch one word, like go cue {number}." The default. You can list several phrases, and any one will do. Any of "Fires when any one of these words or phrases is heard." The list is headed "Words or phrases (any one will do)". Each entry follows the same rules as an exact phrase. All of "Fires when every one of these is heard, in any order." The list is headed "Words or phrases (all must be heard)". All of them must be in the same line. Regular expression "Advanced. One pattern, matched against the cleaned-up text (lower case, no punctuation, numbers as digits)." One Pattern field. See below. Fuzzy "Like exact, but forgives small mis-hearings. Only words of 5 or more letters can differ, by at most 2 letters." Adds a Fuzzy distance (letters) field. See below. In every mode Earshot matches whole words, ignoring case and punctuation. The phrase go does not match "going". Before matching, Earshot tidies the line: spoken numbers become digits ("forty two" becomes 42), "Q42" becomes "cue 42", and "stand by" becomes "standby". So a phrase written cue 1 matches "cue one". The full list is in How Earshot hears numbers.

Type each phrase in a Phrase box. Add a phrase adds another. Put a name in braces to catch one spoken word: go cue {number}. The editor says: "{name} catches exactly one word (go cue {number} hears “go cue 42”) and becomes {{capture.name}}." A capture catches exactly one word. say {word} on "say hello there" catches only "hello". A whole spoken number counts as one word, so cue {number} on "cue forty two" catches 42. A capture name is letters, digits or _, and must be its own word. go{n} is rejected: "{n} must be its own word: put spaces around it." Each capture needs its own name. A name used twice is rejected. A phrase needs at least one real word. A phrase that is only a capture is rejected: "This phrase has no words to listen for, so it would match anything." Earshot refuses a capture if the word it caught is part of a number it is not sure about. See How Earshot hears numbers. Under the phrases the editor lists what you can use in actions, for example "Captures you can use in actions: {{capture.number}}". See Variables.

For people who already know regular expressions. One Pattern, for example: go cue (?P<number>\d+) The editor says: "Matched against lower-case text with no punctuation, and spoken numbers already turned into digits (so use \d+, not “forty two”). Named groups become {{capture.name}}." The match must start and end on whole words. Only the first pattern is used: "Regex mode uses only the first pattern; the others are ignored." If you write a number word in the pattern, the editor warns that it "will never be heard", because numbers arrive as digits. The engine checks the pattern when you save.

Fuzzy matches like Exact phrase, but forgives small mis-hearings in longer words. Fuzzy distance (letters) is "How many letters may differ, 0 to 2. Only words of 5 or more letters are forgiving." The guards that keep short cue words safe: Both the word you wrote and the word heard must have at least 5 letters. Shorter words must match exactly, so "go" never matches "no". Words of 5 to 7 letters may differ by 1 letter. Words of 8 or more may differ by at most 2. The first letter must match. A word containing a digit never fuzzy-matches. A distance of 0 makes Fuzzy the same as Exact, and the editor says so.

"Leave a list empty to listen to everything." List What ticking does Channels Only lines from these channels. Groups Only lines from channels in these groups. People Only lines Earshot is very sure were spoken by these people. Experimental. How the lists combine, as the engine applies them: A line is in range if its channel is ticked under Channels, or its channel belongs to a group ticked under Groups. Ticking a channel and a group widens the range; it does not narrow it. People is a further limit on top of that. The People list carries this warning in the editor: "Experimental. Fires only when Earshot is very sure who spoke. On a noisy comms line that is rare, and someone who sounds very like them can set it off. Do not use this for a cue that must go, or for one that must not go for the wrong person." Read Automations limited to people before you tick anyone.

Field Value Match mode Any of Words or phrases blackout, kill the lights Groups Stage The list shows it as Hears any of "blackout", "kill the lights" in Stage. A line "Kill the lights, please" on Deck Left (a Stage channel) matches. The same words on FOH Audio do not.

One field, OSC address pattern. A new trigger starts as /cue/{number}. The editor says: "Starts with /. * matches any run of characters, ? one character, [a-c] one of a set, {go,stop} either word. A part that is only {name} catches that whole part of the address, and you can use it as {{capture.name}} in actions. Example: /cue/{number}/go hears /cue/42/go." The pattern and the incoming address must have the same number of parts between slashes. * never matches across a /. [!a-c] matches one character that is not in the set. A part that is exactly {name} is a capture. {go} is a capture called "go"; {go,stop} is a choice between two words. // is not supported. Each capture name can be used only once. OSC input must allow it. OSC input is off by default. For an OSC message to fire an automation, Controllers may send OSC to Earshot must be on, the level must be Trigger automations or Full control, and the sending device must be this computer or in the allowed list. See OSC input. Addresses under /earshot/ are Earshot's own controls. Any other address fires the automations whose pattern matches it, so write your patterns outside /earshot/. See the OSC address reference. Variables for actions: {{osc.address}}, {{osc.args.0}}, {{osc.args.1}} and so on, plus your captures.
Field Value OSC address pattern /desk/page/{page}/go A console sending /desk/page/3/go fires it, and {{capture.page}} is 3. The list shows it as Receives OSC /desk/page/{page}/go.

A new MIDI trigger in the mock show's editor. Not a real show. Field Choices Notes Input port Any port, or one named port "Which MIDI input to listen on." A port that has gone is listed as "(not found)". Message Note on, Note off, Control change, Program change MIDI channel Any channel, or 1 to 16 Note, Controller or Program 0 to 127, or empty for any The label follows the message kind. Minimum velocity or Minimum value 0 to 127, or empty ("Any") Fires only at or above this velocity or controller value. The port must also be ticked under Setup, Show control, MIDI input ports, or Earshot is not listening to it. See MIDI. The editor lists the variables: "Variables for actions: {{midi.note}}, {{midi.velocity}}, {{midi.controller}}, {{midi.value}}, {{midi.program}}, {{midi.channel}}." There is also {{midi.port}}. MIDI triggers are exempt from the runaway stop. An automation whose MIDI output comes back in as its own trigger is limited only to about ten firings a second, until you make the show Safe. Not tried on real gear MIDI has been tried only in automated tests against stand-ins on one Mac. See Limits and known behaviour.
Field Value Input port Any port Message Note on MIDI channel 1 Note 60 Minimum velocity (empty) The list shows it as Receives MIDI note on #60 on channel 1.

The automation gets its own web address. Whatever calls that address fires the automation. The path is a password Whoever has the address can fire the automation, in any access mode, without signing in. It still obeys Armed and Safe: in Safe it is a dry run. Treat the address like a password, and do not put it in a show document everyone can read. A new web-request trigger in the mock show. The address shown is the mock's own; a real host shows its own address. Not a real show. Press Generate new path. Earshot makes a long random path. (You can type your own in Path, but a guessable path is a weak password. It cannot contain spaces, ? or #.) The editor shows the full address under "Call this URL (shown now only: after saving, the app cannot show it again)". Press Copy URL and keep it somewhere safe. Save the automation. The address has this shape: http://192.168.1.20:4780/api/v1/webhooks/k3v9q2m7x1c8b5n4z6a0w2e7 From another computer, use the host's address from Setup, Access, Address for the crew in place of the one shown. Send a POST request to it. The body, if there is one, arrives as {{var.body}}: curl -X POST http://192.168.1.20:4780/api/v1/webhooks/k3v9q2m7x1c8b5n4z6a0w2e7 -d "house open" After saving, nobody can read the path back, not even an admin. The editor shows "Hidden. Rotate to get a new URL. The path is a secret, so this app is never given it." To change it, press Generate new path, copy the new address, and save. The old address stops working. See saved secrets. Things to know: Calls are limited to a burst of 20, then 10 a second, from one sender to one path. More than that is answered "too many attempts". A call to a path that does not exist counts as a wrong guess. Five wrong guesses lock that sender out for 30 seconds, doubling up to 15 minutes. An automation started by a web request is subject to the runaway stop: more than 20 real firings in 10 seconds and it is stopped. In an exported show file the path is hidden. After an import the automation arrives switched off until you give it a new path. More on calling Earshot from scripts is in The HTTP API.

Nothing to fill in. The editor says: "Nothing starts this on its own. Press Run now on the list, call it from the HTTP API or an OSC command, or run it from another automation. Whoever calls it can pass values, which arrive as {{var.name}}." Use it for: a button you press yourself (Run now), a set of actions several other automations share (Run another automation, see Actions), something a console starts by name with /earshot/automation/<automation>/trigger (see the OSC address reference), something a script starts through the API, passing values (see The HTTP API). The list shows it as "Run by hand, the API, or another automation". Any automation, whatever its trigger, can also be run these ways. "Manual only" just means it has no other trigger.

Field Choices Channel Any channel, or one channel When it Device lost, Recovered, Silent for a while Seconds of silence Only for "Silent for a while". At least 1. A new trigger starts at 30. Device lost fires when a channel's device is lost. Recovered fires when it comes back. Silent for a while fires when the channel has been silent for at least that many seconds. Variables for actions: {{channel.name}} and {{channel.slug}}. It does not work on channels from another Earshot computer. A linked channel has no audio here, so it is never watched for silence or device health. A trigger set to "Any channel" ignores linked channels. One aimed only at a linked channel never fires, and is reported as a problem: "Silence triggers do not work on channels from another host." Not tried on real hardware Unplugging a USB interface mid-show is untested. See Limits and known behaviour.

Field Value Channel Any channel When it Device lost The list shows it as "Any channel loses its device". Pair it with a Flash an alert action reading Audio lost on {{channel.name}}. The whole automation is in Recipes.

Only if, with no conditions yet. Mock show, not a real show. Conditions are optional. With none, the editor says "No extra conditions: it runs whenever the trigger fires." With several, all of them must be true. To add one, choose its kind in the box and press Add condition. Condition What you set Works with Channel is one of Tick channels. Spoken-phrase and channel-health triggers. Channel is in a group Tick groups. Spoken-phrase and channel-health triggers. Person is one of Tick people. Experimental, with the same warning as the People list above. Spoken-phrase triggers only. Time of day From (local time) and Until (local time). A new one starts at 19:00 to 23:00. "An end earlier than the start wraps past midnight." Every trigger. A flag is set Flag name. Every trigger. A flag is not set Flag name. Every trigger. A condition that cannot apply to the chosen trigger shows an Ignored for this trigger badge, with "People conditions only apply to spoken-phrase triggers." or "Channel and group conditions only apply to spoken-phrase and channel-health triggers." A channel, group or person condition with nothing ticked does nothing, and the editor says so. The time is the host computer's local time.

A flag is a named on/off marker that only automations use. "Flags are set and cleared by “Set a flag” actions." One automation sets the flag; another has a condition that checks it. That makes an interlock: "only fire this after the stage manager has said 'show mode'". The whole pattern is in Recipes. Two things to know: Flags are kept in the engine's memory while Earshot runs. Every flag starts cleared when Earshot starts. A flag is only really set while the show is Armed. In Safe, "Set a flag" is a dry run like every other action, so the flag does not change.

Activity says so, for example: "Go cue" did not fire: condition not met: outside time window 19:00–23:00 "House lights" did not fire: condition not met: flag show-mode is not set A people condition never passes when no voice was heard. Run now, a chained automation, OSC, MIDI, a web request and a channel-health event have no voice, so Activity says "no voice was heard for this trigger".
documents.s: When a condition stops a cue

documents.t: For a spoken phrase, Where to listen and a channel, group or person condition do similar jobs. Use Where to listen for the plain case. The difference: In Where to listen, a ticked channel and a ticked group widen the range (either will do). Conditions must all be true. A "Channel is one of" condition and a "Channel is in a group" condition together narrow the range to channels that satisfy both.
documents.s: Where to listen, or a condition?

documents.t: Two settings at the bottom of the editor change how a trigger behaves. They are described in Actions: Cooldown (milliseconds): after an automation fires, it ignores its trigger for this long. Activity says cooling down (N ms left). Fire on: Final text (recommended) or Draft text (faster, less safe). Only spoken phrases use it.

A variable is a name in double braces, such as {{capture.number}}. When an automation fires, Earshot replaces it with a value from whatever set the automation off: the number that was said, the channel it was said on, an argument from an OSC message. This is how one automation, go cue {number}, can fire any cue number instead of needing one automation per cue.

You write Where It becomes go cue {number} In the trigger's phrase (single braces) A capture called number. /eos/cue/{{capture.number}}/fire In an action (double braces) /eos/cue/42/fire when someone says "go cue forty two". Single braces catch a value in a trigger. Double braces use a value in an action. In the editor, every field that accepts variables has an Insert variable… box under it. It lists exactly the variables your trigger provides, with a description of each, and puts the one you choose at the cursor.

Variable What it holds {{text}} The whole line that was heard. {{match}} The part of the line that matched. {{capture.NAME}} The word heard where {NAME} is in the phrase. With Regular expression, the named group NAME. {{capture.1}}, {{capture.2}} … The same captures by position, counting from 1. {{channel.name}} Name of the channel it came from. {{channel.slug}} Short, OSC-safe name of that channel. {{speaker.name}} Who was speaking, if known. Three things to know: {{text}} and {{match}} are the words as Earshot heard them: numbers and show words tidied ("forty two" is 42, "stand by" is "standby"), but glossary corrections not applied. Automations never see the corrected text. A capture holds one word. A whole spoken number counts as one word, so {number} on "cue twelve point five" is 12.5. {{speaker.name}} is filled in only when Earshot already knows who spoke at the moment the automation fires. A name normally arrives a moment after the line, and an automation that is not limited to people does not wait for it. Expect it to be empty most of the time.

Variable What it holds {{osc.address}} The address that arrived. {{osc.args.0}} First argument (count from 0). {{osc.args.1}} Second argument, and so on. {{capture.NAME}} The part of the address where {NAME} is in the pattern. {{capture.1}}, {{capture.2}} … The same captures by position, counting from 1.

Variable What it holds Filled in for {{midi.port}} Input port the message arrived on. Every message {{midi.channel}} MIDI channel, 1 to 16. Every message {{midi.note}} Note number. Note on, Note off {{midi.velocity}} Velocity. Note on, Note off {{midi.controller}} Controller number. Control change {{midi.value}} Controller value. Control change {{midi.program}} Program number. Program change
Variable What it holds {{var.body}} The request body, as text. Empty if the request had none.

Variable What it holds {{var.NAME}} A value the caller supplied. Replace NAME with the name the caller used. Callers that can supply values: The HTTP API. A request that runs the automation can carry values. See The HTTP API. Run another automation. The first automation's values are handed on with var. in front of each name: its {{capture.number}} is {{var.capture.number}} in the second automation, and its {{text}} is {{var.text}}. Run now on the list supplies no values, so every {{var.NAME}} is empty.
Variable What it holds {{channel.name}} Name of the channel the event is about. {{channel.slug}} Short, OSC-safe name of that channel.

Action Fields that accept variables Send OSC Address, and each argument's value Send MIDI Note, Velocity, Controller, Value, Program HTTP request URL and Body (not header names or values) Flash an alert Alert text Send text to a channel Channel name, short name or number, and Text Add a marker Marker text Control the screen Channel (for Select a channel and Mark as read) Run a shell command None. See below. Flag names, header values and the other fields are used exactly as you typed them.

Write {{name}} or {{ name }}. Spaces inside the braces do not matter. A name is made of letters, digits, _, . and -. A variable your trigger does not provide is replaced with nothing. The editor warns you: "{{capture.cue}} is not filled in by this trigger, so it will be empty." To write two real opening braces, put a backslash first: \{{ comes out as {{. A {{ with no closing }} is sent as plain text. The editor warns: "A {{ has no closing }}, so it will be sent as plain text." There is no nesting, no arithmetic and no formatting. A variable is replaced by its value and nothing else. You cannot add 1 to a cue number or pad it with zeros.
A variable carries something that was said, or something that arrived from the network. Earshot limits what such a value can do.

A value put into an OSC address may not be empty and may not contain any of: / * ? [ ] { } , # or a space If it does, the action is skipped and the reason is logged. The value is never cleaned up and sent anyway. A mis-heard word can therefore never turn /eos/cue/{{capture.number}}/fire into /eos/cue/*/fire. This applies only to values that come from variables. The parts of the address you typed yourself can contain anything. OSC arguments are not addresses, so a text argument may contain anything. A number argument must still read as a number of its type, or the action is skipped.

A value put into a URL is percent-encoded: everything except letters, digits and - . _ ~ is written as % and a code. So a ?, &, / or # in something that was said cannot change which address is called. A value put into a request Body is not encoded. It goes in as it is.

A shell command is not a template. A command containing {{ is refused. Values are passed as environment variables instead, named EARSHOT_ followed by the variable's name in capitals with every other character turned into _: Variable In a shell command {{text}} "$EARSHOT_TEXT" {{capture.number}} "$EARSHOT_CAPTURE_NUMBER" {{channel.slug}} "$EARSHOT_CHANNEL_SLUG" {{osc.args.0}} "$EARSHOT_OSC_ARGS_0" This way spoken text can never become part of the command itself. See Run a shell command.

Phrase go cue {number} Action Send OSC, address /eos/cue/{{capture.number}}/fire Said {{capture.number}} Sent "Go cue forty two." 42 /eos/cue/42/fire "Go Q 7." 7 /eos/cue/7/fire "Go cue twelve point five." 12.5 /eos/cue/12.5/fire "Go cue 7 and 8." (refused) Nothing. Activity: "Go cue" did not fire: the number may be incomplete: … Whether your desk accepts 12.5 in an address is for the desk's documentation to say.
documents.s: A cue number into an OSC address

documents.t: Phrase sound cue {n} go Action Send OSC, address /sound/go, one argument: Whole number, value {{capture.n}} Said Sent "Sound cue nine, go." /sound/go with the whole number 9 "Sound cue nine point five, go." Nothing from this action. 9.5 is not a whole number, so the action is skipped and Activity says why.
documents.s: A cue number as an OSC argument

documents.t: Phrase fade {a} to {b} Action Send OSC, address /fader/{{capture.a}}, one argument: Whole number, value {{capture.b}} "Fade three to five" sends /fader/3 with the whole number 5. Always put a word between two captures. fade {a} {b} is rejected. See How Earshot hears numbers.
Phrase (Any of) blackout, kill the lights Action Flash an alert, text BLACKOUT called by {{channel.name}} "Kill the lights" on Deck Left shows "BLACKOUT called by Deck Left".

Trigger An incoming OSC message, pattern /desk/page/{page}/go Action Add a marker, text Page {{capture.page}}, level {{osc.args.0}} A console sending /desk/page/3/go with the argument 0.8 adds the marker "Page 3, level 0.8".
Phrase (Regular expression) video (?P<n>\d+) go Action HTTP request, POST, URL http://10.0.1.40:8080/play/{{capture.n}} "Video four go" calls http://10.0.1.40:8080/play/4.
documents.s: Something said, into a web address

documents.t: Trigger A web request Action Send text to a channel, a fixed channel, text From the web: {{var.body}} Calling the automation's address with the body house open writes "From the web: house open" into that channel as a typed line.
documents.s: A request body into a channel

documents.t: The Test bench shows each action with its variables already filled in, and never sends. Type the phrase the way it would be said and read what each action would do.

Persistent local desktop diagnostic logs and Open Logs Folder in the Mac app menu and tray. Logging runs off the transcription thread, uses a bounded queue, and retains at most three 10 MiB files. Voice decision logs link each utterance to signal levels, clipping, detected speech, speech-gate thresholds, model readiness, match scores/margins, naming and automation thresholds, learning progress, early exits and final name publication. Logs contain no transcript text, raw audio or voiceprint vectors. Diagnostic comparisons for replies with at least 250 ms of detected speech, exposing their scores even when they are too short to name or learn.

This release adds observability; it does not claim to fix recognition of very short comms replies. Naming and learning still require at least one second of detected speech per observation, and automation thresholds remain unchanged. The synthetic comms measurement found unstable embeddings for isolated single-word replies. macOS Apple Silicon only. Windows and Linux updates remain on hold.

Slow transcription or experimental overlap separation no longer switches off voice naming across every channel. Names continue through their bounded background queue while expensive turn and overlap processing pauses to let transcription catch up. Repeated, consistent unknown replies can now establish a voice even when their similarity to a saved voice falls between recognition and immediate-discovery thresholds. This also combines short replies from the same channel, without mixing channels or dissimilar voices; pending observations expire after two minutes. Setup now identifies CAM++ as the model required to detect and name voices, and explains that MossFormer2 separates audio without recognising people.

Added regressions for automatic naming under load and repeated unknown comms voices, plus a real CAM++ test with synthetic speech through simulated noisy, band-limited comms. These tests do not establish accuracy on real comms feeds. macOS Apple Silicon only; Windows and Linux remain on hold. Overlap separation remains experimental, off by default and slower than real time.

Automatic voice discovery on shared channels: unfamiliar voices appear as Voice 1, Voice 2 and so on without a registration or reading passage. Rename a detected voice in Setup → People; its saved voice and earlier line labels keep the same identity. Separate finished transcript lines for consecutive speakers within one stretch of speech. Clear subsequent turns refine automatically learned voices; controlled voice learning remains available. Optional local separation of two overlapping voices with the MossFormer2 model. Isolated tracks are split at pauses and ordered by onset, with separate replay audio and word timings for each line. Apple Silicon runtime and overlap probes, with reproducible measurements in the developer documentation.

macOS now bundles the Core ML-capable shared speech runtime. CPU remains the default where the installed-model benchmarks were faster. Faster voice processing through reused embeddings, cached FFT and spectral tables, reused scratch buffers, a coarse turn check and four native voice-model threads on Apple Silicon. macOS gives live transcription higher scheduling priority than supporting voice and translation work. Separation prepares in the background and releases its model when switched off. Voice recognition starts enabled on new audio channels. Existing channels keep their previous switch setting. Learned voiceprints remain on the host and are excluded from browsers and exported shows.

This version is released for macOS Apple Silicon only. Windows and Linux builds are on hold; their previous releases remain available. Overlapping-voice separation is experimental and off by default. It recovered both reference phrases in the synthetic trial, but separating four seconds of audio took about 8.6 seconds on the development M3 Pro. It can miss or duplicate speech and is not yet suitable for low-latency live use. Automatic discovery and turn boundaries have been tested with synthetic voices, not real crew or comms feeds. Very short replies, similar voices, noise and more than two simultaneous speakers remain limitations. Names are a reading aid and can be wrong. The macOS app is ad-hoc signed and has a signed updater archive, but is not notarised by Apple.

Offline WAV replay with JSON reports for comparing real console/comms recordings across installed speech models. Expandable transcription timing in Setup → Channels separates first-draft processing time from finished-line delay and shows queued work. Moonshine tiny English as an optional local draft model; finished lines can keep using the main speech model. Select words or use the pencil on a finished line to correct the transcript. Admins can remember confirmed mishearings for future speech; the original remains available, and edits never fire automations. Guided voice learning with a read-along passage, input meter, progress, an explicit processing state, and the option to keep learning in the background. Low-latency and comms/noisy-feed starting points in each channel’s speech detection settings. A cross-platform real-model fixture for isolated “go”, “yes”, “hold”, and “stop”, plus opt-in noise and competing-voice measurements.

Finished lines, including adopted pause decodes, take priority over speculative work on other channels while preserving channel order. Correction retries succeed when the requested text is already saved; remembered spellings cannot invalidate existing glossary aliases. Read-along highlights follow repeated passages and survive hiding enrollment or leaving Setup and returning. Earlier live updates, shorter minimum speech and final waits, and more leading audio. Untuned legacy defaults upgrade on startup; customized settings remain intact. The neural voice detector resets during acoustically quiet pauses instead of resetting during a later word’s delayed onset. Display corrections recognize production cue abbreviations such as “LXQ 912” and distinctive, unambiguous variants of known names. Numbers and automation input stay separate from these inferred corrections. Transcript edits update saved history and search, discard obsolete translations, and reject stale concurrent edits. Voice learning uses a focused, scrollable passage and keeps the channel’s input meter beside progress. Setup reports inputs that are starting or need attention.

Noisy comms and overlapping-voice accuracy remain under evaluation. Isolated commands can still be missed or misheard, and results differ across platforms; detection presets and draft models do not guarantee instant or correct text.

Check for Updates in the tray context menu and macOS app menu, with automatic GitHub Release checks after startup and every six hours. Native update prompts with Update now, Not now and Don't remind me for this update; skipped versions remain available through manual checks. Verified update downloads, download progress and a graceful transcription shutdown before installation and restart on macOS, Windows and Linux AppImage installations. Signed updater artifacts and a GitHub Release manifest in the release scripts, including separate Windows EXE and MSI updates.

Personal keyword alerts in Display → Personal keyword alerts. Enter your name or comma-separated words and phrases to flash this device when a new spoken or typed line mentions them. No automation or Armed mode is needed. Alerts show the matching keyword, channel and transcript line for context. They clear after five seconds or when you press Dismiss. Reduced-motion settings show a steady alert. A changelog in the online manual, linked from Display settings. Release notes now include the changes for their version.

Updated the user guide, display instructions and screenshots for personal keyword alerts. Corrected installation instructions to reflect the published macOS, Windows and Linux downloads. Installers remain unsigned; Windows and Linux installer interfaces and desktop windows have not been tested.

Initial public desktop downloads: macOS Apple Silicon DMG, Windows x64 EXE and MSI, and Linux x86_64 DEB, RPM and AppImage. Local speech transcription, Feed, Lanes, Focus and Archive views, typed messages, show configuration and crew access controls. Phrase automations and show control through OSC, MIDI and HTTP, with Safe/Armed controls and an activity log. Online manual with installation instructions, examples and screenshots.

Installers are unsigned. The headless host passed a demo startup smoke test on all three systems; Windows and Linux installer interfaces and desktop windows have not been tested. No Intel Mac installer. Real comms hardware, real consoles and real venue operation remain untested. See the manual's limits before relying on Earshot at a show.

Go through this before every show. It takes a few minutes, and each item links to the page that explains it. Print the page if you like a pen. danger Finish with the header showing Safe. Arm only when you mean to, and only after every phrase automation has been tried on the Test bench and said out loud on the real channel.

The host computer is on mains power and will not sleep. If the computer sleeps, Earshot stops listening. (Limits) The header says Live, and shows the show name you expect. (Reading the transcript) The speech models show Installed under Setup, Models. A venue with no internet cannot download them. (Models) You know that a restart of the host starts a new session, signs out everyone who used the password, and comes back Safe. (What happens when the host restarts)

Every channel shows a level meter that moves when someone speaks, and no No input, Offline or Error badge. (Status and badges) Say a test line on each channel. Read it in the Feed. (Feed) No channel sits on Behind while people are talking normally. (Troubleshooting) If you use voice names: Separate and recognise voices on this channel is on, detected voices have been named or deliberately learned on that channel, and you know names can be wrong. (People) Names, songs and gear that the recogniser gets wrong are in the glossary, and no entry says "Not applied". (Glossary) If you show another computer's channel: its status line says "Linked to …", and you know whether the link is encrypted (it is not, in practice). (Showing another Earshot computer's channels) Any channel set to cloud speech shows its Cloud mark, you meant it, and a key is saved. Cloud speech has never been tried against the real service. (Cloud & audio) Any channel with Keep audio for replay on is one you mean to record, and the people on it know. (Replay a line's audio, Privacy)

Who can connect is set the way you mean it (Setup, Access). Remember Open means everyone on the network can arm. (Who can connect) Crew have the address from Address for the crew, and each phone shows Live. (Who can connect, Phones and tablets) Anyone who should only read has a Viewer link, not the password. (Invites and personal links, Roles) Old personal links you no longer want are revoked. (Invites and personal links) People who read in another language have picked it under Read in, and know a translation is a reading aid, never a cue call. (Read in another language)

The header shows Safe. (Safe and Armed) The Automations list does not say "… automation is not running." (When an automation is not running) Every phrase automation has been tried on the Test bench, and said out loud on the real channel while Safe, then checked in Activity ("would have fired"). (Run now, the Test bench and Activity) Number calls have been said the way the caller really says them, and none is refused in Activity. (How Earshot hears numbers) Each automation has a Cooldown that suits it. (Building an automation) Each OSC destination has the right address, port and protocol, and the device is on the network. (Actions) No automation that must go, or must not go for the wrong person, is limited to named people. (Automations limited to people) Start armed is off, unless the show runs unattended and you mean it. (Consoles and controllers) Everyone who can press Make safe knows where it is. Alt+Shift+S works from anywhere on the screen. (Safe and Armed)

If a console will send OSC: OSC input is on, at the lowest level that does the job, with the console's IP address in the list, and arming (if used) over TCP. (OSC input) The console's Make safe button has been pressed once, with the show Armed in rehearsal, and the header went to Safe. (OSC examples) Each console cue that triggers an Earshot automation has been fired once while Safe, and shows in Activity as a dry run. (OSC addresses) MIDI controllers are plugged in, their ports are ticked, and a press shows as "MIDI in" in Activity. (MIDI) Allow automations to run shell commands is off, unless you use shell actions and have read each one. (Consoles and controllers)

Press Make safe. Export the session if you want a copy outside Earshot (Archive, Export). (Archive and search) Export the show file if you changed channels, automations or the glossary today. (Show files) Revoke links made for guests. (Invites and personal links)

Everyone else on the show network opens a web address in a browser. There is nothing to install. This page covers the two things you decide first: which address to hand out, and who is allowed in. Both are on one screen: open Setup, then Access. "Decide who can connect to this show from other devices, and hand out access during the show. You can cut anyone off at any time." Earshot starts in Open mode In Open mode everyone on the network is an operator, and an operator can arm the show and fire cues. Change this before you put Earshot on a network you do not control. Who can do this Only admins can open Setup. The desktop window and the Admin: address from earshotd are admin. The mock show. The address 192.168.1.20, the people and the nearby computers are all invented.
documents.s: The address, and who can connect

documents.t: Under Address for the crew, the screen says Crew can open: and gives one address, for example http://192.168.1.20:4780. Press Copy address. Give crew the address shown there. Earshot picks the best one: the address of the network this computer uses to reach everything else. More addresses lists the others this computer has, each with its own Copy button. Some are labelled "Public address" or "VPN or virtual network". Use one of these only if you know the crew are on that network. Do not make up a name for the computer. IP addresses, localhost and the computer's own name work. Anything else is refused. If someone types an address the host does not recognise, their browser shows a card titled "Wrong address": "This address isn't one the host recognises. Use the address shown on the operator's screen." If you need crew to reach Earshot through a name of your own (a venue DNS name, a reverse proxy), see Network. Plain http only Earshot serves plain http in this build. There is no setting to give it a certificate. Anyone on the same network can read what travels between a phone and the host. Keep Earshot on the show network, not the public Wi-Fi.

Under Who can connect there are three cards. Pick one, then press Apply. Until you do, it says "Not applied yet." Mode The card says What it means in practice Open "Anyone on the network can view and operate." No sign-in. Everyone is an operator. Password "One shared password." Everyone who signs in with the password is an operator. Nobody else gets in. Personal links "Each person gets their own link. You can revoke it." Each person has a link with their own role, viewer or operator. You can cut off one person without touching the rest. Apply always asks you to confirm, and says who is affected: Changing to The question What it tells you Open "Open the show to everyone?" "Anyone on the network will be able to view and operate this show." Password "Switch to a shared password?" "Anyone connected right now who has not signed in with the password will be disconnected. They can rejoin once they enter it." Coming from Personal links: "People with a personal link stay connected. Anyone else is disconnected until they enter the password." If no password exists yet: "No password is set yet, so nobody can join until you set one below." Personal links "Switch to personal links?" "Anyone connected right now without a personal link will be disconnected. Make links below, then send them out." Coming from Password: "Everyone signed in with the password will be disconnected. Only people with a personal link can connect." The change applies at once. Your own admin window is never locked out.

Your situation Use Why A closed show network that only crew can join, and you trust everyone on it to arm Open Nothing to hand out. But remember everyone can arm. A network you mostly trust, a small crew, quick to set up Password One thing to say over comms. Everyone still becomes an operator. A shared or venue network, visitors who should only read, or anyone you may need to cut off Personal links Each person has their own role, read-only viewers included, and you can revoke one person without changing anything for the rest. Personal links still work in Password mode, with their own role. So you can run Password for the crew and still hand a read-only viewer link to a guest. In Open mode a viewer link is raised to operator, like everybody else.

Viewer Operator Admin Read the transcript, type where a channel allows it, replay saved audio yes yes yes See Armed or Safe display only yes yes Arm, Make safe, Run now, Test bench, add markers, acknowledge alerts no yes yes See what a changed line was changed from no yes yes Edit automations, and use Setup no no yes How people come by each role: How they connected Role The desktop window, or the Admin: address from earshotd Admin No sign-in, in Open mode Operator The shared password Operator A personal link or a QR invite Viewer or operator, as you chose when you made it The full table is on Roles. The mock show, opened as a viewer. There is no "Hold to arm" control: a viewer sees only whether the show is Safe or Armed. Someone who is not an admin and opens Setup sees this instead: The mock show, opened as an operator.
documents.s: What each kind of person can do

documents.t: You set the show up at home in Open mode. Tomorrow it goes on the venue network, which the front-of-house staff also use. Open Setup, Access. Pick Personal links and press Apply. Read the question and press Switch to personal links. Your own window stays connected. Under People with access, press New personal link for each operator: "Ana, stage manager" as an Operator, and so on. Each link is shown once, so have them scan it or send it straight away. See Invites and personal links. For people who only read, such as the lighting booth, make Viewer links. Press Copy address and put the address on the call sheet. During the show, anyone new gets a QR invite from Invite someone. Anyone who should not be there gets Revoke.
The password Invites and personal links Earshot on a phone Network Safe and Armed: what an operator can set off. Troubleshooting: "A phone cannot connect".

There are two ways to give one person their own way in: Invite someone (QR) New personal link Best for Someone standing next to you with a phone Someone you will send a link to What you hand over A QR code and a join link that work once and run out after 10 minutes A link that keeps working until you revoke it What they end up with A personal link of their own, made when they join That link Shown again later? You can make another No. It is shown once. Either way the person ends up in the list under People with access, where you can Revoke them. Both are on Setup, Access. They work in every mode, and they are the only way in when Who can connect is set to Personal links. Who can do this Only admins make invites and links, and revoke them.

Choice They can Viewer "can read, and type where a channel allows it" Operator "can arm the show, run automations and add markers" Choosing Operator shows a reminder: "An operator can arm the show and fire cues." In Open mode a viewer is not read-only While Who can connect is Open, everyone is at least an operator, including someone holding a viewer link. A viewer link only limits someone in Password or Personal links mode.

"Make a QR code for a phone to scan. It works once and runs out after 10 minutes." Under Invite someone, choose what They can do: Viewer or Operator. Optionally type a Name or label. "Up to 40 characters. It shows next to what they type." Press Make invite. A box opens with the QR code, a countdown ("Expires in 9:59") and the join link. The mock host. The code and the address are invented and lead nowhere. Have them point their phone camera at the code. "No camera? Send the link, or have them open" the crew address "and paste it." Copy link copies the join link. Their phone opens a join page titled "Join" and the Earshot computer's name. "Tap Join to start reading the live transcript." They can type Your name (optional), "Shown next to anything you type in the Feed.", and press Join. Press Done on your screen. What the phone shows after scanning, on the mock host ("FOH Rack" is the mock's name for itself). Not a real show. The rules: A code works once. The moment someone joins with it, it is used up. It runs out after 10 minutes. The box then offers Expired — make a new code. Up to 32 codes can wait at once. After that: "Too many codes are waiting; let some expire." A used code becomes a personal link, listed under People with access under the name they typed, or your label if they typed none. From then on it behaves like any other personal link. A used, expired or mistyped code gets one answer on the phone: "This code is not valid or has already been used. Ask the operator for a new one." iPhone and iPad: add to the Home Screen first The join page tells iPhone users: "Want Earshot on your Home Screen? Add it first (Share, then Add to Home Screen), open it from there, then join. Joining in Safari does not carry over." If they join in Safari and add it to the Home Screen afterwards, they will need a new code. See Earshot on a phone.

Under People with access, press New personal link. Who is it for? "Their name or job, such as “Ana, stage manager”. Up to 40 characters. It shows next to what they type." Choose what They can do. Press Make link. The mock host. The link is invented. The box says "You will not see this again. Copy it or have them scan it now." and "This link is theirs alone. Revoke it from the list if it goes astray." Have them scan the QR, or press Copy link and send it to them. Pressing Done asks "Close?": "You won't be able to see this link again." Choose Close, or Keep it open. The link is the key. Anyone who has it is that person, with that role, until you revoke it. Send it privately, not on a group chat or a call sheet. Unlike a QR invite, a personal link does not expire, and nothing ties it to one device. If someone loses theirs, or it may have been seen by someone else, revoke it and make another.

In Personal links mode, someone who opens the plain address sees: The mock host. "This show needs a personal link or QR code from the operator. Scan the QR code with your camera, or paste the link or code here." They can paste a whole link, or just a code, into Paste link or code.
documents.s: What the crew see without a link

documents.t: Everyone with a personal link is listed, whether they got it from a link you made or from a QR invite. Each row shows: The name or label, for example "Ana (stage manager)". The role: Viewer or Operator. What that means: "Can read, and type where a channel allows it", "Can arm the show, run automations and add markers", or "Can change everything, including Setup". "Made 3 h ago" and "Last used 4 min ago", or "Never used". "Never used" on a link you sent hours ago is worth a question: did they get it? If nobody has one yet, the list says "Nobody has a personal link yet. Make one for each person, and you can cut off any of them later without changing anything for the rest." with a Make the first link button.

Press Revoke next to a name. Earshot asks, for example, "Revoke Lighting booth?" and says "They are disconnected within a second and cannot get back in with this link. You can make them a new one." They are cut off within a second, wherever that link is in use. Everyone else is unaffected. It cannot be undone. Make them a new link if it was a mistake.
Personal links are kept by the host on disk, so they keep working after a restart. That is the big difference from the shared password, which everyone has to type again. See When the host restarts.
documents.s: Personal links and the host restarting

documents.t: When another Earshot computer wants to show one of this computer's channels, the "link code" it asks for is an ordinary Viewer personal link made here with New personal link. Whoever has it can read everything a viewer can, so treat it like a password, and revoke it when the link is no longer wanted. See Showing another Earshot computer's channels.
documents.s: A link code for another Earshot computer

documents.t: Person They can How Ana, stage manager Operator New personal link, sent to her before load-in Deputy stage manager Operator New personal link Sound No. 1 Operator New personal link Lighting booth Viewer New personal link, opened on the booth laptop Followspot 1 and 2 Viewer Invite someone at the half, scanned on their phones A visiting producer Viewer Invite someone on the night. Revoke after the show. On the night, a dresser's phone dies and she borrows another. Make a new invite, she scans it, and you revoke the old entry.
documents.s: Example: a crew of six on personal links

documents.t: The join page and scanning a code have not been tried on real phones and tablets. See Limits and known behaviour.
The address, and who can connect The shared password Earshot on a phone Roles

One Earshot computer can show a channel that another Earshot computer is listening to. The channel appears in the Feed, Lanes and Focus on this computer like any other. Only the text crosses: no audio, and no saved clips. Two words are used on this page: The serving host is the computer that has the audio and does the listening. This computer (the linking host) is the one that shows the other's lines. What has been tried Two Earshot hosts were run on one Mac and linked over plain http through the real screen. Not tried: two separate computers on a real network, finding each other between machines, a link code on a host that requires one, and https. Treat links as not encrypted. Details are at the end of this page. Who can do this Only admins, on both computers.

Open Setup, Channels, the channel, and switch on Shared with other Earshot hosts. Save. Only channels with this switch on can be linked. If that computer's access mode asks people to sign in (Password or Personal links), make a link code: Setup, Access, People with access, New personal link, with They can set to Viewer. Label it so you know what it is for, for example Broadcast truck link. The link it shows you once is the viewer link to give to the other computer. See Invites and personal links. In Open mode no code is needed. A link code is an ordinary Viewer link Whoever has it can open that computer's Earshot as a Viewer and read every channel a Viewer can, not only the shared ones. Treat it like a password. On an unencrypted link it travels readable on the network. To cut a link off for good, revoke it on the serving host, under People with access. Use a personal link, not a QR invite The app's own hint reads "On the other host: Setup → Access → invite a Viewer." What the link box accepts is a viewer link of the kind New personal link makes, with token= in it. A QR invite from Invite someone is a different thing: its join link has code= in it, works once in a browser, and is not a link code. A link code on a host that requires one has not been tried end to end.
Open Setup, Channels, and press From another Earshot host. It has four steps. The mock show. "Main stage" and "Broadcast truck" are invented computers.

Pick one from the list. Each shows its name, its address and a badge, Encrypted or Not encrypted. Look again searches again. If none are found it says "No other Earshot computers were found on this network. If you know the other computer's address, type it below." Choose Type an address and fill in Address and Port (4780 unless the other computer was started on another). You can paste a whole viewer link into Address. Earshot takes it apart: the address and port stay, the code moves to the masked code box, and it says "That was a viewer link. Its address and port are filled in here, and its code is in the Link code step."

Choice The app says Encrypted (https) "Encrypted links have not been proven end to end in this build, and need a certificate this computer trusts." Not encrypted (http) "Lines and the link code travel readable on this network." See Encrypted or not below. In practice, choose Not encrypted (http) on a network you trust.

Link code (optional): "On the other host: Setup → Access → invite a Viewer. Whoever has this code can read everything a Viewer can on that host, so treat it like a password." "Paste the code, or a whole viewer link: Earshot keeps only the code. Leave it empty if the other computer does not ask for one." If you paste a link that belongs to a different computer from the one you chose, the box says "This link is for another computer than the one you chose." Press Find channels.

The screen names the other computer and its address, says "Reached over an encrypted connection." or "Reached without encryption.", and lists the channels it shares. Tick the ones you want and press Add selected channels. A channel you already have says "Already added". If there are none: "That computer shares no channels. On it, turn on “Shared with other Earshot hosts” for a channel." Each result reads "Added name." If some fail, Try the failed ones again. The channels now appear in your channel list with a link icon, and their lines start arriving.

A linked channel… is read-only Nobody can type into it from here. is never shared onward This computer cannot offer it to a third one. Links never chain. never fires automations here Its lines are never matched against a phrase, and a Silence trigger never applies to it. A Silence trigger that listens only to linked channels is reported as a problem: "Silence triggers do not work on channels from another host." has no level meter There is no audio here. has none of the audio settings No saved audio, voice recognition, profanity filter, engine or speech detection. Those are fixed by the serving host. is marked A link icon and "from address". If it is not encrypted it also carries a Not encrypted mark: "Lines from this host travel unencrypted on the network." is stored and searched here Its lines go into this computer's sessions, and can be searched, exported and translated like any line. does not carry names Names of recognised speakers stay on the serving host. A typed line keeps the name of whoever typed it. At most 32 channels can share one link (one address with one code). More than that is refused. A linked line arrives as the text the serving host's readers see. The original of a line that was changed there (by its glossary, a number or a show word) does not come across, so a linked line has no pencil here.
documents.s: What a linked channel can and cannot do

documents.t: Under a linked channel in Setup, Channels, Earshot says what is happening, in these words: The status line Meaning "Connecting to address (not encrypted)." It is trying to reach the other computer. "Linked to name at address (not encrypted). 10 lines received." Working. It adds ", N dropped" if some lines were dropped. "Cannot reach name or address: reason. Retrying." The other computer or the network is down. Earshot keeps trying. "address refused the link: …" The other computer said no, for example because the channel is no longer shared. "The link code was refused. Check the code on the other host, then enter it in this channel again (or switch the channel off and on)." See A refused link code. "This is this host itself …" The address you gave is this computer. A computer cannot link to itself. The other computer's address is shown next to its name because a computer can call itself anything. The mock show with three invented linked channels: one working, one whose code was refused, and one that cannot be reached. In the channel list and the Feed, a linked channel's badge follows the link: Starting while connecting, listening while linked, Error when the other computer refused, and Offline when it cannot be reached. See Status and badges.

The status says "Cannot reach …" and Earshot keeps trying, waiting a little longer each time, up to about half a minute between tries. When the other computer returns, the link comes back by itself, and Earshot catches up on what it missed if it can. If lines may be missing, a line appears in that channel: "Link to name was down for N s; some lines may be missing". The first link after this computer restarts begins from "now", without that notice. A dead link never slows this computer's own channels. A link never brings across lines from before the channel was shared, or from a time when sharing was switched off. If the serving host stops sharing the channel, deletes it or leaves, the link ends at once.
documents.s: When the other computer goes away and comes back

documents.t: If the serving host refuses the code, Earshot does not try again. This is on purpose: every retry would count as a wrong guess on the other computer, and enough of those would lock this computer out of it. The link stays stopped until one of these happens: the channel is saved again on this computer, the channel is switched off and on, or Earshot on this computer is restarted. Fixing the code on the serving host alone does not bring it back. Open the channel here, enter the code under New link code, and save.
documents.s: A refused link code stops the link

documents.t: Open the channel in Setup, Channels. Under "Where this channel comes from" you can change the Address, the Port, how it connects, and the code. A linked channel in the mock show. The other computer's name and address are invented. A linked channel has none of the audio settings. "A link code is saved. Leave the box empty to keep it." A saved code is never shown. See Saved secrets. Remove code removes it when you save ("The link code will be removed when you save."). Keep code undoes that. "Changing the address, port or encryption clears the stored link code. Enter it again." An address with a code must say how it connects: Encrypted or Not encrypted. Switching the channel's Enabled switch off stops showing new lines from the other computer. Deleting it ends the link for that channel.

Choose Not encrypted (http) and "Lines and the link code travel readable on this network." Choose Encrypted (https) and the app says "Encrypted links have not been proven end to end in this build, and need a certificate this computer trusts." That is the honest position: https links have never been tried between two computers. Earshot has no setting to give its own address a certificate, so a serving host normally offers plain http only. A serving host with a self-signed certificate fails unless this computer trusts it. Use plain http on a network you trust, and treat the link code as readable by anyone on it.

The stage rack ("Main stage") hears the Show Caller channel. The broadcast truck runs its own Earshot and wants those lines next to its own channels. On Main stage Setup, Channels, Show Caller: switch on Shared with other Earshot hosts, Save changes. Main stage is on Personal links, so make a code: Setup, Access, New personal link, Who is it for? Broadcast truck link, Viewer, Make link. Press Copy link. It is shown once. Send the link to the truck privately. On the truck Setup, Channels, From another Earshot host. Pick Main stage from the list, or choose Type an address and paste the whole link into Address. Choose Not encrypted (http). If you did not paste the link in step 5, paste it into Link code (optional). Press Find channels. Tick Show Caller and press Add selected channels. "Added Show Caller." Check its status line reads "Linked to Main stage at … (not encrypted)." The truck now sees Show Caller's lines live. Its own automations ignore them. After the show, on Main stage, press Revoke next to "Broadcast truck link". The link stops within a second.
documents.s: Example: the truck reads the stage's Show Caller

documents.t: Two Earshot hosts were run on one Mac and linked through the real screen: The channel's lines, including drafts, appeared live. Stopping the serving host gave "Cannot reach … Retrying." within about 2 seconds. It relinked 12 seconds after the serving host returned, and a gap line appeared ("down for 67 s"). Not tried: two separate computers on a real network, discovery between machines, a link code on a host that requires one, and https. Also known: A linked channel does not say when its last line arrived. A computer can call itself anything, which is why the address is shown beside the name. The first link after this computer restarts has no gap notice.

Channels Network: names, Bonjour and finding other Earshot computers. Invites and personal links: making and revoking the code. Privacy: what goes over the network. Troubleshooting: "A linked channel shows no lines".

This page covers the Network panel at the bottom of Setup, Access, and the rules about which web addresses Earshot answers to. Most shows need none of it: give the crew the address under Address for the crew and carry on. Who can do this Only admins change these settings. The command-line options on this page are for whoever starts earshotd.

Announce on the network (Bonjour) "Lets other Earshot computers on this network find this one." It is on by default. What it is for: when another Earshot computer wants to show one of this computer's channels, its link screen lists the Earshot computers it can find, so nobody has to type an address. See Showing another Earshot computer's channels. What it announces: this computer's Earshot name, its version, its access mode (Open, Password or Personal links) and whether it uses https. Nothing about the show, its channels or the transcript. What it is not: it is not how crew phones find Earshot. Phones use the address you give them. Turn it off if you do not want this computer to be discoverable. Linking still works by typing the address. Earshot does not announce itself at all when it listens only on the computer itself (for example earshotd --bind 127.0.0.1).

Name shown to others: "Crew see this when they join. Leave it empty to use this computer's name." The name appears: On the sign-in and join pages, as "Join" and the name, so people can tell they have the right computer. In other Earshot computers' lists of what is nearby. On a channel linked from this computer, on the other computer's screen. Type a name such as FOH Rack and press Save name. The screen says "Name saved." If you leave it empty, the computer's own system name is used. If that name cannot be used on the network (it is empty, has odd characters or spaces, or is too long), Earshot calls itself "earshot". A name is only a label Any computer can call itself anything. That is why Earshot shows a linked computer's address next to its name. Do not trust a name on its own.

Under Other Earshot computers nearby, Earshot lists what it found on the network. Each entry shows the computer's name, its access mode, its address and port, and its version, for example: Main stage · Password · 192.168.1.31:4780 · Version 0.1.0 Look again searches again. A search takes a second or two. If nothing is found: "No other Earshot computers found on this network." The list is only a view. To use one of those computers' channels, go to Setup, Channels, From another Earshot host. Finding other Earshot computers needs Bonjour (mDNS) to work on your network. If the network blocks it, Earshot finds nothing. Type the address instead. Finding each other between two computers has not been tried Two Earshot hosts have been run and linked on one Mac. Discovery between two separate machines on a real network has not been tried. See Limits and known behaviour.

Earshot checks the address a browser used before it answers anything. It answers to: Any IP address of the computer, for example http://192.168.1.20:4780/. localhost, on the host computer itself. The computer's own name, with or without .local. The name it announces on the network. Any extra name you allowed when starting it (below). Anything else gets the "Wrong address" card: "This address isn't one the host recognises. Use the address shown on the operator's screen." This is a safety check, not a fault. It stops a web page elsewhere from quietly pointing a made-up name at the Earshot computer and talking to it through someone's browser.

If crew must reach Earshot through a name you control, such as a venue DNS name or the name of a reverse proxy, tell Earshot the name when you start the headless program: earshotd --allow-host earshot.venue.example Repeat the flag for more names: earshotd --allow-host earshot.venue.example --allow-host comms.venue.example Give the bare name: no http://, no port, no path. See earshotd for every option. There is no screen for this, and the desktop app has no such setting in this build.
documents.s: Allowing a name of your own

documents.t: Two things follow from how Earshot works, and neither has been tried on a real network: Everyone behind a proxy looks like one device. Earshot counts wrong password tries by the address a connection comes from. Behind a reverse proxy that is the proxy's address for everybody, so one person's five wrong tries lock out new sign-ins for all of them for a while. People already signed in carry on. See The shared password. Do not count on a proxy to give Earshot https in this build. Earshot expects a browser to be talking to it at the same scheme, name and port that it is serving. If a proxy offers https:// to browsers and passes plain http on to Earshot, Earshot sees commands from those browsers as coming from another site and refuses them.
documents.s: If you put something in front of Earshot

documents.t: What How The web port 4780 by default. earshotd --port 4790 chooses another. The desktop app uses 4780, and if that port is busy it starts on another and tells you which in a dialog. Which network interface to listen on All of them by default. earshotd --bind 192.168.1.20 listens on one address only. Listening on the host computer only earshotd --bind 127.0.0.1. Nobody else can connect, Address for the crew is empty, and Earshot does not announce itself. There is no Setup screen for the interface or the port in this build. They can only be set when starting earshotd. Example: a rack machine with a show network card at 10.0.1.5 and a management card you do not want Earshot on: earshotd --bind 10.0.1.5 --port 4780 OSC input listens on the same address as the web app. See OSC input.
documents.s: Choosing the network interface and the port

documents.t: Earshot serves plain http in this build. There is no setting to give it a certificate. What that means for you: Anyone who can listen on the network can read the transcript, passwords as they are typed, and personal links as they are opened. Keep Earshot on a network only the crew can join. Most phones and browsers will not install Earshot as an app from a plain http address. It works the same in the browser. See Earshot on a phone. Links between Earshot computers offer "Encrypted (https)", but that has not been proven end to end. Treat links as not encrypted.
documents.s: No https for Earshot's own address

documents.t: The stage rack and the broadcast truck each run Earshot. On each, open Setup, Access, Network and set Name shown to others: Main stage and Broadcast truck. Press Save name. Leave Announce on the network (Bonjour) on, on both. On the truck, press Look again. If Main stage appears with its address, the two can see each other. If not, the network is probably blocking Bonjour: note the stage rack's address from its Address for the crew and type it when linking. Carry on with Showing another Earshot computer's channels.
documents.s: Example: two Earshot computers in one venue

documents.t: The address, and who can connect Showing another Earshot computer's channels earshotd Privacy: what goes over the network.

In Password mode there is one password for the whole crew. Everyone who signs in with it becomes an operator: they can read, type, arm the show and run automations. This page covers setting it, what the crew see, the lockouts, and when to use personal links instead. Who can do this Only admins set or change the password. Anyone can sign in with it.

Open Setup, Access. Under Who can connect, pick Password and press Apply. Confirm with Switch to password. A Password panel appears. Type the password and press Set password. "At least 8 characters. Share it by voice or message; it is not shown again." A shorter one is refused: "Use at least 8 characters." When it is saved the panel shows a Password set badge and says "Password set. People can join with it now." Until a password is set, nobody can join Switching to Password mode with no password leaves the door shut: "No password set — nobody can join. Only you can connect until you set one." Set the password straight after you switch. The password itself is never stored. Earshot keeps a scrambled form of it (a hash) on the host, and never sends even that to a browser. If you forget the password, set a new one.

They open the crew address and get a sign-in page. The mock host, which calls itself "FOH Rack". Invented, not a real show. The title is "Join" and the name of the Earshot computer, so they can tell they are in the right place. "Enter the show password the operator gave you." Your name (optional): "Shown next to anything you type in the Feed." It is a label people give themselves, not proof of who they are. Join. A wrong password says "That password is not right. Check it and try again."

Button Earshot asks What happens Change password "Change the password?" "Everyone who signed in with the old password is signed out. They will need the new one to get back in." "Password changed. Everyone who used the old one is signed out." Clear password "Clear the password?" "Everyone who signed in with it is signed out, and nobody new can join until you set another." "Password cleared. Nobody can join until you set a new one." Changing the password is how you remove someone in Password mode. It removes everyone, and the rest of the crew need the new one. Saving other settings does not sign anyone out. Only changing or clearing the password does, or leaving Password mode.

What happens Effect on someone signed in with the password They keep using Earshot They stay signed in. Each use renews it. They do not use it for 12 hours The sign-in expires. They enter the password again. The host restarts Everyone is signed out and needs the password again. Password sign-ins are kept only in the host's memory. See When the host restarts. You change or clear the password, or switch to another mode Everyone signed in with it is signed out. They choose Sign out Only they are signed out. Phones can Sign out from the More menu or the display menu. It asks "Sign out?" and says "You'll need the password again to rejoin." At most 256 password sign-ins can be live at once. A 257th pushes out the oldest.

Earshot slows down guessing. Five wrong tries from one device lock that device out for 30 seconds. Each further lockout doubles: 1 minute, 2 minutes, 4 minutes, 8 minutes, up to 15 minutes. The phone shows "Too many tries. Try again in m:ss." and counts down, then "You can try again now." A correct password clears the count. People already signed in are not affected. A lockout only stops new sign-ins from that device. "One device" means one network address. Devices that share an address, for example several phones behind one router or everyone coming through one reverse proxy, are counted together. One person mistyping five times can lock out new sign-ins for the others behind the same address for a short while.

There is one more limit, for the whole show: after 100 wrong password tries within a minute, from all devices together, every new password sign-in is refused for 60 seconds. This stops someone who keeps changing address from guessing without limit. It has a cost, and you should know it: Someone on your network who deliberately sends about 100 bad guesses a minute can keep new password sign-ins refused for as long as they keep it up. People already signed in, personal links, QR invites and the admin window are not affected. A show in progress carries on. What breaks is a crew member trying to join, or rejoin after a restart, while it is happening. On a network you do not trust, use personal links A shared password is one secret that everybody knows, that cannot be taken back from one person, and whose sign-in can be jammed by someone on the network. Personal links have none of those problems: each link is long and unguessable, each can be revoked alone, and they keep working through a host restart. If you must use a password on such a network, make it long.
