Setup, Access, pick Password, Apply, Switch to password. Type harbour hall tonight (20 characters) and press Set password. Say it once on the crew channel, with the address from Address for the crew. Each person opens the address, types the password and their name, and presses Join. The lighting designer's guest only needs to read. Make them a Viewer personal link. Personal links work in Password mode with their own role, so the guest cannot arm. After the show, press Clear password. Everyone is signed out and nobody new can join.
documents.s: Example: a password for a one-night show

documents.t: The sign-in page, like the rest of Earshot on small screens, has not been tried on real phones and tablets. See Limits and known behaviour.
The address, and who can connect Invites and personal links Saved secrets Troubleshooting: "A phone cannot connect".

Crew use Earshot in a phone's or tablet's browser. There is nothing to install: they open the crew address, join, and read. On a narrow screen the same views are laid out for one hand. Not tried on real phones and tablets Nobody has yet tried the join page, installing, or the small-screen layouts on a real phone or tablet, and nobody has confirmed that replayed audio is audible on a phone speaker. The pictures on this page were taken in a desktop browser at phone size. Try your own devices before the show. See Limits and known behaviour.

Join the same network as the Earshot computer. Open the address from the operator (Setup, Access, Address for the crew), or scan the QR code they show you. Depending on how the show is set up, you go straight in, type the show password, or use your personal link or code. See The address, and who can connect. The indicator in the header shows whether the phone is connected to the host (on a wider screen it reads Live). If the phone loses the host it says so, and keeps trying by itself.

The mock show at phone size, in a desktop browser. Invented lines, not a real show. Where What is there Top bar The show name, the connection dot, Safe and Arm (operators and admins; viewers see a display-only Safe or ARMED), and the display button for text size, theme and language. Under it What you are looking at ("All channels") and the Channels button. Middle The transcript. Scroll up to read back. Above the bottom bar On the Feed, the box for typing a line: pick the channel, type, Send. Bottom bar Feed, Lanes, Focus, Archive and More.

The side panel of channels does not fit on a phone, so it is behind the Channels button. The mock show. Channels are listed by group, each with its level meter. Tap a channel to show only that one. Tap more to add them. Tap a group's name to pick all its channels. Show all clears the filter. The cross closes the sheet. "Filtering changes this screen only. Groups are edited in Setup." What you pick here changes nothing for anyone else.

On a phone, Lanes shows one lane at a time with tabs along the top. The mock show. "Swipe sideways or use the tabs to change lane". A tab for a lane you are not looking at shows a count of new lines. More on Lanes.

More opens the rest. The mock show, opened as an admin. Entry What it is Automations "Build, test and arm automations." Activity "Live OSC, MIDI, HTTP and automation log." Setup "Devices, channels, groups, models and access." It needs admin access. API reference Opens /docs on the host. Install app See below. Only shown when it applies to this device. Sign out Only for people who signed in with the shared password. It shows "Signed in as" and your name above it.

Operators and admins have Arm in the top bar. It works like the desktop control: hold it for about 0.7 seconds, or tap it once and then tap Arm now. Safe is one tap. Read Safe and Armed before you give anyone a phone that can arm.
Open More, then Install app. What happens depends on the device.
documents.s: Put Earshot on the Home Screen

documents.t: The menu shows three steps: "Tap the Share button in Safari." "Choose Add to Home Screen." "Open it from the Home Screen, then ask the operator for a new code. Signing in on Safari does not carry over." On iPhone, add it first, then join The Home Screen app does not share Safari's sign-in. If you joined in Safari and then added Earshot to the Home Screen, the app opens signed out, and a QR code that has been used once will not work again. Ask the operator for a new code, or better: add it to the Home Screen first, open it from there, and join then. The join page says the same thing. Other browsers on iPhone and iPad (Chrome, Firefox, Edge) cannot add Earshot to the Home Screen. Use Safari for this.

Browsers only let a page install itself as an app when the page is served securely (https). Earshot serves plain http in this build, so other phones and browsers usually cannot install it. The menu says: "This address can't install apps. Earshot works the same in the browser." That is all there is to it: use the browser. Add a bookmark if you want a quick way back. Nothing is missing. If a browser does offer to install it, Install app opens the browser's own install prompt.

If you signed in with the shared password, Sign out is in the More menu and in the display menu. It asks "Sign out?" and says "You'll need the password again to rejoin." Someone on a personal link has no Sign out: the link is their sign-in. An operator removes them with Revoke.

The phone shows "Reconnecting" and keeps trying. You do not need to reload. When it reconnects, it catches up on the lines it missed. If the phone cannot reach the host at all, it shows "Can't reach the Earshot computer" and "Check that this device is on the same network as the Earshot computer. This page keeps trying by itself." If the host restarted, people on the shared password must sign in again. Personal links carry on. See When the host restarts.

Turn the text up. The display button has Text size from 85% to 175%. See Display. Filter to what you need. A followspot operator rarely needs all eight channels. Use Channels. Keep the screen awake using the phone's own settings if you need to glance at it all show. Earshot does not keep a phone awake. It is a reading aid. Listen to the call. A line can be late, and it can be wrong.
Invites and personal links The shared password Reading the transcript Troubleshooting: "A phone cannot connect".

Sooner or later the Earshot computer restarts mid-rehearsal: a power dip, an update, someone quitting the wrong program. This page says exactly what happens, so you know what to check first. The short version: the show comes back Safe, a new session starts, people on the shared password must sign in again, and people on personal links carry on.
documents.s: What happens when the host restarts

documents.t: Who or what What happens What they must do Every phone and browser Shows "Reconnecting", then if it goes on, "Can't reach the Earshot computer". It keeps trying by itself. Nothing. It reconnects when the host is back. People who signed in with the password Signed out. Password sign-ins are kept only in the host's memory. Type the password again. People with a personal link Still let in. Personal links are kept by the host on disk. Nothing. Someone holding a QR invite they had not used yet The code no longer works. Ask the operator for a new one. The desktop app's own window Signed in as an admin automatically, as always. Nothing. An admin using the Admin: address from earshotd The token in that address is new every time the program starts, unless it was started with --admin-token. The old address stops being an admin's. Use the new Admin: address the program prints. The operator at the Armed control Armed is forgotten. The show comes back Safe, unless Setup, Show control, Start armed is on. Decide whether to arm again. Nothing fires until you do. The transcript A new session starts. The old one is in the Archive. Nothing. Use the Archive to read back. Anything said while the host was down It was not written down. Earshot cannot recover speech it did not hear. Nothing can be done. Channels from another Earshot computer The links connect again by themselves. The first link after this computer restarts begins from "now", with no "some lines may be missing" notice. A link that had stopped because its code was refused is tried again. Check each status line reads "Linked to …". Another Earshot computer reading this one's channels It says "Cannot reach …" and keeps trying, then links again by itself and writes "Link to name was down for N s; some lines may be missing" in the channel. Nothing. Cloud speech and translation counters Start again from zero. They are "Counted since Earshot started". Nothing. Saved audio Kept. The age and size limits are checked again as Earshot starts. Nothing.
documents.s: Who is affected, and what they must do

documents.t: Everything you set up is on disk and comes back as it was: The show: channels, groups, automations, OSC destinations, the glossary, people and their learned voices. This computer's settings: who can connect and the password, OSC and MIDI input, cloud keys, saved-audio limits, Start armed. Every past session, its markers, and saved audio within the limits. Personal links. Downloaded models.
Armed. The show is Safe again. Password sign-ins. Unused QR invites. The live session. A new one begins. An earshotd admin token that was not fixed with --admin-token.

This is different from the host restarting. If a phone walks out of Wi-Fi range and back, or drops for a moment: It shows "Reconnecting" and keeps trying. When it reconnects, it catches up on the lines it missed. Nobody is signed out. The host never went away.
documents.s: A phone that only lost the network

documents.t: Earshot is a program on a computer. If the computer sleeps, Earshot stops listening. Speech during the sleep is not written down, just as if the host were off. Set the host computer not to sleep for the length of the show.

Setup, Show control, Start armed makes automations able to fire as soon as Earshot starts. It is off by default. Leave it off unless the show runs unattended, because with it on, a restart mid-show brings the show back Armed with nobody having chosen that. See Safe and Armed.

The header says Live and shows the show name you expect. The header shows Safe. Arm again only if you mean to. Every channel's level meter moves when someone speaks, with no No input, Offline or Error badge. If you use the shared password, tell the crew to sign in again. Say the password again if they need it. If you use channels from another Earshot computer, each status line reads "Linked to …". If you run headless, note the new Admin: address. Make restarts boring Use personal links rather than the shared password, so the crew are not all signed out at once. Start earshotd with a fixed --admin-token so your own address keeps working. See earshotd.
documents.s: After a restart: a two-minute check

documents.t: The rack loses power for ten seconds in the interval and Earshot starts again. The deck crew's phones, on personal links, show "Reconnecting" for a moment and then the Feed again. They see an empty live transcript, because a new session has started. The followspot operators, who typed the password at the half, get the sign-in page. The stage manager repeats the password on comms. The header shows Safe. The automations that fire lighting cues are logging "would have fired" until the stage manager holds Hold to arm again. The first half is in the Archive, under the earlier session.
documents.s: Example: a power dip in the interval

documents.t: The shared password Invites and personal links Safe and Armed Archive Troubleshooting

Earshot holds a few things that would let someone in, or let them spend your money, if they leaked: the join password, cloud keys, the link codes of channels from other Earshot computers, and two parts of an automation. No browser, not even an admin's, is ever sent one of them. The host sends a marker ("••••") for each secret it holds, and nothing where there is none. That has one consequence you will meet every day: a saved secret cannot be read back. You can keep it, replace it or remove it. You cannot look at it.
documents.s: Saved secrets are never sent to a browser

documents.t: Secret Where you enter it What the screen shows once it is saved The join password Setup, Access, Password A Password set badge. The Deepgram key Setup, Cloud & audio A Key saved badge. "The key is stored on this computer and is never shown again." The DeepL and Anthropic keys Setup, Cloud & audio, Keys for cloud translators A Key saved badge on each. The link code of a channel from another Earshot computer The channel, under "Where this channel comes from" "A link code is saved. Leave the box empty to keep it." An HTTP action's header values in an automation The automation editor, Then, HTTP request, Headers Dots and "(unchanged)", with a Replace button. A webhook trigger's path The automation editor, When, A web request Shown once, when you make it.

Every secret box works the same way. What you want What you do Buttons you will see Keep it Leave the box alone. Saving the rest of the screen does not disturb it. None needed. Remove it Clear it with the button for that. Remove key, Remove code, Clear password Replace it Type a new one and save. Save key, Change password, Replace Leave it alone to keep it. An empty box next to "Key saved" does not mean the key has gone. It means the page was never given it. A saved secret cannot be read back. If you lose a key, get it again from wherever it came from and enter it again. Copy a webhook's address when you create it, because it cannot be shown again. If you lose it, make a new one and update whatever calls it. Personal links are the same. A new link is shown once: "You will not see this again. Copy it or have them scan it now."

Admins still need to edit automations, so they see more than everyone else. Nobody sees the secrets themselves. Viewer and Operator Admin Join password, cloud keys, link codes Nothing A marker that one is saved HTTP header values, webhook paths Hidden A marker that one is saved Web addresses in HTTP actions Cut back to the host name The whole address Request bodies Hidden Shown, so they can be edited Shell commands Hidden Shown, so they can be edited Learned voices Never sent Never sent In the Activity log and in alerts, people who are not admins see a webhook's trigger as just "webhook", without its path. The path is a credential: whoever has it can fire that automation. An exported show file is hidden the same way, for admins too. See Show files.
documents.s: What each role can see of your settings

documents.t: On the host computer, in its data folder: The password is stored as a hash, not as the password. Cloud keys and link codes are stored in the show file there, show.earshot.json. The folder and those files are readable only by your user account (on macOS and Linux). So the secrets are protected from browsers and from the network, not from someone who can sit down at the host computer and read your files. See Data and files and Privacy. Logs never contain a secret, and never contain what was said.

The production's cloud account issues a new key every tour leg. Open Setup, Cloud & audio. The badge under Deepgram API key reads Key saved. The box, Replace the Deepgram key, is empty. That is normal. Paste the new key and press Save key. "Key saved." The old key is gone from this computer. There was never a way to read it here. If the status then reads Key rejected, the new key is wrong. Paste it again and save.

The production manager opens Earshot on her own laptop with the Admin: address from earshotd, to tidy up an automation that posts to the video server with an Authorization header. She can read and edit the web address and the body. The header's value shows as dots and "(unchanged)". She saves her edit without touching it, and the stored value is kept. If she needs to change the value, she presses Replace and types the new one. She still cannot see the old one.
documents.s: Example: an admin on a second laptop

documents.t: On a real host, an admin's view of the settings showed a stored key as "••••". Saving settings with the marker in place kept the real key on disk, and the marker itself was stored nowhere.
Cloud and audio Showing another Earshot computer's channels Show files: what must be typed in again after an import. Privacy

When an admin opens Earshot on a show with no channels, the Set up Earshot box opens by itself. It takes a few minutes and gets you from nothing to a transcript: install a speech model, then choose the inputs to listen to. Who sees it The desktop app gives you admin access automatically. See Get started with Earshot for the complete path from installation to your first transcript. You can reopen the box any time from Setup, button First-time setup… at the bottom of the section list. It has four steps: Welcome, Models, Inputs, Done. Every step can be skipped and redone later under Setup. Skip setup closes the box at any point.

The mock host with an empty show. Not a real show. The box says what Earshot is about to do: "Earshot listens to your intercom and talkback inputs, turns speech into text on this machine, and shows every channel on one screen that the whole crew can open." Press Get started.

Earshot does not come with its speech models. You download them once, then they work offline. The mock host. Its list of models is invented: the real names and sizes are on the Speech models page. Press Install all recommended, or press the download button beside each model you want. Wait for each row to show Installed. The big one is about 487 MB. Press Next. You need internet for this. If you are not on a connection you trust to finish a 500 MB download, press Next and do it later under Setup, Models. Until a speech model is installed, channels cannot transcribe.

This step is the Patch screen inside the box. The mock host and its made-up audio devices. Under Audio device, choose your interface. Tick the inputs that carry comms. Each tick becomes one channel. Type a prefix under Name channels if you want one. The input number is added, for example "USB 1". Press Create (the button reads "Create 4 channels" and so on). Press Next. If you made no channels, the button reads Skip for now. You can rename the channels and give them colours afterwards. Do not spend time on it here.

The last step reads You are ready, and says how many channels are set up, or "No channels yet. You can add them any time under Setup." It also reminds you of the one thing that most often goes wrong: "The first time a channel starts, your operating system may ask for permission to use the microphone. Choose Allow, or Earshot will hear silence." Press Go to the Feed.

The header says Live. In the channel list, each channel's level meter moves when someone speaks on it. Say a test line on each channel and read it in the Feed. If no text appears, go to Troubleshooting. It lists the checks in order.

The box covers the minimum. For a real show, work down this list. Each line is a section of Setup. Order Setup section What to do there Page 1 Models Download the recommended models. Pick the Default speech model. Speech models 2 Patch Choose the audio device and tick inputs. Patch inputs and make channels 3 Channels Rename, colour and tune each channel. Channels 4 Groups Put channels in folders such as Stage and Audio. Groups 5 Access Decide who can connect. Do this before the crew arrive. Who can connect 6 Glossary Add the names, songs and gear the recogniser gets wrong. Glossary 7 People Optional. Name detected voices on a shared channel, or learn one deliberately. People and voices 8 Cloud & audio Optional. Saved-audio limits, translation, cloud speech. Cloud and audio 9 Show control Only if a console or controller will talk to Earshot. Consoles and controllers 10 Show file Name the show. Export a copy when you are happy with it. Show files Then build your automations, if you use them, and run the before-show checklist. Setup in the mock show. The sections are listed down the left.
documents.s: The rest of the setup, in a sensible order

documents.t: Get started with Earshot, from installation to a working transcript. Limits and known behaviour

A group is a named folder of channels, like Stage or Audio. Groups make a long channel list readable, and they let people show a whole department with one press. The Feed and Lanes can filter by group, and an automation can listen to a group instead of naming every channel. Who can do this Admins make and edit groups. Everyone sees them.

A group is a static folder. It changes only when an admin edits it under Setup, Groups. Choosing a channel on the Feed never changes a group. Filtering is a choice on your own screen. A channel can be in more than one group, or in none. Deleting a group does not delete its channels.
documents.s: What a group is, and is not

documents.t: The mock show's three groups. Not a real show. Open Setup, then Groups, and press Add. Under Name and colour, type a Name and pick a Colour. Tick the channels that belong in it. Find a channel narrows a long list. Under Order in the group, use the arrows to put the channels in the order you want them listed. Switch on Pinned if this group should be listed first: "Pinned groups are listed first in the channel rail." Press Create group. The mock show's Stage group. Its four channels are listed in the order they appear in the Feed's channel list. To change a group later, pick it in the list, edit it, and press Save changes. Revert drops changes you have not saved. The arrows beside a group in the list move the group itself up and down.

The mock show in this manual's pictures has eight channels in three groups: Group Pinned Channels Stage Yes Show Caller, Stage Manager, Deck Left, Deck Right Audio No FOH Audio, Monitors Lighting & Video No Lighting, Video Stage is pinned because it is the one everybody watches. On the Feed, a sound operator presses Audio in the channel list and sees only FOH Audio and Monitors. The stage manager's screen is unaffected. The mock show's Feed after pressing the Stage group: "4 of 8 channels".

Place What a group does there Feed Press a group's name in the channel list to pick all its channels. Lanes By group shows one column per group. Automations Where to listen can name groups, and a condition can check "Channel is in a group".

Press the bin beside the group and confirm with Delete group. "The group is removed. Its channels are kept." If automations listen to that group, Earshot tells you which, under "Used by automations:", and warns that "They will still point at a group that no longer exists." Open each one and choose another group or channel, or the automation will not hear what you expect.
Decide who can connect before the crew arrive. Learn the views: Reading the transcript.

Install Earshot on the host computer connected to your audio inputs. Crew members use a browser on the same network. They do not need a copy of the desktop app, a repository checkout or developer tools.

Open Earshot Releases and choose a release. Read its release notes for supported systems, known issues and any upgrade instructions, then download a package from Assets that matches your operating system and processor. GitHub's Source code archives contain only the downloads repository's files; they are not installers or the application source. Release downloads are available for macOS Apple Silicon, Windows x64 and Linux x86_64. Check each release’s asset list: a new version may appear for one system before the others. The installers are unsigned and the macOS app is not notarised. Each platform’s headless host has passed a demo startup smoke test; Windows and Linux installer interfaces and desktop windows have not been tested. There is no Intel Mac package. v0.5.0 is macOS Apple Silicon only. Windows and Linux builds are on hold; their earlier packages remain on the release pages.

Use only a package listed for your system in that release's notes. Package Installation macOS .dmg Open the disk image, drag Earshot to Applications, then eject the disk image. Open Earshot from Applications. The published Mac package is for Apple Silicon only. Windows installer (.msi or .exe) Run the installer and follow its prompts, then open Earshot from the Start menu. Linux .deb or .rpm Install with your system's package manager, then open Earshot from the application menu. Linux .AppImage Give the downloaded file permission to run as a program, then open it. Follow the release notes for any runtime dependencies. The current macOS bundle configuration requires macOS 11 or newer. The release notes should confirm the requirements for each published build. Unsigned builds may prompt an operating system warning on first launch. Check that the download came from the Earshot repository before choosing to open it.

Open Earshot. Its window signs you in as an admin automatically. Allow microphone access when the operating system asks. If you previously denied it, enable Earshot in the system's microphone privacy settings. In the first-time setup, install the recommended Silero VAD and Parakeet TDT models (about 488 MB together). Internet is needed for this download; speech recognition then works offline. Choose audio inputs and create channels under Setup → Patch. Say a test line and check the transcript. Keep the show Safe while setting up automations. Under Setup → Access, choose who may connect and give the crew Address for the crew. Keep the host awake and connected to the show network. Continue with Get started with Earshot for the complete walkthrough. Earshot starts in Open access mode, where anyone on the network can operate the show, including arming it. Set access before using a shared network. The desktop app normally listens on port 4780 and chooses another port if that one is busy. On macOS and Windows, closing the window leaves Earshot running; use Quit from the tray or menu bar icon to stop it.

Earshot checks GitHub Releases shortly after launch and every six hours. To check yourself, choose Check for Updates… from the tray icon's context menu, or the Earshot menu on macOS. When an update is available: Update now downloads and verifies it, stops transcription, installs it and restarts Earshot. Transcription keeps running during the download. Choose a quiet time to install. Not now postpones reminders for this version until you next open Earshot. Don't remind me for this update skips automatic reminders for that version. A newer version can still prompt you, and Check for Updates… still shows the skipped version. In-app installation works on macOS, Windows and Linux AppImage installations. Linux DEB/RPM installations use the package manager. Older Earshot versions without Check for Updates… need one manual update to a version that includes it. You can also update manually: Read the new release's notes for compatibility and migration instructions. Export your show from Earshot. For a complete backup, quit Earshot and copy its data folder as well: a show export does not include history, saved audio, secrets or learned voices. See Privacy and stored data. Download the new package from Releases, quit the running app, and replace or update it using the same installation method. Open Earshot, check your channels and model status, and test your setup while Safe before returning to a show. Do not delete the data folder to update the app. Models and show data are stored separately from the application. Follow release-specific instructions before using an older version with newer data.
For rack computers managed by an administrator, see the headless host reference. The desktop app is the setup path for this guide.

Quit Earshot, then remove the application using your operating system's usual method. The separate data folder contains transcripts, show settings, downloaded models and any saved audio; removing the application does not clear it. See Privacy before deleting data you may need.

Earshot does not come with its models. You download them once under Setup, Models, and after that they work with no internet. This page says which ones you need and what the others are for. Who can do this Admins only. Downloading needs internet on the host computer.

Open Setup, then Models. (In the first-time setup this is step 2.) Press Download next to each model marked Recommended. Wait. The row shows the download's progress, then "Verifying the download…", then the Installed badge. Each download is checked against a checksum before it is used. If a download fails, the row says "Download failed:" with the reason and offers Retry. Do it before you get to the venue You need internet for these downloads, and the speech model is about 487 MB. There is no screen for importing a model from a folder or a USB stick in this build. Download once, on a good connection, on the computer that will run the show. Until a speech model is installed the page says "No speech model is installed. Channels cannot transcribe until you download one." The mock host's Models screen. Its list is invented and does not match a real host: use the table below for the real names and sizes.

The list is in four parts. Part Model Size What it does Do you need it? Voice activity Silero VAD about 0.6 MB Finds speech in the audio. "Install this first." Yes. Recommended. Speech to text Parakeet TDT 0.6b v3 about 487 MB Turns speech into words. English and 24 other European languages. It detects the language itself. Yes. Recommended. Speech to text Moonshine tiny · English about 30 MB Optional faster English drafts; the main model can still produce finished lines. Choose it in the channel’s Draft speech model field. Draft text may change and accuracy is not guaranteed. Optional. Not selected automatically. Speech to text Whisper small about 375 MB An alternative speech model. No. It is marked experimental and has never been run. Leave it alone. Voice recognition Voice recognition (CAM++) about 29 MB Lets Earshot show who is talking when several people share a channel. Only for People and voices. Not marked Recommended. Overlapping voices MossFormer2 (experimental) about 245 MB Separates two simultaneous voices locally before transcription. Can be slower than the audio itself. Only to try experimental overlapping voices. Off by default. Translation Pairs such as "English to Spanish" about 80 to 240 MB each Translates lines for people who read in another language. Only if someone will read in another language. A typical English-language show needs the first two and nothing else: about 488 MB.

Each pair reads one way. "English to Spanish" does not translate Spanish to English. German to English and English to Spanish have been run. German to Spanish works by way of English if both are installed. The other pairs in the list are untested downloads. Their descriptions start with "Untested." Each loaded pair uses about 330 MB of memory while it is in use. Read Read in another language before you download any. Translation is a reading aid, never a cue call.
The voice recognition model's checksum was pinned from the first download, because no published digest exists for it. The other models are checked against published checksums.

At the top of the screen, Default speech model sets the model that channels use unless they pick their own ("Used by channels that do not choose their own."). With only Parakeet installed, choose it here. A single channel can use a different engine or model. That is set on the channel: Setup, Channels, the channel, Engine and Speech model. See Channels. The screen also shows how much disk the installed models use.

Press the bin beside an installed model, then confirm. If it is the default speech model, Earshot warns you first: "This is the default speech model, so channels that use the default will stop transcribing until you choose another."

In the models folder inside Earshot's data folder. On a Mac that is ~/Library/Application Support/Earshot/models. You can put them somewhere else with --models-dir or the EARSHOT_MODELS environment variable. See Where data and models live. Models come from GitHub, and from Hugging Face for Whisper small and the translation pairs. Nothing is downloaded until you press Download. See Privacy.

You see What to do "No speech model is installed. Channels cannot transcribe until you download one." Download Parakeet TDT 0.6b v3 and Silero VAD. "Could not load the model list." The page cannot reach the host. Check the header says Live, then press Try again. "Download failed: …" on a row Check the host's internet, then press Retry on that row. Channels show text, but slowly That is speed, not the model. See the Behind badge in Status and badges.
Patch inputs and make channels.

A channel in Earshot is one stream of comms: a party line, a talkback, a radio. The Patch screen turns the inputs of an audio interface into channels, many at a time. This is the fastest way to set up a show. Who can do this Admins only. Operators and viewers see "Setup needs admin access".

Plug the audio interface in and check the operating system can see it. Know which input carries which comms channel. Earshot numbers inputs from 1, the same as the interface. Download the speech models first, or the channels you make will have nothing to transcribe with. See Speech models.

Open Setup, then Patch. Under Audio device, choose the interface. Earshot opens each device once, however many inputs you use. Tick the inputs to listen to. Each tick becomes one channel. Tick this page ticks a whole page of inputs at once, and Clear ticks unticks them. Under Name channels, type a prefix if you want one. The input number is added, for example "USB 1". Press Create. The button says how many: "Create 4 channels". The mock host's Patch screen, with a made-up two-input device. Under the device, Earshot shows what it found: the number of inputs, the sample rate and the audio system, and the instruction "Tick the inputs you want as channels. Inputs that already have a channel are ticked and named; untick one to delete its channel." A patched input shows its channel's name and a live level meter. Speak on that line and watch the meter move. If it does not, the input number is wrong, the device is not delivering audio, or the operating system has not given Earshot permission to use the microphone.

You have a four-input USB interface. Inputs 1 to 3 carry the stage manager's party line, the audio party line and the lighting party line. Input 4 is not connected. Setup, Patch. Choose the interface under Audio device. Tick inputs 1, 2 and 3. Leave 4. In Name channels, type Comms. Press Create 3 channels. You now have three channels called "Comms 1", "Comms 2" and "Comms 3". Open Setup, Channels, and rename them "Stage Manager", "Audio" and "Lighting", and give each a colour. The Feed shows the new names at once, on every device.

Inputs are shown 32 to a page. Next inputs and Previous inputs move between pages. Tick this page only ticks the page you are looking at, so work a page at a time. Many-input hardware is untested Dante, MADI and other many-input hardware has not been tried with Earshot. Neither has unplugging a USB interface in the middle of a show. Try your own hardware, at full channel count, before you rely on it.

Press Rescan devices after plugging it in. If the screen says "No audio input devices were found. Plug one in, then rescan. You can also add simulator or text-only channels under Channels.", the operating system is not offering any input to Earshot. Check the system's sound settings and microphone permission.
documents.s: If the device is not in the list

documents.t: Untick a patched input. Earshot asks first ("Delete name?") and spells out what goes: "name will be removed from the show, with its settings. This cannot be undone." The same box lists the groups the channel is in ("It is removed from that group.") and any automations that use it ("It will still point at a channel that no longer exists."). Fix those automations afterwards, or they will not hear what you expect.

Patch makes channels with sensible defaults. Open Setup, Channels, and pick a channel to change: its name, colour and short name; its language, or leave it on "Detect automatically"; whether to show words as they are spoken (drafts); Gain and the High-pass filter (100 Hz) for a quiet or rumbly input; whether people can type into it, and whether to keep audio for replay. Every setting is explained in Channels.

Patch is only for audio inputs. Two other kinds of channel are made under Setup, Channels, Add: Source type What it is for Simulator (WAV file) Plays a recording as if it were live. Good for rehearsing automations without the crew. Typed text only No audio. People type lines into it. Useful as a notes channel. A third kind comes from another Earshot computer: see Showing another Earshot computer's channels.
documents.s: Channels that are not audio inputs

documents.t: Every channel in the list shows a meter that moves when someone speaks, and no No input, Offline or Error badge. Status and badges explains each one. A test line on each channel appears in the Feed under the right name.
Groups: put the channels into folders so the crew can filter them.

Start here if you are setting up Earshot for the first time. You will install the app on one computer, turn speech into a transcript, and open that transcript on a crew member's phone. Everything is done through the app and your computer's usual installation screens.

Have these ready: The computer that will run Earshot, connected to power. This is the host; keep it awake while Earshot is listening. An audio input. Your computer's built-in microphone is enough to try Earshot. For a show, connect the audio interface carrying your comms inputs. Internet access to download Earshot and its recommended speech models (about 488 MB). Once installed, local speech recognition works offline. A shared network if you want the crew to read along on other devices. Check supported systems and known limits before choosing a show computer. Earshot has been tested on Apple Silicon Macs. Windows and Linux builds passed a headless demo startup smoke test, but their installer interfaces and desktop windows have not been tested.

Open Earshot Releases. Choose the package for your computer under Assets, rather than a Source code archive. Install it using your computer's usual installer. On a Mac, open the disk image and drag Earshot to Applications. Open Earshot from Applications, the Start menu or your application launcher. See Install and update for package availability and installation details. Downloads are available for macOS Apple Silicon, Windows x64 and Linux x86_64. Check the chosen release’s notes for the packages it includes. The Earshot window gives you admin access automatically. You can set up the host right there.

On a new show, Set up Earshot opens automatically. Press Get started. If you have already closed it, open Setup and press First-time setup… at the bottom of the section list. Screenshots show a sample show. Your devices and channels will have their own names. The assistant has four steps: Welcome, Models, Inputs and Done. Follow them in order for your first setup.

In Models, press Install all recommended. Wait until Silero VAD and Parakeet TDT both show Installed, then press Next. The sample screen illustrates the download controls. Use the models marked Recommended in your app. These downloads happen once. They let Earshot recognise speech on this computer, without choosing a cloud service. Optional translation and voice-recognition models can wait. If a download fails, check the internet connection and retry it under Setup → Models. See Speech models for more help.

In Inputs: Choose your microphone or audio interface under Audio device. Tick the input you want to try. For a built-in microphone, start with input 1. For an interface, use the input carrying your test microphone or comms line. Under Name channels, enter a name such as Test or Comms. Press Create. The button includes the number of channels you selected. Allow microphone access if your computer asks. Earshot needs this permission for audio interfaces as well as microphones. Press Next, then Go to the Feed. The sample screen shows a two-input device. Tick only the inputs you intend to listen to. If your interface is missing, check that it is connected and press Rescan devices. You can add more inputs later under Setup → Patch; see Patch inputs.

Check that the header says Live and Safe. Speak a short sentence into the chosen microphone or comms input, then pause. Watch the channel's level meter. It should move while you speak. Read the line in the Feed. Draft words may change before the line settles. You now have a working local transcript. Speech recognition can make mistakes, so try the names and phrases your crew uses before a show. If the meter does not move, check the input and your computer's microphone permission. If the meter moves but no words appear, check that both recommended models show Installed under Setup → Models. Troubleshooting covers the next checks. Open Setup → Channels to give the channel a useful name and colour. Add your remaining comms inputs under Setup → Patch, and test each one in the same way.

Before sharing, open Setup → Access and choose who can connect. Earshot starts in Open mode, where anyone on the network can operate the show, including arming it. Choose Password or Personal links to control access; personal links let you give someone a read-only Viewer role. Connect the crew member's phone or laptop to the same network as the host. Give them Address for the crew from Setup → Access, together with the password or personal link your chosen mode requires. Open it in their browser and sign in if prompted. Say another test sentence and check it appears on both devices. The crew does not need to install the desktop app. Keep Earshot running on the host while they read. See Who can connect for access modes and Earshot on a phone for phone setup.

Use Feed for one combined timeline, Lanes for channel columns, or Focus for a large view of one channel. Open Display on this device from the header to choose a theme and text size. Each crew member can choose their own display settings. Under Setup → Show file, name the show and export a copy of its settings. See Show files. Your normal show and transcript are saved on the host. Closing the desktop window on macOS or Windows leaves Earshot running. To stop listening, choose Quit from its tray or menu bar icon, or press Cmd+Q on a Mac. Open the app normally next time to continue using your saved setup.
documents.s: 7. Read comfortably and save your setup

documents.t: You have completed the basic setup when: Every input you need has a moving meter and produces readable text. A crew device can connect using the access mode you chose. The host stays awake and the header shows Live and Safe. Work through the before-show checklist before using Earshot in production. Limits and known behaviour explains what has been tested. Automations are optional. When you are ready to explore them, start with Safe and Armed, then Build an automation and Test it.

Read this before you trust Earshot on a show. Earshot is work in progress. It runs and is tested on one Apple Silicon Mac. This page says what has been measured, what has been tried end to end, what has never been tried, and where the known gaps are. Nothing here is softened. The short version Speech recognition makes mistakes. Treat a phrase automation as a convenience beside your normal cue calling, not instead of it. It has not been tried with a real microphone on real comms, a real console, a phone, Windows or Linux desktop windows, two computers on a real network, or in a real venue. Cloud speech has never been run against the real Deepgram service. Safe stops what Earshot would send next. It cannot recall what has already left the computer.

These are planned. They are either not built, or built but not usable from the app. Do not rely on any of them. Feature What you will see "Play a sound" and "Show or hide the window" actions You can add them, but they do not run. The automation shows a problem saying so. The other actions in the same automation still run. A signed installer Unsigned downloads are published for macOS Apple Silicon, Windows x64 and Linux x86_64. The Mac app is signed ad hoc only, not with an Apple Developer ID, and is not notarised. The headless host passed a demo startup smoke test on each system. Windows and Linux installer interfaces and desktop windows have not been tested. There is no Intel Mac installer. Turning on https for Earshot's own address Earshot serves plain http. There is no setting to give it a certificate. Encrypted links between Earshot computers The link screen offers "Encrypted (https)", but it has not been proven end to end in this build, and it needs a certificate this computer trusts. Treat links as not encrypted. Choosing the network interface or web port There is no Setup screen for them. The headless program (earshotd) takes --bind and --port. See earshotd. Importing a speech model from a folder (for a venue with no internet) There is no screen for it. Download the model once while you have internet. See Models.

Measured on one Apple M3 Pro (12 logical CPUs), with the release build, nothing else running. Test recordings played on every channel at the same time, continuously, for 60 seconds. That is far denser than real intercom traffic. "First words" is measured from when the speaker starts. "Final line" is measured from when the speaker stops. Channels First words: typical / slowest 5% Final line: typical / slowest 5% Channels that fell Behind 4 0.46 s / 1.49 s 1.00 s / 1.38 s none 8 0.51 s / 1.73 s 1.24 s / 1.61 s none 16 0.74 s / 2.37 s 1.35 s / 2.00 s 5 of 16, for a while At 16 channels all 224 final lines were transcribed, none lost. About 1.5 to 1.6 GB of memory was in use. One Spotlight indexing job was using about one core at the time. The goals were first words under 0.7 s and a final line under 1.5 s. Typical times meet them at 4 and 8 channels. At 16 channels the typical first words (0.74 s) just miss. The slowest 5% miss the first-words goal everywhere, and miss the final-line goal at 8 and 16 channels. Other computers have not been measured. Intel Macs, Windows and Linux machines may be slower. What Behind means, and what to do about it, is in Reading the transcript and Troubleshooting.

The finished host was run start to finish on one Mac with the real models and recorded speech (the fixture recordings) played into four channels, the show Armed, and a local program listening for the OSC packets. 12 of 12 spoken lines were transcribed, each final line 0.83 to 1.39 seconds after the speaker stopped. "Lighting cue 42, go." sent one OSC packet to the lighting address with the number 42. "Sound cue 7, go." sent one to the QLab address with 7. The two "Standby …" lines sent nothing. Exactly two packets went out. The glossary changed "click ladder" to "click louder" in the stored text and kept what was heard. "Q42" became "cue 42". Clips were saved on the two channels that had them switched on, and the replay address returned a sound file. A line on a channel with clips off had none. 14 translations, none failed: German to English, English to Spanish, and German to Spanish by way of English.
documents.s: One full run of the cue path

documents.t: With the real models and three looping recorded channels: Two voices were learned through the real screen (about 36 seconds each, 16 to 17 seconds of speech). No voiceprint went to the browser. At Balanced, each channel carrying one voice named every line correctly. On a channel mixing five lines from three voices, the two learned voices were named correctly (13 named lines, none wrong) and the third, never learned, got no name in the first run. An admin's view of the settings showed a stored key as "••••". Saving settings with the marker kept the real key on disk and stored the marker nowhere. A bug was found and fixed during this check: in Lanes, the time and name floated beside the text and squeezed it to a sliver. They now sit on their own row. A people-limited automation was tried as described in Automations limited to people.
documents.s: Voices and secrets, on the real host

documents.t: Two hosts were run on one Mac and linked through the real screen. See Showing another Earshot computer's channels.

A real microphone. Comms-quality audio. All the recorded voices are clean, computer-made speech. The voice settings were tuned on them. A real console, and MIDI, web requests and TCP OSC against real gear. They have been tried only in automated tests against stand-ins on one Mac. Phones and tablets. The join page, install, and small screens have not been tried on real devices. Cloud speech with a real key. Windows and Linux. Two separate computers on a real network, including finding each other (Bonjour) between machines, and a link code on a host that requires one. https, for linking. The desktop app running (its tray, pop-outs and the default port) has not been tried by hand. About the pictures in this manual The screenshots in this manual come from the web app's built-in mock show, or from a demo host playing a scripted transcript. They show the real screens with made-up lines. None of them is a real show.

Accuracy in a loud venue is unverified. It has been tried only on synthetic voices and a built-in microphone. The recogniser still makes mistakes on clean recordings: it dropped "du" from "Kannst du bitte…" and "I" from "I need the click…". Treat every cue as something to confirm. The first word can be clipped when an input opens mid-sentence. Earshot keeps 0.3 seconds of audio from before speech starts. That covers live inputs that were already open. It does not cover the first words after an input is (re)connected while someone is already talking. Languages. Parakeet covers English and 24 other European languages. Whisper small is experimental and has never been run. Voice recognition has only been measured on computer-made voices. Several of them share a speech engine and so sound more alike than most people do. Real people on a real noisy party line may do better or worse. The default, Balanced, was kept on the condition that this manual says so plainly, and it may need changing after the first recording of a real party line. See People.

A reading aid, never a cue call. Automations never see a translation. Show jargon is often mistranslated. In the test, "Sound cue 7, go." came out in Spanish as "Suena a señal 7, vamos." and "kick drum" as "tambor de patada". German to English and English to Spanish (and German to Spanish by way of English) have been run. The other pairs in the Models list are untested downloads, and their descriptions start with "Untested." A viewer can pick a language that few lines can reach. The lines that cannot be translated stay in the original, and the host counts them as failed. Translation models were built and run on the Apple Silicon Mac only. See Read in another language.

Cloud speech has never been run against the real Deepgram service. It has been tested against a stand-in server only, and some details of how Deepgram answers are unverified. Before you rely on it, try one channel with a real key. Whether the model-improvement opt-out that Earshot sends by default changes Deepgram's price is also unconfirmed. See Cloud & audio.

Tested: one Apple Silicon Mac, the built-in microphone, and played-back recordings (the simulator). Windows and Linux builds are untested. The desktop app has only been built, unsigned, on macOS. The network socket settings that make Safe discard unsent OSC data are proven on macOS only. Stopping a shell command's child programs when you press Safe is untested on Windows. Dante, MADI and other many-input hardware is untested, as is unplugging a USB interface mid-show. The tray (menu bar) menu, its Armed tick box, pop-out windows and Keep on top have not been tried by hand. The tray's Armed tick arms with one click, without the hold the window requires. Do not use it as your normal way to arm. Replay was checked against the real host, but nobody has yet confirmed that it is audible on a phone or tablet speaker. Earshot is a program on a computer. If the computer sleeps, Earshot stops listening.

Safe cannot recall what has already left the computer. See Safe and Armed. The Armed-from-the-start rule has small edges. Earshot notices the start of speech about 30 milliseconds late, so a cue word that begins that close before you press Arm can still count as armed. The other way round, right after a channel's audio starts, is paused, changes device or has a gap, a cue that begins within about a third of a second after you press Arm can be treated as "heard before the show was armed". Arm first, then speak. Run now and web hooks are tied to Armed or Safe when the engine receives them, a moment (normally under a thousandth of a second) after the request arrives. A Run now pressed as a test in Safe at the very instant someone else arms could really send. Pressing Safe twice. In a very rare tie between two Arm or Safe commands arriving at the same instant, a Safe can be answered with "conflict". The screen then shows the show's real state; press Safe again. A line whose beginning Earshot did not catch (it was restarting that channel) never fires. Activity says "the start of this line was missed". A MIDI send that waits too long is dropped ("not sent: the MIDI port was busy for more than 1 s"), so a MIDI cue is on time or it does not go. Someone on the network who can forge sender addresses can get a real console's trigger messages rate-limited. They cannot stop its Safe. A firing that Earshot refuses (for example because of the runaway limits) still uses up that automation's cooldown. A MIDI feedback loop is limited only to about ten firings a second, until you make the show Safe. See MIDI. The glossary changes finished lines only. Draft text on screen is as heard. Cloud speech does not record, per line, which engine produced it. A linked channel does not say when its last line arrived, and a computer can call itself anything (so the address is shown beside the name). The first link after this computer restarts has no gap notice. Names can be missing while CAM++ is loading, the voice recognition queue is full, or the audio is too short or unclear. Transcription falling behind does not switch off background voice naming.
documents.s: Known gaps in the show-control path

documents.t: Earshot starts in Open mode. Anyone on the network can view and operate the show, including arming it. Change this before you put Earshot on a network you do not control. See Who can connect. Everything travels as plain http. Passwords, link codes and transcripts are readable by anyone who can listen on the network. OSC has no sign-in. OSC input is off by default. Read OSC input before you turn it on. Arming by OSC works only over TCP. Shell-command actions are off unless an admin turns them on. See Consoles and controllers.

Automatic discovery and consecutive-turn detection have been tested with synthetic voices only. Similar voices, noise and short replies can be misidentified or left unnamed. Detected profiles can be renamed without another reading passage; controlled learning remains available. Two-speaker overlap separation is experimental and off by default. The development M3 Pro took about 8.6 seconds to separate four seconds of synthetic audio; it is not yet real time. Quiet speech can be omitted, and isolated outputs may contain artifacts or incorrect words. More than two simultaneous speakers are not supported. Normal transcription continues while the model prepares or is occupied. This release provides a macOS Apple Silicon package only. Windows and Linux builds are on hold.
documents.s: Automatic discovery and overlapping voices in v0.5.0

documents.t: Earshot writes down what people say on comms. This page says what is kept, where, who can read it, and what leaves the computer. The short version. Everything is kept on the host computer, in one folder. Speech is recognised on that computer. If you never choose a cloud option, no audio and no text goes to any company.

Earshot keeps everything on the host computer, in one folder: System Folder macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Earshot Windows and Linux The operating system's data folder, in a folder called Earshot. (Not tested on those systems.) Any The folder you name with the environment variable EARSHOT_DATA_DIR (or --data-dir for earshotd). In that folder What it holds earshot.db The transcripts of every session, markers, and personal link records. For a line changed by the glossary or by number tidying, it holds both the changed text and what was heard. show.earshot.json (and a .bak) The show: channels, groups, automations, glossary, people, settings. The password is stored as a hash. Cloud keys and the link codes of linked channels are stored here too. People's learned voices are stored here as well. None of these is ever sent to a browser, and none is in an export. models/ The downloaded speech and translation models. clips/ Saved audio, for channels with Keep audio for replay on. More about each file, and how to back the folder up, is in Data and files.

The folder is private to your user account. A folder Earshot creates can be opened only by you, and the show file, its backup and the database are readable only by you. (On macOS and Linux. A folder that already existed keeps the permissions it had; the files inside are still made private.) Logs never contain what was said, or any secret. Lines sent for translation are logged by length only. Earshot does not use a proxy for speech, translation or automation web requests, even if this computer has one set in its environment. Only model downloads use it.

Audio is not saved unless you ask. Earshot turns audio into text and does not keep the audio. The exception is a channel with Keep audio for replay switched on. It saves the audio behind each spoken line on the host, in clips/. Typed lines have none. Anyone who can read that channel can replay it. See Replay a line's audio. Saved audio is limited. Under Setup, Cloud & audio, Keep for (days) and At most (MB) set the limits (0 means no limit). Clips older than the limit are deleted. If the total is over the size limit, the oldest go first. The limits are checked when Earshot starts, every 10 minutes, when you change them, and as clips are added. Clearing a transcript makes its audio unreachable at once. The files are deleted as well. A clip that finishes being written after its line was cleared is deleted and never announced. Live audio never goes to a phone, tablet or another computer. Only text does. The one thing a browser can fetch is the saved clip behind a single line, on a channel where you switched that on.

Who can read the transcript. Anyone who can connect. In Open mode that is everyone on the network. Roles control who can do things, but any role can read. See Who can connect and Roles. Who can see what was heard. The original text of a changed line goes to Operators and Admins only. In an Open show, and with the shared password, everyone is an Operator, so everyone sees it. Only personal-link Viewers do not. (On a channel with "Filter profanity" on, the original is never shown, because it would show the words the filter hid.) Learned voices identify people. They stay on the host, are never sent to any browser, and are never in an export. Names on lines go to every role. See People. What others see of your settings. Nobody, including an admin, is sent a saved cloud key, link code or password. Viewers and operators also get web header values, webhook paths and shell command text hidden, and web addresses cut back to the host name. Exports are hidden the same way. See Saved secrets. warning Earshot starts in Open mode, and serves plain http. On a network you do not control, anyone on it can read the transcript, and anyone listening on it can read what travels. Choose Password or Personal links before the show. See Who can connect.

What When The transcript, to the browsers of the people connected Whenever someone has Earshot open. It goes to devices on your network that connected to the host. Speech and translation model downloads (GitHub; Hugging Face for Whisper small and the translation models) When you press Download. The messages your automations send (OSC, MIDI, web requests, shell commands) While the show is Armed. Bonjour announcements If Announce on the network (Bonjour) is on. It is on by default. Lines from a linked channel, and its link code Between the two Earshot computers, while a link is on. With Not encrypted (http) both travel readable on the network. https links have not been proven. Audio from a channel set to "Deepgram (cloud)", to Deepgram Only for channels you set to cloud speech and confirmed, and only if a key is saved. Words from your glossary travel with it, in the request address. Drafts stay on this computer. Every request also carries Deepgram's model-improvement opt-out. The text of each translated line, to DeepL or Anthropic (Claude) Only if you chose that translator under Cloud & audio and confirmed. Audio is not sent. Nothing else leaves the computer. If you never choose a cloud option, no audio and no text goes to any company.

Cloud speech is per channel. There is no switch that sends every channel out. Each one asks you to confirm. See Cloud & audio. While cloud speech is paused after repeated failures, Earshot sends one short piece of audio about every 30 seconds to test the service. A little audio therefore still leaves while it says Paused. Your glossary travels with cloud speech. On a Deepgram channel, the words in your glossary (which may be crew names) are sent to Deepgram as hints. Cloud speech has never been run against the real Deepgram service. See Limits and known behaviour. A cloud translator sees the text of every line it translates, for every viewer reading in another language.
documents.s: Things worth knowing about the cloud options

documents.t: There is no button for deleting past sessions in this build. To start a fresh history: Stop Earshot. In the data folder, delete earshot.db and the files beside it whose names start earshot.db. Delete the clips folder. Start Earshot again. This also removes the personal links. Everyone who joined with a personal link or an invite will need a new one. Deleting those files does not touch the show (show.earshot.json): your channels, automations, glossary, people and settings stay. To remove lines without stopping Earshot, a transcript can be cleared: by an automation with the action Clear the transcript, or by a console at the Full control level. Clearing deletes the lines of the current session, for one channel or for every channel, and their saved audio with them. Past sessions are not touched.

Everyone on a channel Earshot listens to is being written down, and on a channel with Keep audio for replay on, recorded. Depending on where you work, the law or a union agreement may require you to tell people, or to get their agreement, before you do that. Earshot does not tell them for you.

Earshot's macOS build uses the shared, Core ML-capable sherpa-onnx / ONNX Runtime libraries. The previous static runtime explicitly disabled Core ML. Both dylibs are included in the app's Frameworks directory; development binaries and tests resolve their copies beside the executable. Windows and Linux retain the static speech runtime. Enabling an execution provider does not mean every operator runs on the GPU or Neural Engine. Unsupported operations can remain on CPU. Core ML performance also depends on model shapes and conversion. See ONNX Runtime's Core ML documentation.

Transcription: CPU, with one cached recognizer per model, shared across decode workers. Live decode workers use macOS User Initiated QoS. Keep the existing worker budget for many simultaneous channels; isolated single-line results do not establish the best many-channel setting. VAD: one CPU thread. Its small, frequent windows were faster on CPU in the local probe. Voice recognition: up to four native CPU threads on Apple Silicon, on a supporting-work thread. Automatic discovery reuses the identification embedding. FFT plans, spectral interpolation tables and mel weights are cached across lines; per-frame FFT scratch is reused. An initial coarse turn check avoids dense overlapping windows when the voice strongly agrees throughout. Overlapping speech: native ONNX Runtime on Apple Silicon, with four CPU threads by default. Model preparation happens in the background. Only one separation runs at a time; other lines keep normal transcription while it is preparing or occupied. The portable interpreter remains available on other platforms but is not proven suitable for live use. Translation: the existing Apple Accelerate / Ruy build and INT8 compute remain in place. Translation work and voice identification use supporting-work QoS, while transcription has higher scheduling priority. QoS is restored when a reused blocking-pool thread returns. Translation concurrency stays bounded. Translation speed was not remeasured in this pass. The scheduler and its threads do not pin work to particular cores. macOS chooses cores using these QoS hints. The defaults preserve CPU execution where it won the installed-model measurements. Core ML remains available for component-specific experiments.

Measured on the development Apple M3 Pro, 12 CPU cores (6 performance and 6 efficiency), 18 GB RAM, on 19 November 2026. Each row uses a four-second, 16 kHz mono synthetic recording from fixtures/audio/showcaller.wav. Times are medians of five warmed runs. VAD time covers all 125 windows, not one window. Core ML rows include its CPU fallback operations. Component CPU, 1 thread CPU, 4 threads Core ML, 1 CPU thread Parakeet TDT v3 INT8 258 ms 107 ms 334 ms CAM++ including audio preprocessing 63 ms 24 ms 30 ms Silero VAD, whole four-second clip 8.7 ms 8.9 ms 50 ms Parakeet produced the same text in those three runs. This is a small diagnostic, not a transcript accuracy evaluation or a guarantee for other M-series chips. Initial Core ML model preparation was slower than CPU loading. Early trials performed during compilation were discarded from this table. The standalone four-second CMN diagnostic measured about 5.3 ms after caching and scratch reuse. The spectral-table test checks every cached interpolation value against the original calculation. The real-model turn probe found the known 3 s and 6 s changes exactly in the three-turn synthetic recording. These tests do not establish accuracy with real crew or comms noise. A 16-channel, 20-second simulator run with the real models and the default 8 workers × 1 ONNX thread published 72 speech finals, with no decode failures and no channels Behind. Final-text latency was 839 ms median and 1,238 ms p95; first text appeared after 790 ms median measured from the segment start including pre-roll. Process CPU averaged 700% of one core (58% of the 12-core machine), with about 1.23 GB resident memory. This is a short local fixture run, not venue validation.

Run from the repository root with the installed models directory: cargo run --release -p earshot-speech --example apple_runtime_probe -- /path/to/models cpu 1 cargo run --release -p earshot-speech --example apple_runtime_probe -- /path/to/models cpu 4 cargo run --release -p earshot-speech --example apple_runtime_probe -- /path/to/models coreml 1 EARSHOT_MODELS=/path/to/models cargo test --release -p earshot-speech consecutive_unregistered_fixture_voices_have_turn_boundaries -- --ignored --nocapture cargo test --release -p earshot-speech normalisation_cost -- --ignored --nocapture Run benchmarks separately from builds and other model probes. Use examples/loadtest.rs for channel throughput before changing the default worker plan. The EARSHOT_STT_PROVIDER, EARSHOT_VOICE_PROVIDER, EARSHOT_VAD_PROVIDER, and EARSHOT_SEPARATION_PROVIDER environment variables accept cpu or coreml on Apple Silicon. EARSHOT_ONNX_PROVIDER is the fallback for components without an override. These are development controls; macOS Finder launches do not automatically inherit a terminal's environment. Restart the host after changing a provider. EARSHOT_SEPARATION_THREADS accepts 1–8. An optional EARSHOT_ONNXRUNTIME_LIB points separation at an explicit compatible runtime dylib. The native separation Core ML path uses fixed input shapes and MLProgram format, and caches compiled models beside the installed ONNX file in .coreml-cache. MLProgram requires macOS 12 or newer. The normal CPU path retains the app's macOS 11 requirement. Core ML compilation can consume substantial time and memory; it is experimental and is not the default.

The MossFormer2 model is a pinned 245 MB ONNX conversion of Alibaba's two-speaker model. Its input is a fixed four-second window. Adjacent windows are aligned by their overlap before being blended, since output speaker order can change between windows. Isolated tracks are then split using the channel’s pause policy and sorted by onset, so an A–B–A conversation keeps three turns and text cannot join across long gaps on one voice’s track. Very faint regions relative to that track’s own voice are rejected to reduce cross-speaker bleed; unusually quiet utterances can also be missed. cargo run --release -p earshot-speech --example overlap_probe -- /path/to/models /path/to/mossformer2_ss_16k.onnx /tmp/earshot-overlap-trial The isolated CPU run took 8.6 seconds to separate four seconds of audio, with roughly 1.7 GB maximum resident memory for the full probe (including transcription). A Core ML MLProgram trial loaded in about 80 seconds but did not finish within the 90-second test budget. It remains opt-in. Overlap separation is therefore not yet real time on this Mac; leave it off for normal low-latency operation. This mixes the two repository fixtures at equal RMS, writes the mixture and two isolated WAVs, reports scale-invariant signal-to-distortion improvement, and transcribes all three. One synthetic trial recovered both phrases, with about 22 dB improvement for each source; the mixture produced no transcript in that run. That establishes recovery on this fixture, not real-show reliability. More than two simultaneous speakers, duplicate speech and similar voices remain limitations. Check the isolated runtime and memory results before using separation live.

This page is for developers and people who need a custom build. To install Earshot for use, start with installation and updates. You do not need Rust, Node.js, pnpm or a repository checkout to use a release build.

git clone https://github.com/RVLT-Labs/earshot.git cd earshot To reproduce a release, check out its tag before installing dependencies. The commands below run from the repository root unless stated otherwise.

Rust 1.98.1. rust-toolchain.toml pins it and asks for rustfmt and clippy. With rustup installed, the first cargo command in the repository installs it. Node.js and pnpm. pnpm-lock.yaml is lockfile version 9. The CI workflow selects Node 24 and pnpm 12; local work has also used Node 26. CMake (3.15 or newer) and a C++17 compiler. The translation crate (earshot-translate) builds CTranslate2 from source. The first build takes a few minutes. On macOS that means the Xcode command-line tools and CMake; on Windows, MSVC; on Linux, gcc or clang. Nothing is downloaded for this step. The C++ SentencePiece library is no longer part of normal builds: the tokenizer is written in Rust, and the C++ one is kept only as a dev-dependency for a test that compares the two. (Linking both SentencePiece and sherpa-onnx into one program made the speech model fail to load, so CI checks that sentencepiece-sys stays out of the program.) Network access at build time. The speech crate's dependency, sherpa-onnx, fetches its prebuilt runtime when it builds. macOS uses Core ML-capable shared libraries, which are included in the desktop app bundle. Other platforms retain the static speech runtime. Linux only: ALSA development headers for audio capture, and the packages Tauri 2 needs for the desktop app. See Tauri's prerequisites. The CI workflow lists the packages it installs. Linux has not been built here. The desktop bundle is built for macOS 11 or newer. See Apple Silicon performance for model runtime choices and reproducible probes.
Install the web dependencies once, from the repository root: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

pnpm build:web # builds apps/web/dist For development, run the Vite server, which proxies /api to a host on 127.0.0.1:4780: pnpm dev:web Open the address Vite prints with ?mock=1 on the end (for example http://localhost:5173/?mock=1) to use the built-in mock host and no engine at all. Other mock options are described in apps/web/src/runtime/runtime.ts.

cargo run -p earshotd -- --demo --bind 127.0.0.1 Then open http://localhost:4780/. It plays a scripted transcript. Your own data is not read or written. earshotd serves apps/web/dist if it exists, so build the web app first.
documents.s: The demo (no models, no audio hardware)

documents.t: cargo run -p earshotd --release To build a headless executable without starting it: cargo build --locked -p earshotd --release The executable is target/release/earshotd (earshotd.exe on Windows). It does not embed the web app. Keep a copy of apps/web/dist alongside the executable, for example as a folder named web, and pass its path explicitly when running outside the checkout: ./earshotd --web-dir ./web It prints an Open: address and an Admin: address. Use the Admin address. In the app, open Setup, then Models, and download the models you need. They are downloaded once and checked against a checksum. Model Size Needed for Silero VAD about 0.6 MB Finding speech. Recommended. Parakeet TDT 0.6b v3 about 487 MB Speech to text. Recommended. Voice recognition (CAM++) about 29 MB Names on lines (optional). Its checksum was pinned from the first download; no published digest exists. Whisper small about 375 MB Experimental, never run. Translation pairs (Opus-MT) about 80 to 240 MB each Reading in another language (optional). German to English and English to Spanish have been run. Then choose inputs under Setup, Patch. The user guide walks through it. earshotd options (cargo run -p earshotd -- --help): --port (default 4780), --bind (default 0.0.0.0), --data-dir, --models-dir, --web-dir, --admin-token, --allow-host, --demo. IP addresses, localhost and the computer's own name always work as web addresses. Anyone typing another name (a venue DNS name, a reverse proxy) is refused until you add it with --allow-host NAME (repeat the flag for more). The speech tests that use real models are marked ignored. To fetch the recommended models for them (about 488 MB): EARSHOT_MODELS=$PWD/.models cargo test -p earshot-speech -- --ignored download_recommended.

Build the web app first (the desktop bundle packs apps/web/dist), then: pnpm --filter desktop tauri build The bundle is written to target/release/bundle/ (unless you override Cargo's target directory). The app bundles the built web files as resources and serves them through its local host. A local build is not signed or notarised. To run it in demo mode, set EARSHOT_DEMO=1.

Path What it is crates/earshot-core Shared types, events, commands and the show-file schema. No I/O. crates/earshot-audio Audio devices, capture, resampling, level meters, voice detection, the WAV simulator. crates/earshot-speech Speech engines (sherpa-onnx), the model manager, text post-processing, the glossary library, voice recognition, a Deepgram cloud client with a local fallback. crates/earshot-translate Local translation models (a Rust tokenizer feeding CTranslate2), the optional DeepL and Claude translators, and the translation router. crates/earshot-automation Triggers, matching, number safety, conditions, actions, the Safe gate. crates/earshot-io OSC (UDP and TCP), MIDI and outbound HTTP. crates/earshot-store SQLite history, search, export, the show file, tokens, clip storage. crates/earshot-server The HTTP, WebSocket and SSE API, access control, QR invites, Bonjour, the API reference page, and the web app files. crates/earshot-engine Wires the crates together: state, the audio-to-speech pipeline, the glossary, voice recognition, saved audio, translation, cloud speech, links to other hosts, the automation host, OSC input, demo mode. apps/desktop The Tauri 2 desktop app (src-tauri). apps/headless earshotd, the engine and server with no window. apps/web The React and TypeScript web app. It is the only UI. docs/ user-guide.md, api-contract.md (HTTP and WebSocket), osc.md (OSC addresses), screenshots/, and superpowers/specs/ (the design spec). fixtures/audio Synthetic speech recordings used by the simulator, tests and demos.

Run tests for one crate at a time while you work: cargo test -p earshot-core cargo test -p earshot-audio cargo test -p earshot-speech cargo test -p earshot-translate cargo test -p earshot-automation cargo test -p earshot-io cargo test -p earshot-store cargo test -p earshot-server cargo test -p earshot-engine cargo test -p earshotd cargo test -p earshot-desktop cargo clippy -p earshot-engine --all-targets -- -D warnings # swap in any crate cargo fmt -p earshot-engine --check Or everything: cargo test --workspace. Tests marked #[ignore] need downloaded models (set EARSHOT_MODELS) and are run with -- --ignored. Web app: pnpm -C apps/web test pnpm -C apps/web lint pnpm -C apps/web build The TypeScript types in apps/web/src/api/types/ are generated from the Rust types. Do not edit them. Regenerate with pnpm types.

The Build workflow tests the web app and Rust workspace. Starting it manually also builds unsigned desktop bundles and uploads them as workflow artifacts. These artifacts are temporary CI outputs; the workflow does not publish GitHub Releases or headless packages. Check the workflow run for its actual platform results. Local release builds for Windows and Linux have passed a headless demo startup smoke test. Their installer interfaces and desktop windows have not been tested.

The web app has a mock host built in. It needs only Node.js and pnpm, and it runs entirely in your browser. pnpm install pnpm dev:web Open the address it prints with ?mock=1 on the end, for example http://localhost:5173/?mock=1. The mock plays a different made-up show, "Spring Tour at Harbour Hall". It is the one in this manual's pictures. It already has six sample automations, four people with voices, a glossary and two OSC destinations, so you can look at every screen. It is a stand-in for the engine, not the engine: its model list, its translations and its matching are simplified. Use the demo above when you want to see how Earshot really behaves. A few extras for looking around, added to the address after ?mock=1: Add What you get &fresh=1 An empty show, so the first-time setup opens. &role=viewer or &role=operator The screens as a viewer or an operator sees them. &access=password A host that asks for a password. The mock's password is show-time-1. &access=tokens A host that asks for a personal link or code. &linked=1 Three channels linked from other hosts: one working, one refused, one unreachable. &problems=1 One automation reported as not running.
