Earshot keeps everything on the host computer, in one folder: the data folder. Nothing is kept on the crew's phones and laptops except their own display choices and their sign-in.

System Folder macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Earshot Windows and Linux The operating system's data folder, in a folder called Earshot. (Not tested on those systems.) To put it somewhere else: for the desktop app or earshotd, set the environment variable EARSHOT_DATA_DIR before starting; for earshotd you can pass --data-dir instead. EARSHOT_DATA_DIR=/Volumes/Show/earshot earshotd earshotd --data-dir /Volumes/Show/earshot earshotd writes the folder it is using to its log when it starts ("data directory: …"). See earshotd. Demo mode In demo mode (earshotd --demo, or the desktop app with EARSHOT_DEMO=1), the data folder is not read or written at all. Nothing you do in a demo is kept.

Earshot/ ├── earshot.db transcripts, markers, personal links ├── earshot.db-wal (beside the database while Earshot runs) ├── earshot.db-shm (beside the database while Earshot runs) ├── show.earshot.json the show, and this computer's settings ├── show.earshot.json.bak the show as it was before the last save ├── models/ downloaded speech and translation models └── clips/ saved audio, one file per line Path What it holds earshot.db The transcripts of every session, markers, and personal link records, in one SQLite database. For a line changed by the glossary or by number tidying, it holds both the changed text and what was heard. The files beside it whose names start earshot.db belong to it. show.earshot.json The show: channels, groups, automations, OSC destinations, glossary, people. And this computer's settings: who can connect, OSC and MIDI input, cloud options, saved-audio limits. The password is stored as a hash. Cloud keys and the link codes of linked channels are stored here. People's learned voices are stored here as well. show.earshot.json.bak The show file as it was before the most recent save. Each save writes a new file, then swaps it in, and keeps the previous one as this backup. models/ The downloaded speech and translation models, one folder per model. Set EARSHOT_MODELS, or pass --models-dir to earshotd, to keep them somewhere else. clips/ Saved audio, for channels with Keep audio for replay on: one WAV file per spoken line.

What Size Silero VAD About 0.6 MB Parakeet TDT 0.6b v3 About 487 MB Voice recognition (CAM++) About 29 MB Each translation pair About 80 to 240 MB Saved audio Up to the limit under Setup, Cloud & audio, At most (MB). It starts at 2048 MB, and clips are kept for 14 days. 0 means no limit. Transcripts Text only. Small beside everything else. See Models and Replay a line's audio.

There are two things called a show file. They are not the same. show.earshot.json in the data folder The file from Export show file What it is for Earshot's own working copy Carrying a show to another computer The password, cloud keys, link codes Stored in it Not in it Learned voices Stored in it Not in it Webhook addresses, HTTP header values, shell commands Stored in it Hidden This computer's settings (access, OSC and MIDI input, Start armed) Stored in it Ignored when imported Safe to send to someone No Yes danger Never hand someone the show.earshot.json from the data folder. It holds your cloud keys, link codes and the crew's learned voices. To share a show, use Setup, Show file, Export show file. See Show files. Do not edit show.earshot.json by hand. Earshot writes the whole file on every save, so a change made while it runs would be lost. And if the file is there but cannot be read, Earshot does not start with an empty show in its place: it reports the error and does not start.
documents.s: The show file in the folder is not the show file you export

documents.t: The folder is private to your user account. A folder Earshot creates can be opened only by you, and the show file, its backup and the database are readable only by you. That holds on macOS and Linux. A folder that already existed keeps the permissions it had; the files inside are still made private. Other user accounts on the same computer, and anyone with administrator rights, are a matter for the computer, not for Earshot. See Privacy for who can read the transcript through the app.

Everything worth keeping is in the data folder. To back up a show completely: Stop Earshot. The database is being written while it runs, and a copy taken mid-write may not open. Copy the whole data folder somewhere safe. Start Earshot again. You can leave models/ out of the copy: models can be downloaded again (with internet). Everything else cannot be made again. warning A copy of the data folder contains your cloud keys, link codes, the password hash, every transcript and the crew's learned voices. Keep it as carefully as the host itself. Two lighter copies you can take while Earshot runs, from the screens: What Where What you get The show Setup, Show file, Export show file Channels, groups, automations, destinations, glossary, people's names. No secrets, no voices, no transcript. One session's transcript Archive, Export TXT, CSV, JSON or SRT. See Archive and search.

On the old computer: Setup, Show file, Export show file. On the new one: install Earshot, download the models, then Setup, Show file, Choose a show file…. Then, on the new computer, do again by hand everything an export leaves out: who can connect, and the password (Setup, Access); cloud keys (Setup, Cloud & audio); OSC and MIDI input (Setup, Show control); link codes of linked channels; webhook addresses, HTTP header values and web addresses in automations, which arrive empty and switched off; every learned voice. Voices are never exported. See Show files for exactly what an import brings and what it leaves alone. Copying the whole data folder to the new computer instead brings everything, secrets and voices included. That has not been tried between two computers.

There is no button for deleting past sessions in this build. Stop Earshot. In the data folder, delete earshot.db and the files beside it whose names start earshot.db. Delete the clips folder. Start Earshot again. This also removes the personal links, so everyone who joined with a link or an invite needs a new one. It does not touch the show: channels, automations, the glossary, people and settings stay. To start completely clean, delete the whole data folder with Earshot stopped. The next start makes a new one, with an empty show, and the first-time setup opens. You will need to download the models again unless you kept models/. For a clean transcript without deleting anything, use Setup, Show file, New session…. The old session stays in the Archive.

Earshot treats the two cases differently: The file is missing. Earshot starts with a new, empty show. The file is there but cannot be read (it is damaged, or was written by a build with a different show version). Earshot does not start, and its log names the file and says what is wrong. It never quietly replaces your show with an empty one. The copy from before the last save is beside it as show.earshot.json.bak. With Earshot stopped, move the damaged file somewhere else, copy the .bak file to show.earshot.json, and start Earshot. You lose only the most recent change. Earshot does not do this for you, and this recovery has not been rehearsed for this manual: keep your own exported show file as well.
documents.s: If the show file is damaged

documents.t: Each phone, tablet and laptop keeps a little of its own, in the browser it used: display choices: theme, text size, the language under Read in, which channels and lanes are shown; its sign-in (a personal link's token, or a password session). None of that is on the host, and clearing the browser's site data removes it. A person who clears it needs their link or the password again.
documents.s: What is kept in the browser

documents.t: earshotd is Earshot with no window: the same engine and the same web screens as the desktop app, for a rack machine with no monitor. You run it from a terminal, and everyone, including you, opens it in a browser. For packages and installation, see Install and update. For a custom build, see Building from source.

From the extracted package folder, with its web files in web: ./earshotd --web-dir ./web On Windows, use .\earshotd.exe --web-dir .\web in PowerShell. The examples below use earshotd for the installed executable; use its path if it is not on your PATH. It prints this, then keeps running: Earshot is running Open: http://localhost:4780/ Admin: http://localhost:4780/?token=3f9a1c0e5b7d42a68c1e0f2a9b4d6c7e Other devices on the network can use this machine's address on port 4780. Line Meaning Earshot is running In demo mode it says Earshot is running (demo mode). Open: The plain address. Whoever opens it gets whatever the access mode gives them: an operator while the show is Open. Setup shows "Setup needs admin access". Admin: The same address with the admin token on the end. Use this one for setup. Whoever opens it is an admin, in every access mode. Other devices… Printed when it listens on every network address (the default). Give crew the address shown in the app under Setup, Access, Address for the crew, not localhost. Treat the Admin address like a password Anyone who has the Admin: address can change everything, including who can connect. Do not paste it into a chat or leave it on a shared screen. The token is new every time the program starts, unless you set one with --admin-token. When you open the Admin address, the app takes the token out of the address bar and remembers it in that browser, so it does not stay in the address you see or share. That browser stays an admin until the token changes (the next start, unless you set one) or you sign out.

Usage: earshotd [OPTIONS] Option Default What it does --port <PORT> 4780 The TCP port for the web app and API. --bind <BIND> 0.0.0.0 The network address to listen on. 0.0.0.0 means every address this computer has. 127.0.0.1 means this computer only. --data-dir <DATA_DIR> The operating system's data folder + Earshot Where the show file and history live. Also read from the environment variable EARSHOT_DATA_DIR. See Data and files. --demo Off Play a scripted demo show. Your own data is not read or written. --models-dir <MODELS_DIR> EARSHOT_MODELS, else <data-dir>/models Where speech models live. --web-dir <WEB_DIR> apps/web/dist, if it exists The built web app to serve. --admin-token <ADMIN_TOKEN> Random, printed at startup The token that makes a client an admin. --allow-host <NAME> None An extra name people may use to reach this host (a DNS name, or a reverse proxy's name). Repeat the flag for more names. -h, --help Print the options. -V, --version Print the version. Things there is no option for in this build: a certificate (Earshot serves plain http), and the OSC ports (set those in the app, under Setup, Show control).

There is no Setup screen for the network address or the web port. These two options are the only way to set them for the headless program. If the port is already in use, earshotd stops with an error ("could not start the server"). Choose another with --port. With --bind 127.0.0.1, only a browser on the same computer can connect, and Setup, Access has no address to offer the crew. The OSC TCP port cannot be the same as the web port.

Earshot refuses any request made to a name it does not recognise as its own. People who type such a name see "This address isn't one the host recognises. Use the address shown on the operator's screen." These always work, with no option needed: any IP address, localhost, the computer's own name (also with .local). Any other name, such as a venue DNS name or the name of a reverse proxy in front of Earshot, is refused until you add it: earshotd --allow-host earshot.venue.example --allow-host comms.venue.example

Without it, a new random token is made at every start, so yesterday's Admin: address stops working. Set your own to keep one address working across restarts, for example on a rack machine that starts Earshot by itself: earshotd --admin-token "a-long-random-string-you-keep-secret" Use a long random string. It is the key to everything.

earshotd --web-dir ./web --demo --bind 127.0.0.1 Demo mode plays a scripted transcript on made-up channels. It needs no models and no audio hardware, and your own data folder is not read or written. For the desktop app’s setup walkthrough, see Get started with Earshot. The Feed on a demo host, playing its scripted show. It is not a real show.

Variable What it does Read by EARSHOT_DATA_DIR The data folder. The same as --data-dir. earshotd and the desktop app EARSHOT_MODELS The models folder, when --models-dir is not given. Otherwise models go in models inside the data folder. earshotd and the desktop app EARSHOT_LOG How much goes in the log, for example EARSHOT_LOG=debug. Without it the level is info. earshotd and the desktop app EARSHOT_DEMO Set to 1 (or true) to start the desktop app in demo mode. earshotd uses --demo instead. The desktop app EARSHOT_LOG=debug earshotd --data-dir /srv/earshot Logs never contain what was said, or any secret. See Privacy.
earshotd --web-dir ./web --demo --bind 127.0.0.1 Open the Admin: address it prints. Nothing is reachable from the network, and nothing of yours is touched.
documents.s: Try it, on this computer only

documents.t: earshotd \ --data-dir /srv/earshot \ --admin-token "a-long-random-string-you-keep-secret" \ --web-dir /opt/earshot/web The show, the transcripts and the models are kept in /srv/earshot. The admin address is the same after every restart: http://<this machine's address>:4780/?token=<your token>. --web-dir points at the built web app (the contents of apps/web/dist). Without a web app to serve, there are no screens to open. Then, from a laptop, open the admin address, download the models (Setup, Models), patch the inputs (Setup, Patch), and set who can connect (Setup, Access). See First-time setup.
documents.s: A rack machine for a show

documents.t: earshotd --port 8080 Crew then open http://<this machine's address>:8080/.
earshotd --models-dir /Volumes/Models/earshot The speech model alone is about 487 MB, and each translation pair is 80 to 240 MB.
earshotd --allow-host earshot.venue.example

Press Ctrl-C in its terminal, or send it the terminate signal (kill <pid>, or however your service manager stops a program). It shuts the engine down in order, then stops. Nothing fires while Earshot is shutting down.

A new session starts. The earlier ones stay in the Archive. The show comes back Safe, unless Setup, Show control, Start armed is on. People who signed in with the password must sign in again. Personal links keep working. Unless you set --admin-token, the admin token is new. See What happens when the host restarts.

earshotd has been tested on one Apple Silicon Mac and has passed a demo startup smoke test on Windows and Linux. It has not been tested as a system service or behind a reverse proxy. See Limits and known behaviour.

Everyone connected to Earshot has one of three roles: viewer, operator or admin. The role decides what they can do. It does not decide what they can read: any role can read the transcript. The host enforces roles on every request. The screens only reflect what the host allows, so hiding a button is never the only thing standing between a viewer and arming the show.

Viewer Operator Admin Read Feed, Lanes, Focus, Archive, Activity yes yes yes Search and export the Archive yes yes yes Type lines into channels that allow typing yes yes yes See Armed or Safe yes (display only) yes yes Replay saved audio yes yes yes Read in another language one language several, up to the host's limit several, up to the host's limit See names on lines yes yes yes See what a changed line was changed from (the pencil) no yes yes Hold to arm, Make safe no yes yes Run now, Test bench, acknowledge alerts, add markers no yes yes Edit automations; use Setup (Channels, Patch, Groups, Models, People, Glossary, Cloud & audio, Access, Show control, Show file) no no yes An operator who opens Setup sees "Setup needs admin access". danger An operator can arm the show and fire cues. When you hand out operator access, by invite, personal link, the shared password or Open mode, you are handing out the Armed control.

It depends on the access mode (Setup, Access, Who can connect) and on how the person got in. How they connect In Open mode In Password mode In Personal links mode The desktop app's own window Admin Admin Admin The Admin: address that earshotd prints Admin Admin Admin Just the address, nothing else Operator Sent to the password page Sent to the "needs a personal link" page The show password Not used: nobody is asked for one Operator Not accepted A personal link or a scanned invite made as Viewer Operator (raised) Viewer Viewer A personal link or a scanned invite made as Operator Operator Operator Operator Three things in that table surprise people: Earshot starts in Open mode, and in Open mode everyone on the network is an operator. That includes the ability to arm. Change the mode before you put Earshot on a network you do not control. See Who can connect. In Open mode a viewer link is raised to operator. There are no viewers in an Open show. If you need real viewers (people who can read but not arm, and who are not sent what was heard), use Personal links, or Password with viewer links. The shared password always makes an operator. There is no viewer password. The Access screen makes invites and personal links for two roles only: Viewer ("can read, and type where a channel allows it") and Operator ("can arm the show, run automations and add markers"). Admin access stays with the host's own window and the Admin: address. (The API can make a link with the admin role. Such a link is listed as "Can change everything, including Setup".)
documents.s: How a sign-in becomes a role

documents.t: earshotd prints an Admin: address with a token on the end when it starts. Whoever opens it is an admin, in every access mode. The token is new each time the program starts, unless you set one with --admin-token. Treat it like the keys to the building. See earshotd.

The name beside a typed line is whatever that person typed when they joined, or the label on their personal link. Earshot does not check it. The role comes from the link or password, never from the name.

Revoke next to a person (Setup, Access, People with access) cuts off that one link. They are disconnected within a second. Changing or clearing the show password signs out everyone who used it. Changing the access mode applies at once, to everyone, and asks you to confirm first. If a person's role changes while they are connected, their screen reconnects and picks up the new role. See Invites and personal links and The show password.

Some things never leave the host, whoever asks. Never sent to What Anyone, admins included A saved cloud key, a saved link code, the show password (it is stored as a hash), an automation's web-request header values, and a webhook's path. Where one is saved an admin sees "••••", and can keep it, clear it or replace it, but never read it back. Anyone, admins included Learned voices. They stay on the host, are never sent to any browser, and are never in an exported show file. Anyone, admins included A show file export always has secrets hidden, even when an admin exports it. Operators and viewers Web addresses in automations are cut back to the host name, and request bodies and shell command text are hidden. Admins see those, because they need to edit them. Operators and viewers Webhook paths in the Activity log and in alerts. They show as plain "webhook". Viewers What was heard: the original text of a line that was changed by the glossary, number tidying or the profanity filter. Viewers get no pencil. In the JSON export it is empty for them. Viewers Voice-learning progress and which people have a learned voice. Because everyone in an Open show is an operator, everyone in an Open show can see what was heard. See Privacy and Saved secrets.
documents.s: What no role is ever sent

documents.t: A console sending OSC has no sign-in and no role. What it may do is decided by where the message came from and the level chosen under Setup, Show control: Make safe only, Trigger automations, or Full control, including arming. See OSC input. Similarly, anyone who has a webhook's address can fire that one automation, in any access mode, though it still obeys Armed and Safe. See Triggers.
documents.s: What OSC can do is separate

documents.t: The mock show plays a venue whose network the production does not control. The stage manager runs the host from the desktop app's window: admin. Access is set to Personal links. The deputy stage manager and the lighting programmer each get a personal link made as Operator, because either may need to press Make safe. Dressers, follow-spot operators and the company manager scan an invite made as Viewer. They can read, type notes into channels that allow it, and replay calls. They cannot arm, and they see no pencil. The lighting desk sends OSC at the Trigger automations level, with its address in the allowed list. It has no role at all. When the programmer leaves the tour, the stage manager presses Revoke beside their name. Nobody else is affected.
documents.s: A worked example: a touring show

documents.t: Who can connect Invites and personal links Safe and Armed Privacy
Earshot says a great deal with small labels. This page lists them all, by where you meet them. The wording is exactly what the app shows.

It says What it means What to do Live This screen is connected to the host. Nothing. Connecting The page has just opened and is reaching the host. Wait a moment. Reconnecting "Connection lost. Reconnecting (attempt N)." Wait. It keeps trying by itself and catches up on missed lines. Engine unreachable "No connection to the engine. Retrying (attempt N)." Check this device's network, and that the host is running and awake. Demo Connected, but to a demo show: a host started in demo mode ("The engine is running its demo show."), or the built-in mock ("Showing the built-in demo show, not a live engine."). Nothing, unless you expected a real show.

It shows What it means Safe (lit), with Hold to arm beside it Automations that match are only logged. Nothing is sent. On a narrow screen the second button reads Arm. ARMED in red, with Make safe beside it, a red band across the header and "ARMED" in the browser tab title Automations that match really send. Arming… Your arm is on its way to the host. Making safe… Your Safe is on its way to the host. Safe? or ARMED? (with a question mark) "Safe — connection lost, state unknown" (or "Armed — …"). The screen has lost the host and is showing the last state it knew. Arming is not possible. Press Make safe anyway. "Could not confirm Safe — the host may still be armed." Earshot could not confirm your Safe. Press Retry until it clears. "The host is armed. Your Safe was overtaken — press Make safe again." Someone armed after your Safe. Press Make safe again. A viewer sees Safe or ARMED as a display only, with no buttons. The whole subject is in Safe and Armed.
It shows a language code (for example ES) while you are reading in another language.

These appear in the Feed's channel list, on lane headers, in Focus and in Setup. A channel that is listening normally shows no badge in the transcript views. In Setup, where the absence of a badge would be unclear, it shows Listening.

Badge Tone What it means What to do (none) / Listening The channel is hearing its input and transcribing. Nothing. Idle grey The channel is switched off, or has not started. Check it is enabled under Setup, Channels. Starting grey The channel is opening its input, or a linked channel is connecting. Wait. Paused grey Someone, or an automation, paused it. It is not listening. Resume it when you want it back. Behind amber "Transcription is running behind; live drafts are paused until it catches up". Every line is still transcribed, but late. See below. No input red The audio device is not delivering audio. Check the interface, its cable, and the operating system's microphone permission. Offline red A channel from another Earshot computer, whose computer cannot be reached. Earshot keeps retrying. Check the other computer and the network. Hover the badge for the detail. Error red Something went wrong. For a linked channel, the other computer refused. Hover the badge: the detail says what. Disabled grey In Setup's channel list only: the channel is switched off and does not listen. Switch it on under Setup, Channels. Hover any badge for the detail the host gave. Behind comes on when the backlog on that channel goes over 3 seconds, and goes off when it falls under 1 second. While it is on: no draft text, final lines arrive late, cues set to fire on final text fire late, and lines get no names. Help is in Troubleshooting. Where one lane or one Focus covers several channels (a group), the badge is that of the channel in the worst state.

The bar under a channel's name shows how loud its input is, on a scale from -60 dB to 0 dB, with a thin mark at the peak. The meter What it means Moves when someone talks The input is alive. Never moves Wrong input number, a dead line, or no microphone permission. Turns amber Peaks are within 6 dB of the top. Loud, still fine. Turns red Peaks are within 1 dB of the top. The input is clipping: turn it down at the source, or lower Gain. A channel from another Earshot computer has no meter, because no audio comes across.

Mark What it means A number Lines you have not read on that channel ("unread lines" in the Feed, "new lines" on a lane). Speaking now Lanes: someone is talking on it at this moment. Pinned Lanes: the lane is pinned to the left. A cloud, reading Cloud The channel is set to cloud speech. Either lines are coming back from the cloud ("Cloud speech: audio from this channel is sent to Deepgram, outside this building, to be transcribed."), or that is simply how it is set ("Set to cloud speech: this channel’s audio may be sent to Deepgram, outside this building."). A cloud, reading Cloud paused "Cloud speech is paused after failures. Lines are transcribed on this computer; Earshot tests the service with one short piece of audio about every 30 seconds." A cloud, reading On this computer The channel is set to cloud speech but is being transcribed locally, because "Deepgram rejected the key" or there is "No key saved". No audio is sent. A link mark The channel comes from another Earshot computer. It says "From" and the address. Not encrypted That link is plain http: "Lines from this host travel unencrypted on the network." People who cannot read diagnostics (viewers) only ever see the plain Cloud mark. See Cloud & audio and Showing another Earshot computer's channels.

Mark What it means Soft grey text A draft: the person is still talking and the words may change. Screen readers hear "still speaking". Solid text A final line. A dimmed word with a dotted underline Earshot was unsure of that word. A name with a coloured dot Earshot recognised the voice. "Recognised by voice. May be wrong." Typed, with a name Someone typed the line. Typed lines never fire phrase automations. A small pencil "Changed from what was heard. Show the original." Operators and admins only. A small play control "Play the audio of" the channel and time. The channel keeps its audio. Original, before muted text under a line You are reading a translation, and this is what was actually said. Translating… A translation is on its way (up to 10 seconds). Not translated No translation arrived, or the line cannot be translated. More on each in The screen at a glance.
Badge What it means Live now The session that is running at this moment. Other sessions show how long they ran instead. Highlighted words in a search result The words you searched for.

Mark Where What it means Problem Automations list The automation cannot run, or needs fixing. The line under it starts "Not running:" or "Needs fixing:" and says what to change. See When an automation is not running. Would have fired Test bench The phrase matched. The test bench is always a dry run. Really sent A firing's card It was a live firing, not a dry run. Would run / Ran / Skipped Beside each action of a firing What that action did, or would have done. A skipped action gives its reason. Dry run Activity The automation matched while the show was Safe (or the firing was held back), so nothing was sent. Failed Activity The send was tried and did not succeed. Open the row for the reason. Ignored for this trigger Automation editor, on a condition The condition cannot apply to this kind of trigger. See Run now, the Test bench and Activity.

documents.t: Badge Where What it means Recommended Models Install this one. Installed Models Downloaded, checked and ready. Before that a row may say "Verifying the download…". In use now Names on lines, Translate with, What incoming OSC may do The choice in force, as opposed to the card you have picked but not yet applied. Voice learned People Earshot has that person's voice. No voice yet People The person exists but no voice has been learned. No name will appear for them. Voice needs learning again People A stored voice no longer fits the voice model. Learn it again. Pinned Groups The group is listed first. Password set / No password set Access Whether a show password exists. Until one is set, nobody can join by password. Key saved / No key / Checking… Cloud & audio Whether the host holds a key for that service. The key itself is never shown. Working, Waiting, Paused, Key rejected, No key, Not used Cloud & audio, cloud speech status How cloud speech is doing. See Cloud & audio. Encrypted / Not encrypted From another Earshot host Whether that computer offers https. Not connected Show control, MIDI input ports A MIDI port you ticked is not plugged in at the moment. "••••" Anywhere a secret is saved A key, code or password is saved. It cannot be read back. See Saved secrets.
The screen at a glance Troubleshooting Words used in this manual
Plain definitions, in alphabetical order. Each links to the page that covers it properly.

Action. One thing an automation does when it fires: send OSC, send MIDI, make a web request, flash an alert, add a marker, and so on. An automation has a list of actions, run in order. See Actions. Activity. The live log of what came in, what went out and what every automation did or would have done. It is where you look to find out why a cue did or did not fire. See Run now, the Test bench and Activity. Admin. The role that can change everything, including Setup. The desktop app's own window is an admin. See Roles. Armed. The state in which automations that match really send their cues. Shown in red, as ARMED. The opposite of Safe. See Safe and Armed. Automation. A rule: a trigger, optional conditions, and a list of actions. "When the show caller says 'go cue' and a number, send that cue to the lighting desk." See Building an automation. Behind. A channel badge meaning transcription is running late on that channel. Every line is still written down, but later than usual, and drafts stop until it catches up. See Badges and marks. Bonjour. The way computers announce themselves on a local network (also called mDNS). Earshot uses it so other Earshot computers can find this one. See Network. Channel. One source of speech that Earshot listens to and writes down: usually one audio input carrying one comms line. A channel can also be a recording played in as if live (a simulator), a typed-text-only channel, or a channel shown from another Earshot computer. See Channel settings. Clip. The saved audio behind one spoken line, on a channel with Keep audio for replay on. See Replay a line's audio. Cloud speech. Sending one channel's audio to an outside company (Deepgram) to be transcribed, instead of doing it on the host. Off unless you choose it for a channel and confirm. See Cloud & audio. Condition. An extra check on an automation ("Only if"): the channel, the group, the person, the time of day, or a flag. All conditions must be true for the automation to fire. Cooldown. How long an automation ignores its trigger after it fires, so that a repeated call does not send the cue twice. A new automation has 2 seconds.

Demo. A host started in demo mode plays a scripted, made-up transcript, needs no models or audio hardware, and does not touch your own data. The header says Demo. See Quick tour. Destination. A named place OSC is sent to: a lighting desk, a video server, a QLab machine. It has a name, an address, a port and a protocol. Draft line. A line shown in soft grey while the person is still talking. Its words can change. Also called a partial. See The screen at a glance. Dry run. An automation that matched but sent nothing, because the show was Safe (or because the test bench was used, which is always a dry run). Activity marks it Dry run and says what would have fired. earshotd. The host program with no window, for a rack machine. See earshotd. Final line. A line whose text has settled, because the person stopped speaking. Shown solid. Glossary corrections, names and cues set to "Final text" all wait for it. Firing. One occasion on which an automation's trigger matched, with the result of each of its actions. A firing is either live (really sent) or a dry run. Flag. A named on/off switch that one automation can set and another can check. Used for things like "we are in act two". Glossary. Your list of words Earshot often mis-hears (names, songs, gear), each with the right spelling and the ways it tends to come out. It corrects what people read. It never changes numbers, and never changes what automations hear. See The glossary. Group. A named folder of channels, like Stage or Audio. The Feed and Lanes can filter or arrange by group. Groups are only edited in Setup. See Groups.

Host. The one computer that runs Earshot: it has the audio inputs, runs the speech models, keeps the transcript and serves the screens. Everyone else is just a browser looking at it. Invite. A QR code (and link) that lets one person join once. It runs out after 10 minutes. Once used, it becomes a personal link. See Invites and personal links. Line. One stretch of speech, or one typed message, on one channel. Link code. What one Earshot computer needs to read another's shared channels, when that other computer asks for a sign-in. It is an ordinary viewer invite of the other computer, so treat it like a password. See Showing another Earshot computer's channels. Linked channel. A channel that comes from another Earshot computer. Read-only, text only, and its lines never fire automations here. Marker. A labelled point on a session's timeline, like "Act two, cue 42". See Archive, search and export. MIDI. A long-established way for music and show equipment to send short control messages (notes, controllers, program changes). Earshot can send MIDI as an action and be triggered by it. See MIDI. Model. A downloaded file that does one job on the host: finding speech in audio, turning speech into words, recognising voices, or translating between two languages. See Models.

Operator. The role that can arm the show, make it safe, run automations and add markers, but cannot change Setup. See Roles. OSC. Open Sound Control: the network message format most lighting desks, sound desks and playback systems use for remote control. An OSC message is an address like /eos/cue/42/fire with optional values. Earshot sends OSC as an action, and can be controlled by it. See OSC addresses. Patch. Choosing which inputs of an audio device Earshot listens to. Each ticked input becomes a channel. See Patch and channels. People. The crew members Earshot knows by voice. Each has a name, a colour, and (once learned) a voice. See People: recognise voices. Personal link. A web address that signs in one person, with a role you chose. You can revoke it without affecting anyone else. Phrase. The words a spoken-phrase automation listens for, for example go cue {number}. The part in braces stands for one spoken word, which the actions can then use. Role. Viewer, operator or admin. See Roles. Run now. Running one automation by hand from the Automations list. A dry run while Safe; it asks before sending while Armed.

Safe. The state in which automations that match are only logged as "would have fired". Nothing is sent. Earshot starts Safe, and Safe always wins over Armed. Serving host. When two Earshot computers are linked, the one that has the channel and shares it. Session. One continuous run of the transcript. Every time Earshot starts it begins a new session. The Archive lists them. Show. Everything you set up: channels, groups, automations, destinations, glossary, people and settings. Show file. The show saved as one file (ending .earshot.json), so it can be carried to another computer. It holds no passwords, keys, link codes, learned voices or transcript. See Show files. Simulator. A channel that plays a recording (a WAV file) as if it were a live input. Good for rehearsing automations without a crew. "Sounds like". In the glossary, the wrong spellings a word tends to come out as. Only the spellings you list are replaced.

Test bench. A screen where you type a phrase and see which automations would fire and what each would do. Always a dry run. Trigger. What sets an automation off: a spoken phrase, an incoming OSC message, an incoming MIDI message, a web request, a channel's health, or nothing but a manual press. See Triggers. Typed line. A line someone typed into a channel instead of saying it. It carries a Typed badge and never fires a phrase automation. Utterance. The technical word for a line: one stretch of speech from when the person starts to when they stop. You will meet it in the API and in JSON exports. VAD. Voice activity detection: deciding when someone is speaking, so that only speech is sent to the recogniser. Earshot uses a small model (Silero VAD) for it. The channel settings under Advanced: speech detection adjust it. Viewer. The role that can read, type where a channel allows it, and replay saved audio, but cannot arm or run anything. See Roles. Voice. What Earshot learns about how a person sounds, so it can put their name on their lines. Learned voices never leave the host. Webhook. A web address that fires one automation when something calls it. The address is a secret: whoever has it can fire that automation, though it still obeys Armed and Safe. See Triggers.
Badges, marks and indicators Roles What Earshot does

On the Mac running the Earshot host, choose Earshot → Open Logs Folder…, or Open Logs Folder… in the Earshot tray menu. Browser clients do not hold the host’s logs. The default Mac folder is ~/Library/Logs/Earshot/. The current file is earshot.log; older files are earshot.1.log and earshot.2.log. If EARSHOT_DATA_DIR is set, logs go into its logs subfolder instead.

Keep the current channel and People settings so the log reflects the problem. Let several people speak normally on the comms channel. Include a few longer replies if possible, and a clean PGM comparison. Open the logs folder and keep earshot.log. Include the rotated files if the relevant time has moved into them. Note the channel and approximate time of a reply that should have had a name. Send the log with that information when reporting the issue.

Entries with the earshot_voice target share an utterance ID and channel ID, so the input, comparison, learning and final result can be followed together. Event What it tells you model_ready Which voice model loaded, its execution provider, thread count and embedding size. input Channel name, sample rate, audio duration, RMS and peak levels in dBFS, clipping, invalid samples, and whether recognition, discovery and the model are enabled/installed. speech_gate The loud and noise RMS estimates, effective gate floor and accepted 20 ms frames. A long recording can still contain very little speech according to this gate. comparison Detected speech duration, availability of a usable observation, saved voice count, best and runner-up speaker IDs/scores, confidence margin, and the exact duration/score/margin thresholds for display and automations. candidate_rejected Why an observation cannot enter the learning pool, including the required speech duration. candidate_started / candidate_progress Pending voice similarity, number of consistent observations, total speech, and the requirements to establish a voice. candidates_expired Pending observations were discarded after two minutes without matching speech. learning_not_saved / learning_save_failed An observation did not qualify for saving, or saving failed. decision The speaker selected for display and the separate, stricter automation result. answer The automation answer, including early exits such as recognition off, missing model, startup, missing audio or a full recognition queue. name_published / name_publish_failed Whether a selected name was actually stored and announced to clients.

Replies with less than one second of detected speech remain unnamed under the current matching rules. For diagnostics, discovery can extract an observation from at least 250 ms of detected speech, so its scores can be inspected, but that does not lower the naming or automation thresholds. The current learning pool still requires at least one second per observation. This distinction matters on comms: “go” may contain only a few hundred milliseconds of usable speech even when its recorded segment is much longer. Single-word samples are not a reliable basis for claiming that two people are the same voice. Diagnostics expose the actual reason instead of assuming that every missing name is a model installation problem.

Logging is enabled by default, writes off the transcription thread and keeps at most three 10 MiB files. Its memory queue is bounded; extreme overload can drop log entries. A normal app shutdown records the dropped-entry count and flushes the writer. Logs include channel names, IDs, timestamps, numeric signal measurements and decision scores. They do not record transcript text, raw audio, voice embeddings, stored voiceprints or credentials. Existing replay clips are separate from these logs. Developers can override the filter with EARSHOT_LOG. The default is info,earshot_voice=debug; EARSHOT_LOG=warn suppresses normal voice diagnostics. Cloud HTTP request logging remains clamped to info so request URLs containing glossary terms are not exposed at trace level.

Everything the Earshot screens do, they do through a web API on the host. A script, a show-control tool or another service can use the same API: read the transcript, follow it live, send a typed line, drop a marker, make the show Safe, run an automation. This page is a guided tour with examples. The full reference is on the host itself, described next.

Open Setup, then Show control, and press API reference at the top right. It opens /docs on the host in a new tab (for example http://192.168.1.20:4780/docs). On a phone it is under More. The API reference served by a demo host on one computer. It is not a real show. It has: A Safety box (Safe always wins; arming is a deliberate act; automations fire only when Armed). Every route, grouped by task: Transcript, Typing and markers, Automations and Armed/Safe, Show setup, Access, History and export, System. Each has the role it needs and a curl example with this host's own address filled in. A walk-through of the live WebSocket connection. The OSC address list. Download openapi.json, the same description as an OpenAPI 3.1 document, for tools that read one. The page asks you to sign in to Earshot in that browser first, unless the show is Open. It reads the sign-in the Earshot web app keeps in that browser. Opening /docs with a token on the end of the address does nothing: the page accepts no credential of its own.
documents.s: The API reference on the host

documents.t: Base address http://<host>:4780/api/v1 Bodies JSON, in and out Errors {"error": {"code": "...", "message": "..."}} with the matching HTTP status Encryption None in this build. Earshot serves plain http. See Limits and known behaviour. The examples below use these two lines. Set them once in your shell. export EARSHOT=http://192.168.1.20:4780 export EARSHOT_TOKEN="paste-your-token-here" Use the address from Setup, Access, Address for the crew. Do not make up a name for the computer: see "The address must be one the host recognises" below.

Send your token in a header: Authorization: Bearer <token> Every route also accepts ?token=<token> on the end of the address, but that is meant for the WebSocket and the event stream, where a browser cannot set a header. Prefer the header: addresses end up in browser history and in logs. Never put a real token in a script you share. Read it from an environment variable, as these examples do. Where a token comes from Token How to get it Role The admin token earshotd prints it at start, in the Admin: address (the part after ?token=). Set your own with --admin-token. See earshotd. Admin A personal link Setup, Access, New personal link. The token is the part of the link after ?token=. It is shown once. See Invites and personal links. Viewer or Operator, as you chose A password session POST /auth/login with the show password (example below). It is forgotten when the host restarts, and expires after 12 hours without use. Operator What you are without a token depends on who can connect (Setup, Access): Mode With no token With a token Open Operator Its own role, but at least Operator Password Refused (401) A password session is an Operator. A personal link keeps its role. Personal links Refused (401) The role the link was made with So in an Open show you can leave the Authorization header out of every example on this page. Roles. Reading and typing need Viewer. Live operation (Safe and Armed, running automations, markers, pausing a channel) needs Operator. Changing the show and managing access need Admin. See Roles. Check what you are: curl -sS \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/auth/whoami" {"credential":"open","mode":"open","name":"Guest","role":"operator","token_id":null} Sign in with the show password, to get a session token: curl -sS \ -X POST \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"password":"the show password"}' \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/auth/login" The reply is {"token":"...","role":"operator"}. Use that token as $EARSHOT_TOKEN.

These two need no token in any mode. curl -sS "$EARSHOT/api/v1/health" {"name":"Earshot","ok":true,"version":"0.1.0"} curl -sS "$EARSHOT/api/v1/auth/mode" {"mode":"open","name":"FOH Rack","version":"0.1.0"} name is the Name shown to others from Setup, Access, or the computer's own name if that is empty. (The name in this example was changed.)

curl -sS \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/state" The reply is one large object: the show (channels, groups, automations, settings, with secrets hidden), the current session, whether the show is armed, each channel's status, open alerts, and any automations that are not running. It is the place to look up the ids the other calls need: show.channels[].id for a channel, show.automations[].id for an automation, session.id for the current session.

Lines of the current session, oldest first: curl -sS \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/utterances?limit=20" Only some channels (ids, separated by commas): curl -sS \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/utterances?channels=01JC8Z4M2Q7K9R3VX5TB6N1WDE&limit=20" One line looks like this (the list of single words is cut short here): { "id": "01M7H1QYCAN2VNFFGPXTJMHGB8", "session_id": "01M7H1EDP38RJNA0R63AQPMZZP", "channel_id": "demo-video", "started_at": 1794794846602, "ended_at": 1794794849012, "text": "Recording paused for the interval.", "raw_text": null, "words": [{"text": "Recording", "confidence": 0.976672, "t0_ms": 181, "t1_ms": 666}], "language": "en", "speaker_id": null, "kind": "speech", "author": null, "keyword_hits": [], "has_clip": false, "latency_ms": 491, "confidence": 0.95143384, "translations": {} } Times are milliseconds since 1970 (UTC). kind is speech, typed or system. raw_text is what the recogniser heard before the glossary, number tidying and the profanity filter changed it. It is null when nothing was changed, and always null for anyone below Operator. limit is 200 unless you say otherwise, and at most 1000. You get the newest lines that fit, still listed oldest first. Other query options: session= (a session id; the current one if left out), and before= or after= with a line's id, to page backwards or forwards from that line. Past sessions, newest first: curl -sS \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/sessions"
curl -sS \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/search?q=cue%20twelve&limit=10" Add &session=<id> to search one session. Without it, every session is searched.

format is txt, csv, json or srt. Without session= it is the current session. channels=a,b keeps only those channels. curl -sS -o transcript.srt \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/export?format=srt" The start of an SRT export from the demo host: 1 00:00:00,506 --> 00:00:05,433 SM Desk: Good evening all, this is your five minute call for beginners. 2 00:00:04,205 --> 00:00:07,563 ASM Stage Left: Stage left copies, all cast are in position. And the same lines as format=txt. The times in a text export are in UTC. [02:02:15] SM Desk: Good evening all, this is your five minute call for beginners. [02:02:18] ASM Stage Left: Stage left copies, all cast are in position. See Archive and search for the same exports from the screen.

GET /stream is a server-sent event stream: one event for each finished line, for as long as you keep the connection open. -N stops curl from holding the output back. curl -sSN \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/stream" Each event is an id: line and a data: line. This one is cut short where the ... is: id: 7580 data: {"seq":7580,"at":1794794857756,"event":{"type":"utterance_final","data":{"id":"01M7H1R4QFD73MAJTRA8K5X1J6","channel_id":"demo-sm","text":"Good evening all, this is your five minute call for beginners.", ...}}} It carries finished lines only. Drafts, names on lines, alerts and Armed or Safe changes are on the WebSocket (below). It ends when its token is revoked or its role changes. Connect again. A few lines of Python that print each line as it is finished: import json import os import urllib.request request = urllib.request.Request( os.environ["EARSHOT"] + "/api/v1/stream", headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ.get("EARSHOT_TOKEN", "")}, ) with urllib.request.urlopen(request) as stream: for raw in stream: line = raw.decode().strip() if line.startswith("data:"): event = json.loads(line[5:])["event"] if event["type"] == "utterance_final": print(event["data"]["channel_id"], event["data"]["text"])

Needs Viewer, on a channel that allows typing. The id in the address is the channel's id. curl -sS \ -X POST \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"text":"standby cue 12"}' \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/channels/01JC8Z4M2Q7K9R3VX5TB6N1WDE/messages" The reply is the line as stored, with "kind":"typed" and "author" set to your name. Your name comes from the personal link's label, or from the header X-Earshot-Name (up to 40 characters; "Guest" if you send none). A typed line never fires a phrase automation, however it arrives.

Needs Operator. curl -sS \ -X POST \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"label":"Act 2 start"}' \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/markers" {"id":"01M7H1RSPTFFQE9HHZBQ80456T","session_id":"01M7H1EDP38RJNA0R63AQPMZZP","at":1794794874586,"label":"Act 2 start","author":"Guest"}

Needs Operator. curl -sS \ -X PUT \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"armed":false}' \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/armed" {"type":"ok"} {"armed":true} arms. danger Arming lets automations really send cues. A script that arms the show is a script that can fire them. Read Safe and Armed. Arm and Safe from every source (screens, API, OSC) are applied in the order the host receives them. The last one wins. A request that was overtaken by a later one answers 409 ("a later arm/safe command was received first"), unless it asked for the state that now holds. A request the engine does not finish within 2 seconds answers 503. A stuck Arm therefore cannot hold back a Safe for more than about 2 seconds. After a 409 or a 503 on a Safe, read /state and send Safe again if armed is still true.

Needs Operator. This is the Test bench: always a dry run, whether the show is Safe or Armed. Nothing is sent. curl -sS \ -X POST \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"channel_id":"01JC8Z4M2Q7K9R3VX5TB6N1WDE","text":"go cue twelve"}' \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/test-phrase" channel_id is optional. The reply lists what would fire. From the demo host, whose one automation listens for standby lighting cue {number}, the text "standby lighting cue five" gave: [ { "id": "01M7H1RSNNBCGY9WGR2K2SFQHH", "automation_id": "tour-standby", "automation_name": "Standby marker", "at": 1794794874549, "dry_run": true, "trigger": "phrase \"standby lighting cue 5\" on SM Desk", "utterance_id": null, "results": [ {"summary": "would add marker \"Standby LX 5\"", "ok": true, "skipped": "dry run: nothing was sent"} ] } ] An empty list ([]) means no automation would fire.

Needs Operator. This is Run now. The id in the address is the automation's id (from /state). Its name or short name does not work here. curl -sS \ -X POST \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"vars":{"cue":"12"}}' \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/automations/01JC8Z5A7P3D2H9TQ4WZ8F6KCB/trigger" While the show is Safe this is a dry run. The reply has "dry_run": true and each result says "dry run: nothing was sent". While Armed it really sends. vars is optional. Each value you send can be used in the automation's actions as {{var.<name>}}: here, {{var.cue}}. See Variables. It can take up to 2 seconds to answer. Two runs of one automation less than 0.1 seconds apart: the second is refused. An automation limited to named people never fires this way. See Automations limited to people.

An automation whose trigger is A web request has its own address: POST http://<host>:4780/api/v1/webhooks/<path> curl -sS \ -X POST \ -d 'scene 3' \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/webhooks/lights/go" It needs no token, in any access mode. The path is the secret. Whoever has it can fire that automation. Earshot shows the address only once, when you make the trigger. Copy it then. See Triggers and Saved secrets. It still obeys Safe and Armed. While Safe the reply is a dry run. Whatever you send as the body is passed to the automation as text, as {{var.body}}. An unknown path answers 404 ("no automation uses this webhook path") and counts as a wrong guess (see "Limits" below). An automation started by a webhook that fires more than 20 times in 10 seconds is stopped. See When an automation is not running.

One WebSocket carries everything the screens show live: draft and finished lines, levels, alerts, automation firings, Armed and Safe changes. It also takes commands. It is at: ws://<host>:4780/api/v1/ws?token=<token> Messages are JSON text. In outline: Direction Message Meaning You send {"op":"hello","resume_from":null} Start. resume_from is the last seq you processed, or null the first time. Host sends {"op":"snapshot","snapshot":{...},"resync":false,"role":"operator","name":"Guest"} Always first: the whole state, as /state gives it. Host sends {"op":"event","seq":1235,"at":1700000000000,"event":{"type":"utterance_final","data":{...}}} One thing that happened. Keep the seq. You send {"op":"command","id":7,"command":{"type":"send_typed","data":{"channel_id":"...","text":"copy"}}} Do something. id is yours, to match the reply. Host sends {"op":"reply","id":7,"ok":true,"reply":{"type":"ok"}} The answer to command 7. Replies can arrive out of order. You send {"op":"ping"} The host answers {"op":"pong"}. If you reconnect with resume_from set, the host replays what you missed (it keeps the last 5 000 events), then carries on live. If resync is true, too much was missed or the host restarted: throw away what you have and read the history again with /utterances. An utterance_partial with empty text means "remove that draft line". A connection that falls too far behind (1 000 messages waiting) is closed. Connect again. Close code 4401 means your token is no longer accepted: sign in again. 4403 means your role changed: connect again. Any command can also be sent without a WebSocket, to POST /command: curl -sS \ -X POST \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $EARSHOT_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"type":"set_armed","data":{"armed":false}}' \ "$EARSHOT/api/v1/command" The API reference on the host has a short working example in JavaScript and the full list of events and commands.

What Limit Wrong guesses from one device (a wrong password, an unknown token, a bad invite code, an unknown webhook path) 5, then that device is locked out for 30 seconds, doubling each time up to 15 minutes Webhooks A burst of 20, refilled at 10 a second, per sender and per path Password sign-ins and invite claims, all devices together 20 at once, and 20 started a second Failed password sign-ins, all devices together After 100 in a minute, new password sign-ins are refused for 60 seconds Connections 64 from one device, 192 from all other devices together. A WebSocket or an event stream holds one for its whole life. WebSocket Commands 16 at a time per connection. A message over 2 MiB closes it. Every limit answers 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header (in seconds) and: {"error":{"code":"rate_limited","message":"too many attempts; try again in N s"}} A token that is already in use keeps working while a device is locked out. Only new sign-ins and unknown tokens are refused. Devices behind one router or one proxy count as one device.

Status error.code Meaning 400 bad_request The body or the query is not valid. 401 unauthorized No token, or an unknown, expired or revoked one, and the show is not Open. 403 forbidden Your role is too low, or the request came from another website (below). 404 not_found No such channel, automation, alert, token, code or clip. 409 conflict For example, a later Arm or Safe was received first. 421 misdirected The address used is not one the host recognises (below). 429 rate_limited A limit or a lockout. Wait Retry-After seconds. 500 internal Something went wrong inside the host. 503 unavailable The engine did not answer in time, or is shutting down.

Earshot refuses any request whose address names a computer it does not know it is. The answer is 421: {"error":{"code":"misdirected","message":"this server does not answer to that host name"}} These always work: any IP address, localhost, and the computer's own name (also with .local). Any other name (a venue DNS name, a reverse proxy) is refused until you add it when starting the headless program, with --allow-host NAME. See earshotd. This is what stops a web page on someone's laptop from reaching Earshot under a made-up name.
documents.s: The address must be one the host recognises

documents.t: There is no cross-site access. A web page that is not Earshot's own cannot change anything: a request that changes something (anything but a read), or a WebSocket, that carries a browser's Origin header from another site is refused with 403 ("cross-origin requests are not allowed"). Scripts and tools that send no Origin header, such as curl, are not affected. Webhooks are the exception: they accept a request from anywhere, because the path is the secret.
documents.s: Requests from other websites are refused

documents.t: No reply contains a saved password, cloud key, link code, web request header value or webhook path, for any role. An admin gets the marker •••• where one is saved. When you write settings back, send the marker back unchanged to keep the saved value, an empty string to remove it, or a new value to replace it. Everyone below Admin also gets web addresses in automations cut back to the host name, and shell commands hidden. The show file from GET /show/export is hidden the same way for everyone, admins included. See Saved secrets.

The read, typed-line, marker, Safe, test-phrase and run examples on this page were run with curl against a demo host on the same computer, with that host's own ids in place of the long example ids. The replies shown are what came back (the ids and times are that run's), apart from the computer's name. The password sign-in and the webhook example were not run. The API has not been tried from another computer on a real network, or with real show-control software. See Limits and known behaviour.

Earshot uses MIDI in two ways. A MIDI message coming in can trigger an automation: a pad, a key, a fader or a program change. An automation can send a MIDI message out as one of its actions. warning MIDI has been tried only in automated tests against stand-ins on one Mac. It has never been tried against real gear. See Limits and known behaviour.

Open Setup, then Show control. Only admins can. Under MIDI inputs the screen says "Earshot listens to the ports you tick. MIDI messages from them can trigger automations." Tick each port you want Earshot to listen to. If you plugged a controller in after Earshot started, press Refresh. No port is ticked to begin with, so no MIDI message is listened to. If no ports are found, the screen says "No MIDI inputs found. Plug in or switch on a controller, then choose Refresh." A port you ticked that is not plugged in right now stays in the list with the badge Not connected. The ticked ports are a setting of this computer. An imported show file does not change them. See Show files. MIDI has no levels and no allowed-device list, unlike OSC input. Whatever arrives on a ticked port can trigger the automations that listen for it. MIDI cannot arm the show, cannot make it Safe and cannot run Earshot's own controls: it only triggers automations.
documents.s: Choose the MIDI inputs to listen to

documents.t: A new MIDI trigger in the mock show's editor. Not a real show. In the automation editor, under When, choose An incoming MIDI message. See Building an automation for the rest of the editor. Field Choices Notes Input port Any port, or one named port "Which MIDI input to listen on." The port must also be ticked in Setup, Show control. A port that is not there right now shows as "(not found)". Message Note on, Note off, Control change, Program change MIDI channel Any channel, or 1 to 16 Note, Controller or Program 0 to 127, or empty for any The label follows the message type. Minimum velocity or Minimum value 0 to 127, or empty ("Any") The message must be at least this strong. Use it to ignore a fader until it passes a point, or a soft touch on a pad. The Automations list then describes it in words, for example "Receives MIDI note on #60 on channel 1 from IAC Bus 1". Actions in that automation can use what arrived: Variable Holds {{midi.port}} The input port the message arrived on {{midi.channel}} The MIDI channel, 1 to 16 {{midi.note}} The note number (note messages) {{midi.velocity}} The velocity (note messages) {{midi.controller}} The controller number (control change) {{midi.value}} The controller value (control change) {{midi.program}} The program number (program change) See Variables.

Tick the pad controller's port under Setup, Show control, MIDI inputs. Automations, New automation. Name it "Standby pad". When: An incoming MIDI message. Message: Note on. Note: 60. Leave the port and channel on Any. Then: add Flash an alert with the text STANDBY. Save. While the show is Safe, press the pad and look in Activity: the row says Would have fired Standby pad with Dry run. Every MIDI message that arrives on a ticked port is logged in Activity as "MIDI in", so you can press the pad first and read off its note and channel.

An automation limited to named people never fires from MIDI, because no voice was heard. Activity says "no voice was heard for this trigger". See Automations limited to people. Like every automation, it sends nothing unless the show is Armed.
documents.s: What a MIDI trigger cannot do

documents.t: Add the action Send MIDI under Then. See Actions. Field Notes Output port One of this computer's MIDI output ports. A port that is not there right now shows as "(not found)". Message Note on, Note off, Control change, Program change, or Raw bytes MIDI channel (1 to 16) For every message except Raw bytes. Note, Velocity Note on (Note off has only Note). 0 to 127. Controller, Value Control change. 0 to 127. Program Program change. 0 to 127. Raw bytes (hex) "Like 90 3C 7F: status byte, then data bytes." Only hex digits, separated by spaces. The first byte must be a status byte. The note, velocity, controller, value and program boxes accept a variable, so a spoken number can become a program change: with the phrase preset {n}, set Program to {{capture.n}}. The result must be a whole number from 0 to 127. If it is not, that message is not sent, and Activity says why.

If the MIDI port is busy for more than 1 second, the send is dropped. Activity says "not sent: the MIDI port was busy for more than 1 s". It is never sent late and reported as sent. A MIDI cue is on time or it does not go.
documents.s: A MIDI send is on time or it does not go

documents.t: Pressing Make safe stops a MIDI message even while its port is still opening. The message is checked again right before it goes to the driver. Safe cannot recall a MIDI message already handed to the driver. See Safe and Armed.

A feedback loop is an automation whose MIDI output comes back in as its own trigger: for example, it sends note 60 to a port that is also a ticked input, and it is triggered by note 60. The runaway stop (20 firings in 10 seconds) applies to automations started by OSC or a web request. MIDI is exempt from it. A MIDI loop is limited only by the rule that any two firings of one automation from anything other than speech are at least 0.1 seconds apart. That is about ten firings a second. It carries on until you make the show Safe. To avoid one: do not tick, as an input, a port that an automation sends to. If you must, give the automation a Cooldown long enough to break the loop, and trigger on a different note from the one it sends.

Is the port ticked under Setup, Show control, MIDI inputs? Press Refresh if the controller was plugged in late. Does Activity show "MIDI in" rows when you press the control? If not, the message is not reaching Earshot. Do the message type, channel and number in the automation match what Activity shows? Is there a Minimum velocity or Minimum value the control is not reaching? Is the show Armed? In Safe, Activity shows the row as a Dry run. Is the automation on, with no Problem badge? See When an automation is not running.

Worked examples of the messages in the address list. Read OSC input first: nothing here works until OSC input is switched on, and most of it needs the level Trigger automations and the sending device on the allowed list. What has been tried The Python examples on this page that use only Python's own library were run against a demo host on the same computer (over 127.0.0.1), and the results shown are what came back. The oscsend and python-osc lines send the same messages but were not run for this manual. Nothing here has been tried against a real console, or between two computers on a real network. Try your own gear in rehearsal. See Limits and known behaviour. The examples use these values. Change them to yours. Value In the examples Where to find yours The host's address 192.168.1.20 Setup, Access, Address for the crew UDP port 4781 Setup, Show control, UDP port TCP port 4782 Setup, Show control, TCP port (optional). Empty until you set one. A channel Show Caller, short name show-caller, first in the list Setup, Channels An automation Go cue, short name go-cue Automations

oscsend comes with liblo (on a Mac with Homebrew, brew install liblo). Its form is: host, port, address, then the argument types and the arguments. oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/armed/off The type letters are s for a string, i for a whole number, f for a decimal number, and T and F for true and false (which take no value). oscsend only sends. It cannot show a reply.
from pythonosc.udp_client import SimpleUDPClient earshot = SimpleUDPClient("192.168.1.20", 4781) earshot.send_message("/earshot/armed/off", [])

An OSC message is small enough to build by hand. This helper is used in the rest of the page. It needs only Python 3. import socket import struct def pad(data: bytes) -> bytes: """OSC strings end with a zero byte and are padded to a multiple of four.""" return data + b"\0" * (4 - len(data) % 4) def osc(address: str, *args) -> bytes: """Build one OSC message. Arguments may be str, int, float, True or False.""" tags, data = ",", b"" for arg in args: if arg is True: tags += "T" elif arg is False: tags += "F" elif isinstance(arg, int): tags += "i" data += struct.pack(">i", arg) elif isinstance(arg, float): tags += "f" data += struct.pack(">f", arg) else: tags += "s" data += pad(str(arg).encode()) return pad(address.encode()) + pad(tags.encode()) + data EARSHOT = ("192.168.1.20", 4781) udp = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/armed/off"), EARSHOT)

This works from any device, at every level, over UDP or TCP. It is the one message worth putting on a button on every desk. oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/armed/off The other spelling takes one argument: false, the number 0, or the string "off". oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/armed F oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/armed i 0 oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/armed s off udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/armed/off"), EARSHOT) udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/armed", False), EARSHOT) There is no reply. Look at the header of any Earshot screen: it shows Safe. tip Send Safe as a small message on its own, not inside a large bundle. See "Safe always wins" in OSC input.

/earshot/ping comes back as /earshot/reply/pong with the arguments you sent. /earshot/version comes back as /earshot/reply/version with the app version. Both work from any device at every level, so they are the way to prove that the address, the port and the network are right before you try anything else. The reply goes to the address and port the message came from, so listen on the same socket you sent from: udp.settimeout(2) udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/ping", 7, "hello"), EARSHOT) print(udp.recvfrom(4096)[0]) udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/version"), EARSHOT) print(udp.recvfrom(4096)[0]) What came back from the demo host: b'/earshot/reply/pong\x00,is\x00\x00\x00\x00\x07hello\x00\x00\x00' b'/earshot/reply/version\x00\x00,s\x00\x000.1.0\x00\x00\x00' That is /earshot/reply/pong 7 "hello" and /earshot/reply/version "0.1.0". If nothing comes back within two seconds, OSC input is off, the port is wrong, or something between the two computers is blocking UDP.
documents.s: Check the connection: ping and version

documents.t: Needs the level Trigger automations. This changes the Earshot window on the host computer only. It is never sent to phones or other computers, and it does nothing while someone on the host is in Setup, Automations, Archive or Activity. By name, as an argument: oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/channel/select s "Show Caller" By short name, in the address: oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/channel/show-caller/select By position (1 is the first channel), in the address or as an argument: oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/channel/1/select oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/channel/select i 1 Step through the channels, and get back to the newest line: oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/channel/next oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/channel/previous oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/scroll/live
documents.s: Select a channel on the host's screen

documents.t: Needs Trigger automations. The line appears in that channel with a Typed badge, as if someone had typed it in the Feed. oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/channel/show-caller/send s "Front of house is clear" oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/channel/send ss "Show Caller" "Front of house is clear" udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/channel/show-caller/send", "Front of house is clear"), EARSHOT) udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/channel/send", "Show Caller", "Front of house is clear"), EARSHOT) A typed line never fires a phrase automation, so a console cannot use this to "say" a cue. To fire an automation from a console, see "Run an automation" below.
documents.s: Send a typed line into a channel

documents.t: Needs Trigger automations. The first argument is the text. The second, if you send one, is a colour. The third, if you send one, makes the alert stay until an operator presses Acknowledge. oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/flash s "Five minutes" oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/flash ss "HOLD" "#ff4639" oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/flash ssT "HOLD" "#ff4639" udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/flash", "Five minutes"), EARSHOT) udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/flash", "HOLD", "#ff4639", True), EARSHOT) The last one stays on every screen until someone acknowledges it. The until-ack argument can be true or false, or the numbers 1 or 0.
documents.s: Flash an alert on every screen

documents.t: Needs Trigger automations. The marker goes into the current session at this moment. The label is optional. oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/marker/add s "Act two" oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/marker/add Find it afterwards in the Archive, in the session's marker list. Do not confuse this with /earshot/channel/mark, which means mark read: it clears the unread counts on the host's screen.

Needs Trigger automations. This is the same as pressing Run now. While the show is Safe it is a dry run: Activity shows what would have been sent, and nothing is sent. By short name, in the address: oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/automation/go-cue/trigger By name, short name or id, as an argument: oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /earshot/automation/trigger s "Go cue" udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/automation/go-cue/trigger"), EARSHOT) Things to know: A manual run carries no spoken words, so a value such as {{capture.number}} is empty. An automation that puts a spoken number into an OSC address has nothing to put there when you run it this way. Use an OSC-triggered automation instead (next section) if the console needs to pass a value. Press it twice less than 0.1 seconds apart and the second is refused. An automation started by OSC that fires more than 20 times in 10 seconds is stopped. See OSC input.

An automation whose trigger is An incoming OSC message listens for an address of your own choosing, outside /earshot/. Put a name in braces where a value goes. In the automation editor, under When, choose An incoming OSC message and give it the pattern /cue/{n}/go. Give it an action that uses the value, for example Add a marker with the label Cue {{capture.n}} called from the desk. From the console, send: oscsend 192.168.1.20 4781 /cue/7/go The automation fires with {{capture.n}} set to 7. The arguments of the message are available too, as {{osc.args.0}}, {{osc.args.1}} and so on, and the whole address as {{osc.address}}. See Triggers and Variables. This needs the level Trigger automations and the console on the allowed list. Like every automation, it sends nothing unless the show is Armed.
documents.s: Fire an automation with a value from the console

documents.t: Needs Trigger automations. The reply is /earshot/reply/automation/list with one string per automation: its short name. udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/automation/list"), EARSHOT) print(udp.recvfrom(4096)[0]) From the demo host, which has one automation: b'/earshot/reply/automation/list\x00\x00,s\x00\x00standby-marker\x00\x00'

A device that is allowed to control gets an error back when a message cannot be carried out. It is /earshot/error with two strings: the address you sent, and the reason. udp.sendto(osc("/earshot/nonsense"), EARSHOT) print(udp.recvfrom(4096)[0]) b'/earshot/error\x00\x00,ss\x00/earshot/nonsense\x00\x00\x00unknown Earshot OSC command\x00' A device that is not allowed to control gets no error back. Look in Activity on the host instead: refused OSC is logged there with the sender's address and the reason, for example "OSC from 10.0.0.9 refused: this source is not allowed to trigger".

danger Arming lets automations really send cues. Read Safe and Armed first. Most shows should arm from the screen, by hand, and use OSC only to make Safe. Arming by OSC needs all of these: the level Full control, including arming, a TCP port set and saved, the sending device on the allowed list (or it is the host itself), and a TCP connection. Sent over UDP, /earshot/armed/on does nothing, and Activity says "Arming by OSC needs the TCP port". Earshot's TCP port speaks OSC 1.1: each message is wrapped in SLIP framing. That means a byte 0xC0 before and after each message, with any 0xC0 inside the message written as 0xDB 0xDC and any 0xDB as 0xDB 0xDD. Many consoles and OSC libraries offer this as "TCP (SLIP)" or "OSC 1.1". The older style, where each message starts with its length, is not accepted. With the osc() helper from the top of the page: import socket END, ESC = b"\xc0", b"\xdb" def slip(message: bytes) -> bytes: """Wrap one OSC message in SLIP framing (OSC 1.1 over TCP).""" return END + message.replace(ESC, b"\xdb\xdd").replace(END, b"\xdb\xdc") + END tcp = socket.create_connection(("192.168.1.20", 4782)) tcp.sendall(slip(osc("/earshot/armed/on"))) # arms # ... the show runs ... tcp.sendall(slip(osc("/earshot/armed/off"))) # makes Safe tcp.close() Run against the demo host on the same computer, with the level at Full control: /earshot/armed/on over UDP left the show Safe; the same message over TCP armed it; /earshot/armed/off made it Safe again. /earshot/armed with true over TCP arms as well. Replies come back over the same connection, framed the same way. A ping sent over TCP came back as: b'\xc0/earshot/reply/pong\x00,i\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x01\xc0' Things to know about the TCP connection: It must begin with an OSC message. Anything else closes it at once. One bad frame closes it. It is closed after 60 seconds with nothing sent. Send /earshot/ping every so often to keep it open, or open a new connection each time.

Arm and Safe are applied in the order they arrive, and the last one wins. You send The show ends Arm, then Safe, as two packets (or two TCP frames) Safe Safe, then Arm, as two packets over TCP Armed Arm and Safe in one bundle, in either order Safe. The Arm is ignored: "Arm ignored: the same OSC packet also made the show Safe". Safe by UDP while an Arm is still on its way by TCP Whichever the host receives last wins. If you mean both, send them as separate packets. If you mean "definitely Safe", send Safe on its own, and send it again if you are unsure: making Safe is never rate-limited.
documents.s: Arm and Safe: the order matters

documents.t: Every console words this differently, so these are the things to enter, not the menus to find them in.
