Enter Value Destination address The host's address, for example 192.168.1.20 Destination port The UDP port from Show control (4781 unless you changed it) Type OSC message, UDP Message, to make Safe /earshot/armed/off with no arguments Message, to add a marker /earshot/marker/add with one string argument, for example Act two Message, to run an automation /earshot/automation/go-cue/trigger with no arguments On Earshot: OSC input on, the level at Trigger automations (for the marker and the automation), and the playback machine's IP address under Devices allowed to control.
documents.s: A playback machine sending a network cue (for example QLab)

documents.t: Enter Value OSC output address (the "TX" address) The host's address OSC output port (the "TX" port) The UDP port from Show control The string or command the macro sends /earshot/armed/off, or your own plain address such as /cue/7/go Many desks add their own prefix to every address they send, or send their own messages on every cue. Look at Activity on the Earshot host while you press the button on the desk. Every message Earshot lets through is logged there as "OSC in", with its address, its arguments and where it came from, so you can see exactly what the desk sent and match your automation's pattern to it. A message that was refused is logged with the reason.
documents.s: A lighting desk macro or OSC output

documents.t: To have Earshot send a cue to the desk when it hears a phrase, you do not need OSC input at all. Add the desk as an OSC destination and use a Send OSC action. See Actions and Recipes.

Send /earshot/ping and wait for the pong. No pong means the message is not reaching Earshot: check that OSC input is on, the port, the network, and any firewall on the host. A pong but nothing else works: check the level, and that the sending device's IP address is on the allowed list. Look in Activity on the host. Refused OSC is logged with the reason. Check the spelling against the address list. There are no aliases. The full list is in Troubleshooting.

OSC input lets a lighting desk, a show controller or an app send messages to Earshot: to make the show Safe, to trigger an automation, to add a marker, or (at the highest level, over TCP) to arm. OSC carries no sign-in. Earshot decides what a message may do by where it came from and by the level you choose here. Open Setup, then Show control. Only admins can. Show control in the mock show. It is not a real show. The mock show uses UDP port 53000; a new show uses 4781. warning OSC input has been tried only in automated tests against stand-ins on one Mac. No real console has been connected. See Limits and known behaviour.

OSC input is off by default. While it is off there is no listener at all. No OSC message does anything, not even Make safe. The screen says "OSC input is off, so no device can control Earshot by OSC — not even to make it Safe." Under Controllers, turn on Controllers may send OSC to Earshot. Its hint reads "Lighting desks, show controllers and apps can send Earshot OSC messages. What they may do is set below." If the level is already above Make safe only, Earshot asks "Switch on OSC control?" first and says what listed devices will be able to do. Press Switch on OSC control to confirm. Set the ports (below) and press Save ports. Once it is on, the screen says "When OSC input is on, any device can make the show Safe."

Setting Default Notes UDP port 4781 What most devices send. TCP port (optional) Empty Empty means TCP is off. It cannot be the same as the web port (4780): the screen says "TCP port: That is the port the web app uses. Choose another." Type the ports, then press Save ports. Until you do, the screen says "Not saved yet." Afterwards it says "Ports saved." A port is a whole number from 1 to 65535. The screen's own hint: "UDP is what most devices send. Arming works only over TCP, and a TCP sender's address cannot be faked. Leave the TCP port empty to switch TCP off." TCP uses SLIP framing (OSC 1.1). Most consoles call this "TCP (SLIP)" or "OSC 1.1". The older "length prefix" TCP style (OSC 1.0) is not accepted. Which network address it listens on. OSC listens only on the network address the show is set to (all of this computer's addresses by default). If that address is not a usable IP address, or a port cannot be opened, OSC input stays off and an alert says why. It never falls back to listening everywhere.

Under What incoming OSC may do, pick a card, then press Apply. Until you do, the screen says "Not applied yet." Apply always asks you to confirm, and says what changes. The card in force carries the badge In use now. Level The card says What a message may do Make safe only (the default) "Any device can make the show Safe. Nothing else." Any device can make the show Safe, and send ping and version. Nothing else, from anyone, including this computer. Trigger automations "This computer and listed devices can also fire OSC-triggered automations, run an automation by name, send a typed line to a channel, add markers and use the view controls. They cannot arm and cannot clear transcripts. Typed lines never fire automations." This computer and the devices you list can also do everything marked Trigger in the address list. Full control, including arming "Listed devices can do everything an operator can. Arming works only over the TCP port." Listed devices can also clear transcripts, and arm. Arming works only over the TCP port. What Apply asks: Moving to Question Button Trigger automations (up from Make safe only) "Let listed devices trigger automations?" Allow triggers Trigger automations (down from Full control) "Stop listed devices arming?" Stop arming by OSC Full control, including arming "Allow full control by OSC?" It says: "OSC has no sign-in. Any listed device will be able to arm the show and fire cues. Arming works only over the TCP port." If no TCP port is set it adds "No TCP port is set, so nobody can arm by OSC until you set one." Allow full control Make safe only "Go back to making the show Safe only?" It says: "Devices will only be able to make the show Safe. Triggers and arming by OSC stop working." Make safe only tip Use the lowest level that does the job. A desk that only needs a panic button needs Make safe only. A desk that fires Earshot automations needs Trigger automations. Very few shows need Full control.

The mock show with OSC input switched on, Trigger automations in use and one device allowed. The mock's UDP port reads 53000; a real host starts at 4781. Not a real show. Under Devices allowed to control the screen says "This computer and these devices can do more than make the show Safe. Use each device's IP address." The list starts empty, shown as "Only this computer". Type an address under Add a device (for example 192.168.1.40) and add it. Earshot asks "Let 192.168.1.40 control Earshot?" and says "That device will be able to trigger automations. OSC has no sign-in, so anything using that address can." (the middle of the sentence follows the level in force). Press Add device. One IP address per device. No ranges, no wildcards, no names, no port. The screen tells you which rule you broke, for example "Type one address, not a range. Add each device on its own." or "Host names are not accepted. Type the device's IP address, like 192.168.1.40." IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are both accepted. The list holds at most 64 devices. To take a device off, press the bin next to its address. "This computer" always counts as allowed. That is safe because the operating system does not accept a packet with a loopback address (127.0.0.1 or ::1) from the network. macOS, Linux and Windows all drop such packets. The list matters only above Make safe only. At Make safe only, nobody can trigger anything, listed or not, and that includes this computer.

Make Safe works from any device, over UDP or TCP, whatever the level, as long as OSC input is on. So do ping and version. The device does not have to be on the list. There are two ways to send it: /earshot/armed/off /earshot/armed false (or the number 0, or the string "off") See OSC examples for how to send them.

Arming by OSC works only over TCP, never UDP. A UDP sender's address can be faked by anyone on the same network. A list of allowed devices therefore cannot protect arming over UDP: anyone could pretend to be your console. A TCP connection has to be answered by the real device, so its address cannot be faked the same way. To arm by OSC you need all four of these: OSC input switched on. The level set to Full control, including arming. A TCP port set and saved. The sending device on the Devices allowed to control list (or it is this computer), and connected by TCP. If the TCP port is empty, nobody can arm by OSC. Activity says so ("Arming by OSC needs the TCP port"). At the Trigger automations level, UDP is allowed from listed devices, but remember that a UDP sender can be forged. Use TCP for anything that matters.

Arm and Safe take effect the moment they arrive, in the order they arrive. They are never queued behind other messages, so an Arm followed by a Safe always ends Safe. OSC, the app and the API share one order: a Safe from any of them beats an Arm from any of them that was received earlier. Other controls wait in a short queue. Making the show Safe empties that queue. A control that arrived before the Safe never runs after it, even if the show is armed again in the meantime. An automation trigger that arrived while the show was Safe runs as a dry run: nothing is sent. Inside one packet: A Safe anywhere in a packet or bundle, at any depth, is applied even if the rest of the packet is refused: too many messages, nested too deep, timed too far ahead, next to a bad address, from a sender over its limit or not allowed. Only a packet over the size limit is not looked into. A damaged bundle (one that cannot be read as OSC) that visibly contains a make-Safe message still makes the show Safe. Earshot looks for the exact Safe message inside it. Nothing else in a damaged bundle is ever acted on. Only damaged bundles are searched this way. A single damaged message that is not in a bundle is ignored. A packet or TCP frame over 8 KiB is refused unread (on TCP, the connection is closed), so a Safe inside either is not applied. Send Safe as a small, plain message. A packet that contains a Safe never arms. Every Arm in the same packet is ignored, in any order and at any depth. Activity says "Arm ignored: the same OSC packet also made the show Safe". Send Arm and Safe as separate packets (or separate frames on one TCP connection) if you mean both: they are then applied in the order they arrive. If a bundle contains a Safe, any automation trigger in it runs as a dry run. While Earshot is shutting down, nothing fires and the show cannot be armed. danger Safe stops what Earshot would send next. It cannot recall anything that has already left this computer. See Safe and Armed.

Limit Value Messages from one sender 50 a second (bursts of 100). The rest are dropped and counted. Making Safe is never limited. Packet size Up to 8 KiB. Bundles Up to 32 messages, nested at most 4 deep. Bundle time tags Not scheduled. A bundle timed more than 1 second ahead is refused. Anything else runs at once. Address patterns Addresses containing *, ?, [, ], { or } are refused: one message does at most one thing. Senders remembered for these limits 1 024. Refusal lines in Activity At most once per sender every 10 seconds, with a count, and at most 10 lines every 10 seconds in all (then one line counting the rest). A refusal in Activity reads like "OSC from 10.0.0.9 refused: this source is not allowed to trigger". The reasons you may see: Activity says What it means "OSC control is set to Safe only" The level is Make safe only. "this source is not allowed to trigger" The sender is not on the list. "this source is not allowed to arm" The sender is not on the list, and it tried to arm. "this control needs full OSC control" The address is marked Full (clearing a transcript) and the level is Trigger automations. "Arming by OSC needs the TCP port" The level is Full, but the Arm came over UDP. "arming over OSC needs full OSC control (and the TCP port)" An Arm at the Trigger automations level. "address patterns are not accepted" The address had pattern characters in it. "messages dropped (more than 50 a second)" The sender is over its limit. "not run: the show was made Safe after this arrived" A control was waiting in the queue when a Safe arrived. Changing OSC input (off, ports, level, allowed devices) closes every open connection and restarts the listener. Every message is checked against the settings in force when it arrives.

A connection must start with an OSC message or bundle. If its first bytes look like a web request (GET, POST and so on) or a secure-connection hello, it is closed at once and nothing in it is acted on. This stops a web page in a browser on the host computer from posting OSC to the port. Activity says "a TCP connection that does not speak OSC (HTTP or TLS?) was closed". The first frame that is not a well-formed SLIP-framed OSC message or bundle (it must start with / or #bundle), or is over 8 KiB, closes the connection. Nothing after it is read. A connection idle for 60 seconds is closed. Send a /earshot/ping now and then to keep one open. At most 32 connections are open at once.

Replies go back to the sender, under /earshot/reply/.... On UDP they go to the address and port the message came from, so the sending program must listen on the port it sends from. On TCP they come back over the same connection. Errors come back as /earshot/error with two strings: the address received and the reason. For example, /earshot/nonsense is answered /earshot/error "/earshot/nonsense" "unknown Earshot OSC command". Errors are sent only to senders allowed to control. Earshot never answers anything under /earshot/reply or /earshot/error, never replies to a multicast address or to its own port, and sends at most 10 replies a second to one destination. Two Earshot computers therefore cannot ping-pong. Only three addresses reply at all: /earshot/ping, /earshot/version and /earshot/automation/list. See OSC addresses.

An automation fired by OSC or a web request (and anything it chains) that really fires more than 20 times in 10 seconds is stopped. An alert reads "'Name' fired 20 times in 10 seconds and was stopped". It stays stopped until the show is made Safe and armed again, or the automation is edited. This is aimed at loops, for example a console that echoes OSC back into Earshot. Any two firings of one automation from anything other than speech are at least 0.1 seconds apart. MIDI and speech are exempt from the stop. See MIDI for what that means for a MIDI feedback loop. See When an automation is not running.
Work down the list in Troubleshooting.

This is the complete list of OSC addresses Earshot accepts. It is the same table as docs/osc.md in the repository, which a test checks against the engine, so the spellings here are exactly what Earshot accepts. Spellings are exact. There are no aliases. /earshot/safe, /earshot/arm and /Earshot/armed/off do nothing. Everything here applies only when OSC input is on. It is off by default. See OSC input for how to turn it on, what the levels mean and which devices are allowed.

Column Meaning Address What to send. <channel> and <automation> are placeholders: see below. Arguments What to send with it. "none" means the message must have no arguments: an unexpected argument is refused ("takes no arguments"). Reply What Earshot sends back to the sender, if anything. Level The lowest setting of What incoming OSC may do that allows it. Any device works at every level, from any sender. Trigger needs Trigger automations or higher, and a sender on the allowed list (or this computer). Full needs Full control, including arming, and a sender on the list. Transport UDP, TCP, or both. TCP is SLIP-framed (OSC 1.1).

Address Arguments Reply Level Transport /earshot/armed/off none none any device UDP or TCP /earshot/armed one: false, 0 or "off" (makes Safe) none any device UDP or TCP /earshot/ping any /earshot/reply/pong, with the same arguments any device UDP or TCP /earshot/version none /earshot/reply/version, the app version (string) any device UDP or TCP /earshot/channel/next none none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/channel/previous none none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/channel/select channel (string or int) none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/channel/<channel>/select none none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/channel/<channel>/send text (string or number) none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/channel/send channel (string or int), text (string or number) none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/channel/<channel>/mark none none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/channel/mark optional channel (string or int); none marks every channel none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/channel/<channel>/clear none none Full UDP or TCP /earshot/channel/clear optional channel (string or int); none clears every channel none Full UDP or TCP /earshot/scroll/up none none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/scroll/down none none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/scroll/live none none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/font/up none none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/font/down none none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/flash text (string), optional colour (string), optional until-ack (true/false or 1/0) none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/marker/add optional label (string) none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/automation/trigger automation id, slug or name (string) none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/automation/<automation>/trigger none none Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/automation/list none /earshot/reply/automation/list, one string per automation slug Trigger UDP or TCP /earshot/armed/on none none Full TCP only /earshot/armed one: true, 1 or "on" (arms) none Full TCP only /earshot/armed appears twice on purpose. With false, 0 or "off" it makes the show Safe, from any device. With true, 1 or "on" it arms, and that needs the Full level, an allowed device and TCP.

A channel can be named three ways: Way Example Notes Its name Show Caller Any case. Its short name show-caller The Slug box in the channel's settings (Setup, Channels). Its position 1 1 is the first channel in show order. As an argument (/earshot/channel/select, /earshot/channel/send, /earshot/channel/mark, /earshot/channel/clear) all three work. A position can be sent as a number or as a string. Inside an address (/earshot/channel/<channel>/select and the others) use the short name or the position, for example /earshot/channel/show-caller/select or /earshot/channel/1/select. An OSC address cannot contain a space, so a name with a space in it has to go as an argument instead.

An automation's id, its short name or its name. Inside an address use the short name, for example /earshot/automation/go-cue/trigger. As an argument (/earshot/automation/trigger) the name works too, for example the string Go cue. The short name is the Short name in the automation editor. /earshot/automation/list replies with every automation's short name.

/earshot/armed/off and /earshot/armed with false make the show Safe. They work from any device, over UDP or TCP, at every level, and are never rate-limited. /earshot/armed/on and /earshot/armed with true arm the show. They need the Full level, an allowed device, and TCP. Over UDP they are refused, whatever else is set. A packet or bundle that contains a Safe never arms. See OSC input.

/earshot/ping is answered with /earshot/reply/pong and the same arguments you sent. /earshot/version is answered with /earshot/reply/version and the app version as a string. Both work from any device. Use them to check a cable, a port number or a firewall.

/earshot/channel/<channel>/send and /earshot/channel/send put a typed line into a channel, as if someone had typed it in the Feed. Typed lines never fire phrase automations, however they arrive. /earshot/flash flashes a message across every screen. The optional second argument is a colour, such as #ff4639. If the optional third argument is true (or 1), the message stays until an operator presses Acknowledge. /earshot/marker/add adds a marker to the session at this moment, with the label you send, if any. See Archive and search.

/earshot/automation/trigger and /earshot/automation/<automation>/trigger run one automation, like pressing Run now. While the show is Safe this is a dry run: Activity shows what would have been sent, and nothing is sent. /earshot/automation/list replies with one string per automation: its short name. An automation limited to named people never fires from OSC, because there is no voice. See Automations limited to people.

/earshot/channel/<channel>/clear and /earshot/channel/clear clear a channel's transcript (or every channel's, if you send no channel). The lines of the current session are deleted. Past sessions are not touched. They need the Full level. danger Clearing a transcript also makes its saved audio unreachable at once, and deletes the files. See Replay a line's audio.
mark means mark read: /earshot/channel/<channel>/mark and /earshot/channel/mark clear the unread counts. They do not add a marker. To add a marker, use /earshot/marker/add.

An address that does not start /earshot/ is a plain address. It fires the automations whose OSC trigger matches it. That needs the Trigger level and an allowed device, over UDP or TCP. For example, an automation whose trigger is An incoming OSC message with the pattern /cue/{n}/go fires when a console sends /cue/7/go, and its actions can use {{capture.n}}, {{osc.address}} and {{osc.args.0}}. See Triggers and Variables. An incoming address may not itself contain pattern characters (*, ?, [, ], {, }): one message does at most one thing.

These addresses are view controls: /earshot/channel/next, /earshot/channel/previous /earshot/channel/select, /earshot/channel/<channel>/select /earshot/channel/mark, /earshot/channel/<channel>/mark /earshot/scroll/up, /earshot/scroll/down, /earshot/scroll/live /earshot/font/up, /earshot/font/down They are carried out by the Earshot window on the host computer (and by a browser open on that same computer). They are never sent to phones, tablets or other computers. They change what is shown, not the show. On the host's window: Select channel changes the Feed's filter if one is set. It shows that channel in Focus. If the window is on the Feed with all channels showing, or on Lanes, it switches to Focus on that channel. Next and previous step through the channels in show order and wrap round. Scroll up and down move the Feed one page. Scroll to live returns to the newest line. Font up and down change the text size on that window. Nothing happens while someone is in Setup, Automations, Archive or Activity. A cue never throws someone out of an editor.
documents.s: View controls change the host computer's own window only

documents.t: On a running host, the API reference (Setup, Show control, top right, or /docs) includes the same OSC list. See HTTP API. For worked examples of sending these messages, see OSC examples.
documents.s: Where else to find this list

documents.t: Earshot talks to other show gear in both directions. Messages come in from a console, a controller or a script, and can trigger automations or operate Earshot. Messages go out from automations to lighting desks, playback machines and web services. Everything that comes in is set on one screen: open Setup, then Show control. The page says "Decide how lighting desks, controllers and other devices may drive Earshot, and what Earshot does when it starts." Who can do this Only admins can open Setup. Operators and viewers see "Setup needs admin access". See Roles. The Show control screen in the mock show. It is not a real show. The mock show uses UDP port 53000; a new show uses 4781.
Nothing on the right-hand side happens while the show is Safe. In Safe, an automation that matches is logged as "would have fired" and nothing is sent. See Safe and Armed.
documents.s: What goes in and what comes out

documents.t: I want to… Use Read Make the show Safe from a button on a desk or controller OSC input, at any level OSC input Fire an Earshot automation from a console cue OSC input at Trigger automations, and an automation with the trigger An incoming OSC message OSC input, Triggers Run an automation by name from a console /earshot/automation/<automation>/trigger at Trigger automations OSC addresses Flash a message on every screen from a console /earshot/flash at Trigger automations OSC examples Drop a marker in the transcript from a console /earshot/marker/add at Trigger automations OSC examples Change what the host computer's own screen shows (channel, scroll, text size) The view controls at Trigger automations OSC addresses Arm the show from a console OSC input at Full control, including arming, over TCP only OSC input Fire an automation from a pad or a fader A ticked MIDI input port, and an automation with the trigger An incoming MIDI message MIDI Fire an automation from a script or another service A web request trigger (a webhook), or the HTTP API HTTP API Read the transcript from a script The HTTP API HTTP API Send a cue to a desk when a phrase is heard An automation with a Send OSC, Send MIDI or HTTP request action Actions

A new show accepts nothing from other gear until you say so. Setting Starts as What that means Controllers may send OSC to Earshot Off Nothing listens. No OSC message does anything, not even Make safe. What incoming OSC may do Make safe only Once OSC input is on, any device can make the show Safe, and nothing more. Devices allowed to control "Only this computer" No other device can trigger or arm until you add its IP address. TCP port (optional) Empty TCP is off, so nobody can arm by OSC. MIDI inputs None ticked No MIDI message is listened to. Start armed Off Earshot starts Safe. Allow automations to run shell commands Off Shell-command actions are refused. The show itself also starts Safe, so even a fully set-up automation sends nothing until someone arms it.

Part What is there Read Controllers The switch Controllers may send OSC to Earshot, the UDP port, the TCP port (optional) and Save ports OSC input What incoming OSC may do Three cards (Make safe only, Trigger automations, Full control, including arming) and Apply OSC input Devices allowed to control The list of IP addresses and Add a device OSC input MIDI inputs The ports to listen to, and Refresh MIDI Starting up and shell commands Start armed and Allow automations to run shell commands Below Earshot's OSC addresses A pointer to the address list in the API reference OSC addresses API reference (top right) Opens /docs on the host in a new tab HTTP API

Start armed makes automations able to fire as soon as Earshot starts. The switch says "Automations can fire as soon as Earshot starts. Leave this off unless the show runs unattended." Turning it on asks "Start Armed?" and says: "Automations can fire as soon as Earshot starts, before anyone has looked at the show. Leave this off unless the show runs unattended." danger With Start armed on, a restart of the host brings the show back Armed. Without it, a restart always comes back Safe. See What happens when the host restarts. An imported show file never changes this switch. It is a setting of this computer, not of the show. See Show files.

An automation can run a shell command on the host computer. This is off until an admin turns on Allow automations to run shell commands. The switch says "Automations will be able to run programs on this computer with your user account's rights." Turning it on asks "Allow shell commands?" and says: "Automations will be able to run programs on this computer with the rights of the account Earshot runs as. Shell automations that were refused until now will start working, and run for real when the show is Armed." Press Allow shell commands to confirm. A shell command runs on the host, with the rights of the account Earshot runs as. It runs for real only while the show is Armed. Pressing Make safe stops a running shell command, together with the programs it started. (Stopping the child programs is untested on Windows.) Importing a show file never turns this switch on, and every automation with a shell action arrives switched off. Read what each one does, then switch it on yourself. See Actions for how a shell action is written.
documents.s: Allow automations to run shell commands

documents.t: At the top right of Show control, API reference opens /docs on the host in a new tab. It lists every web address Earshot answers, with an example for each, a walk-through of the live connection, and the OSC address list. It asks you to sign in to Earshot in that browser first, unless the show is Open. See HTTP API.

warning No real console has been connected to Earshot. MIDI, web requests and TCP OSC against real gear have been tried only in automated tests against stand-ins on one Mac. Try your own desk in rehearsal before you rely on any of this. See Limits and known behaviour.

A channel is one thing Earshot listens to: an input on your audio interface, a recording played in for rehearsal, or a place where people only type. This page covers the Channels screen and every setting in the channel editor. To make many channels at once from an audio interface, use Patch instead. See Patch and channels. Come here afterwards to rename, colour and fine-tune them. Who can do this Only admins can open Setup. Everyone else sees "Setup needs admin access". The desktop window and the Admin: address from earshotd are admin. See Roles.

Open Setup, then Channels. The mock show "Spring Tour at Harbour Hall". Invented channels, not a real show. Each row shows the channel's name in its colour, where its audio comes from (for example "Simulator: demo/show-caller.wav"), and a live level meter. The buttons on a row are: Control What it does The row itself Opens the channel in the editor on the right. Up and down arrows Move the channel up or down. This is the show order, which "next channel" and "previous channel" from a console step through. Duplicate Makes a copy called "name copy" with a new short name. A copy of a cloud-speech channel is made as a local channel, and the editor says "This copy uses speech on this computer. Choose cloud speech again if you want it." A channel from another Earshot computer cannot be duplicated. Delete (the bin) Asks "Delete name?" first. See below. The switch Turns the channel on or off without opening it. A disabled channel does not listen. Add at the top opens an empty editor. Fill it in and press Create channel. From another Earshot host adds a channel that another Earshot computer is listening to. That has its own page: Showing another Earshot computer's channels. If the show has no channels, the list says "No channels yet. Add one here, or tick inputs in Patch to make many at once." with an Open Patch link.

The confirmation says "name will be removed from the show, with its settings. This cannot be undone." It also warns you about two things if they apply: In groups: the channel is removed from those groups. Used by automations: the automations are named, and "will still point at a channel that no longer exists". Open each one and choose another channel, or it will never hear anything.

Press a channel to open it. The editor has a bar at the bottom with Save changes (or Create channel), Revert, and a note that reads "Unsaved changes" or "Saved". Nothing changes on the host until you save. If you try to leave with unsaved changes, Earshot asks first. If a save fails, the form stays exactly as you left it and the host's message appears above the button. The mock show. The channel plays a recording through the Simulator, so there is no real audio device here. At the top is the channel's live status: its level meter and badge. A new channel says "Save the channel to see its live level here."

Setting Notes Name What everyone reads in the Feed, for example "Show Caller". Required. Slug The channel's short name: lower-case letters, digits and single hyphens, like stage-left. Consoles use it in OSC addresses, and automation actions can use it as {{channel.slug}}. Leave it alone on a new channel and the host makes one from the name (the hint shows roughly what it will be). Two channels cannot share one: "Already used by name. Slugs must be unique." Colour Pick a swatch, or type a colour as #rrggbb. Changing a slug breaks what uses the old one Once a channel is saved, renaming it does not change its slug. That is deliberate. If you type a new slug yourself, the editor warns: "Used in OSC addresses and automations. Changing it breaks anything that uses the old one." A console sending /earshot/channel/show-caller/select stops working the moment the slug becomes something else. A name with no letters a to z or digits (for example a name in another script) cannot be turned into a slug. The editor says "This name has no letters or digits a to z, so type a slug yourself, like stage-left."

Source type has three choices. Source type What it is Its settings Audio device input One input of an audio interface on the host computer. Device (each is listed with its input count, for example "USB Audio Interface (2 in)") and Input number, counted from 1 "as labelled on the device". If another channel already uses that input, the hint says "Input 1 is also used by name." A device that has been unplugged is shown as "(not connected)". Simulator (WAV file) A recording played in as if it were live. Good for rehearsal and for testing automations with no crew on comms. WAV file path: "A path on the machine running Earshot." Loop the file plays it again and again. With the switch off, the channel goes Idle when the file ends. Typed text only No audio at all. "This channel has no audio. It only shows messages people type." None. The Simulator accepts a WAV file of any sample rate and any number of channels. It mixes the file to mono and plays it at normal speed through the same processing a real input gets.

Setting Notes Language "Detect automatically", or one of the listed languages, or Other… to type a language tag "such as sv or de-CH". Leave it on automatic unless a channel is always in one language and is being heard as another. Engine Local (on this machine) uses a speech model installed on the host. Demo (scripted text) plays made-up lines and needs no model. Deepgram (cloud) sends this channel's audio to a company outside the building, and asks you to confirm first. See Cloud and audio. Speech model Only for the local engine ("Only the local engine uses a model."). Default follows the Default speech model chosen under Setup, Models. If none is installed the hint says "No speech model is installed yet. Install one under Models." See Models. Show words as they are spoken "Partial text appears dimmed, then firms up. Uses more processing." With it off, a line appears only when the person has finished. See draft and final lines.

Setting Notes Gain A slider from -24 dB to +24 dB in half-decibel steps. "Trim before speech detection. Most inputs need none." Raise it for a quiet input whose speech is not being picked up. High-pass filter (100 Hz) "Cuts rumble and handling noise."

Switch What it does Enabled "A disabled channel does not listen." Allow typed messages "People can type lines into this channel." With it off, the Feed's typing box shows the channel as "(no typing)". Separate and recognise voices on this channel Separates consecutive speakers and discovers unfamiliar voices automatically. Requires CAM++. On for new audio channels; existing channels keep their previous setting. Give detected voices names in People. See People. Filter profanity Masks a short list of words in the transcript. It matches exact words only: other forms of a word are not masked unless they are on the list, and a listed word that is also someone's name is masked too. A channel with this on never shows what a changed line was changed from, because that would show the hidden words. Keep audio for replay "Saves the audio behind each line on the host computer so anyone who can read this channel can replay it." Off by default. See Replay a line's audio and the limits under Cloud and audio. Shared with other Earshot hosts Lets another Earshot computer show this channel. See Showing another Earshot computer's channels.

Install Moonshine tiny · English in Setup → Models, then choose it as the channel's Draft speech model for faster English live text. The main speech model still produces finished lines. Drafts may be revised; this option is not a guarantee of accuracy and falls back to the main model if unavailable. Expand Transcription timing in the Channels list to see median and 95th-percentile timing across this host over the last minute. Draft timing starts after detection; finished-line timing starts at the detected end of speech. Neither includes delivery to the screen. Queue depth shows work waiting to transcribe.

Open Advanced: speech detection at the bottom of the editor. "These control when a channel decides someone is speaking. The defaults suit most rooms." Each box shows its default beneath it, and Reset to defaults puts them all back. Setting Default What it decides Sensitivity (0 to 1) 0.5 How sure the detector must be that a moment of audio is speech. A higher number makes it pickier, so it ignores more noise and may miss quiet speech. A lower number picks up more, including noise. Pre-roll (ms) 500 How much audio from just before speech was noticed is kept with the line, so the first word is not clipped. Hangover (ms) 350 How long the channel must be quiet before Earshot decides the person has stopped and finishes the line. A longer hangover keeps a slow speaker's pauses in one line, and makes every final line arrive later. Shortest speech (ms) 64 How much speech must be heard before it counts as someone talking. Shorter bursts are ignored. Longest segment (ms) 15000 The longest a single line may run. Someone who talks without a pause is cut into lines of this length. It cannot be shorter than the shortest speech. Low latency applies the defaults above and enables live drafts. Comms / noisy feed uses a lower detection threshold and longer lead-in and pause allowance. These are starting points; neither separates overlapping voices or guarantees detection of every word. Existing untouched legacy defaults are upgraded on startup; custom settings are retained. Change one thing at a time If a channel misses quiet speech, check the input meter and adjust Gain only if the feed is too quiet. Gain also raises noise; avoid clipping. Save before judging its effect. If it writes lines out of background noise, raise Sensitivity a little (for example from 0.5 to 0.6) and listen again. Cues set to fire on final text wait for the hangover, so a long hangover slows your cues down.

You want to try an automation for "Lighting cue 42, go" tonight, and nobody is on comms. The repository carries a few short recordings of computer-made voices in fixtures/audio. One of them, showcaller.wav, says "Standby lighting cue forty two.", "Lighting cue forty two, go.", "Standby sound cue seven and video cue twelve." and "Sound cue seven, go." Open Setup, Channels, and press Add. Name: Rehearsal caller. Leave Slug empty. Pick a colour. Source type: Simulator (WAV file). WAV file path: the full path to the file on the host computer, for example /Users/you/earshot/fixtures/audio/showcaller.wav. Switch Loop the file on, so the lines come round again. Engine: Local (on this machine), with a speech model installed. (Choosing Demo (scripted text) would ignore the recording and play made-up lines.) Press Create channel. The level meter starts moving and the lines appear in the Feed. Leave the show Safe and watch Activity: each line that matches an automation is logged as "would have fired". See Testing automations. When rehearsal is over, switch the channel off with its switch, or delete it. These recordings are computer-made voices They are clean speech from a text-to-speech voice. A real party line is noisier, and recognition on it will be worse. See Limits and known behaviour.
documents.s: Example: a rehearsal channel from a recording

documents.t: A channel that comes from another Earshot computer is marked with a link icon and "from address". Its editor is much shorter: Audio source is replaced by "Where this channel comes from": the other computer's Address and Port, how it connects, and its link code. It has only Name, Slug, Colour and Enabled. There is no language, engine, gain, typing, voice recognition, profanity filter, saved audio, sharing or speech detection. Those belong to the computer that hears the audio. It has no level meter, because there is no audio here. It says "Lines from another host never fire automations here." The mock show with three invented linked channels: one working, one whose code was refused, and one that cannot be reached. Everything about them is on Showing another Earshot computer's channels.

Patch and channels: make many channels from an interface at once. Groups: put channels into folders. Status and badges: what Behind, No input, Offline and the others mean. Troubleshooting: when no text is appearing.

Open Setup, then Cloud & audio. The screen says what it is for: "Where audio and text may leave this computer, and how long saved audio is kept. Each cloud service is off until you choose it." It has three parts: Part What it controls What leaves the building if you turn it on Cloud speech (Deepgram) Speech recognition by an outside service, one channel at a time. That channel's audio, and your glossary words. Translation Which translator turns lines into other languages, and how many languages at once. With DeepL or Claude: the text of each translated line. No audio. Saved audio How long replay audio is kept, and how much. Nothing. Saved audio stays on the host. If you never choose a cloud option, no audio and no text goes to any company. Who can do this Only admins. Operators and viewers cannot open Setup. Viewers see only a "Cloud" mark on a cloud channel. The mock show. The key shown as saved is a stand-in, the counters are invented, and the saved-audio limits are the mock's, not the real defaults.

Cloud speech has never been run against the real Deepgram service It has been tested against a stand-in server only, and some details of how Deepgram answers are unverified. Before you rely on it, try one channel with a real key. Whether the model-improvement opt-out that Earshot sends changes Deepgram's price is also unconfirmed.

By default every channel is transcribed on the host computer by a local model. Cloud speech sends one channel's audio to Deepgram, a company outside the building, to be transcribed there instead. It is chosen per channel, never for the whole show. Only finished lines' audio goes to Deepgram. Drafts always stay on this computer. Your glossary words are sent with it, as hints. They travel in the request address. Every request carries Deepgram's model-improvement opt-out.

Save a key first (below), or the channel will carry on being transcribed locally. Open Setup, Channels, and the channel. Under Engine, choose Deepgram (cloud). Earshot asks "Send this channel's audio to Deepgram?" and says: "Audio from this channel will be sent to Deepgram, a company outside this building, to be transcribed. Words from your glossary are sent with it. Drafts stay on this computer." Press Send audio to Deepgram to confirm, or Cancel. Press Save changes. Until you save, the editor says "When you save, audio from this channel will be sent to Deepgram, outside this building, to be transcribed." The mock show: choosing Deepgram for the Monitors channel. Nothing is sent anywhere by the mock. If no key is saved, the confirmation adds: "No Deepgram key is saved yet, so this channel will be transcribed on this computer until you add one." A copy of a cloud channel (Duplicate) is made as a local channel. Choose cloud again, and confirm again.
documents.s: Turn it on for a channel

documents.t: Under Deepgram API key a badge says Key saved or No key. Type the key in Enter the Deepgram key (it reads Replace the Deepgram key if one is saved). Press Save key. The screen says "Key saved." "The key is stored on this computer and is never shown again." No browser, not even an admin's, is sent a saved key. See Saved secrets. Remove key asks "Remove the Deepgram key?" and warns: "Channels set to Deepgram will be transcribed on this computer until a key is saved again."

A channel set to cloud speech carries a small mark wherever it is listed. Hover it for the long form. Mark Meaning Cloud "Cloud speech: audio from this channel is sent to Deepgram, outside this building, to be transcribed." Cloud paused "Cloud speech is paused after failures. Lines are transcribed on this computer; Earshot tests the service with one short piece of audio about every 30 seconds." On this computer Either "Deepgram rejected the key, so this channel is transcribed on this computer. No audio is sent." or "No key saved, so this channel is transcribed on this computer." People who cannot read diagnostics (viewers) see only Cloud, meaning "Set to cloud speech: this channel's audio may be sent to Deepgram, outside this building."
documents.s: The mark on a cloud channel

documents.t: At the top of the Cloud speech part, a status box gives one of six states. Status The screen says Not used "No channel is set to cloud speech. Choose “Deepgram (cloud)” as a channel's engine, under Channels." No key "No key saved, so the channel set to cloud speech is being transcribed on this computer. Save a key below." Waiting "Set to cloud speech. Nothing has come back from Deepgram yet." Working "The channel set to cloud speech is sending audio to Deepgram." Paused "Paused after failures. Lines are transcribed on this computer; Earshot tests the service with one short piece of audio about every 30 seconds." Key rejected "Deepgram rejected this key. Enter the key again and save it to try once more." Under it are four counters, "Counted since Earshot started": Counter Counts Lines from the cloud Lines Deepgram transcribed. Lines from this computer "Lines from this computer are ones the cloud did not answer, or that were sent there while it was paused." Audio sent How much audio has gone out. Failures Requests that failed. The most recent reason is shown as Last problem:.

No line is lost. If Deepgram does not answer, the line is transcribed on this computer instead. After repeated failures cloud speech pauses. While it is paused, lines are transcribed on this computer. A little audio still leaves while it is Paused. Earshot sends one short piece of audio about every 30 seconds to test whether the service is back. If Deepgram rejects the key, uploads stop and everything is transcribed on this computer. Saving the key again makes Earshot try again. Cloud speech does not record, line by line, which engine produced a line. The counters are the only tally.

Viewers choose a language to read in from the display menu. This part of the screen decides what does the translating and how many languages at once. How it looks to a reader is on Read in another language.

Three cards. The one in use carries an In use now badge. Pick a card, then press Apply (until then it says "Not applied yet."). Card The app says This computer (the default) "Translates with the models installed under Models. Text never leaves this computer." DeepL "Sends the text of each translated line to DeepL, outside this building. Needs a DeepL key. If DeepL fails, models on this computer are used." Claude "Sends the text of each translated line to Anthropic, outside this building, to be translated by Claude. Needs an Anthropic key. If Claude fails, models on this computer are used." Choosing DeepL or Claude asks first, for example "Translate with DeepL?": "The text of each line that is translated will be sent to DeepL, a company outside this building. Audio is not sent." If no key is saved it adds "No DeepL key is saved yet, so DeepL will not be used until you add one below." Press Use DeepL to confirm. The screen then says "Now translating with DeepL." This computer needs a translation model for each language pair, installed under Setup, Models. German to English and English to Spanish have been run. The other pairs in the list are untested downloads. See Models.

"How many languages are translated at the same time, for everyone reading. Another language is refused while all of them are in use. 0 turns translation off." It starts at 4. Type a whole number and press Save. Everyone's choices share this limit: if four people are reading in four different languages, a fifth language is refused and that reader sees the host's own sentence saying so. Each loaded local pair uses about 330 MB of memory on the host, so a small computer may want a lower number.

Two key boxes, DeepL and Anthropic, work exactly like the Deepgram one: a Key saved or No key badge, Save key, Remove key, and "The key is stored on this computer and is never shown again." Removing one warns that the translator "will not be used for translation until a key is saved again".

A status box with four counters, "Counted since Earshot started": Counter Counts Languages in use The languages people are reading in at this moment. Lines translated Translations that worked. Lines that failed Lines that could not be translated. If someone picks a language that few lines can reach, the lines that cannot be translated stay in the original and are counted here. Lines skipped "A line is skipped when translation is busy, and then shows only the original." If a cloud translator has failed, the box says "The cloud translator is paused after a failure, so it is being skipped for now." and the models on this computer are used meanwhile. The most recent reason is shown as Last problem:. A reading aid, never a cue call Show jargon is often mistranslated. In testing, "Sound cue 7, go." came out in Spanish as "Suena a señal 7, vamos." and "kick drum" as "tambor de patada". Automations never see a translation. Do not call a cue from translated text.

A channel with Keep audio for replay on (Setup, Channels) "saves the audio behind each line on this computer, so anyone who can read that channel can replay it." Setting Starts at Meaning Keep for (days) 14 Clips older than this are deleted. At most (MB) 2048 If the total is over this size, the oldest go first. "0 means no limit." Type whole numbers and press Save (until then it says "Not saved yet."). The limits are checked when Earshot starts, every 10 minutes, when you change them, and as clips are added. Clearing a channel's transcript makes its audio unreachable at once, and the files are deleted. Anyone who can read the channel can replay it. That includes viewers. The audio is kept in the clips folder inside the host's data folder. See Data and files. How replay looks and behaves for a reader is on Replay a line's audio.

The FOH Audio channel is hard for the local model, and the production has agreed to send that one channel out. Setup, Cloud & audio: type the key under Deepgram API key, press Save key. The badge reads Key saved and the status reads Not used. Setup, Channels, FOH Audio: set Engine to Deepgram (cloud), confirm with Send audio to Deepgram, press Save changes. Back on Cloud & audio, the status reads Waiting, then Working once a line has come back. Lines from the cloud starts to count. In the Feed, FOH Audio now carries the Cloud mark. The other seven channels have none: their audio never leaves the computer. Tell the crew on that channel. Their voices are now going to an outside company. If the status turns to Paused mid-show, nothing needs doing: lines keep arriving, transcribed locally. If it turns to Key rejected, enter the key again.
documents.s: Example: one cloud channel, everything else local

documents.t: Every channel showing a Cloud mark is one you meant, and a key is saved. Translate with is on the card you meant. If it is DeepL or Claude, the production knows the text of lines is leaving the building. Keep for (days) suits the show's rules about recordings.
Channels: the Engine and Keep audio for replay settings. The glossary: its words travel with cloud speech. Privacy: the full list of what goes over the network. Limits and known behaviour.

The glossary is for "words Earshot often mis-hears — names, songs, gear". You give the right spelling and the ways it tends to come out wrong, and Earshot corrects the transcript. The one rule to remember: corrections change what you read. Automations hear what was said. Who can do this Only admins can open the Glossary. Everyone reads the corrected transcript.

Open Setup, then Glossary. Press Add a word. Type the Right spelling, for example Alesha. Choose a Kind: Name, Song, Cue, Gear or Other. Under Sounds like, type how it tends to come out, for example a lesha, and press Add. Add one for each wrong spelling you have seen. Press Save glossary. Until you save, the screen says "Not saved yet". Revert drops changes you have not saved. Search the glossary filters a long list by a word or a spelling. The mock show. The three entries are invented, and the mock host does not check them the way a real host does. The mock show's glossary has three entries: Right spelling Kind Sounds like Alesha Name aleesha, a leash a Leko Gear lecko, le co House Of The Rising Sun Song house of the rising son With the first two saved, a line the recogniser heard as "aleesha, the lecko on the front truss is flickering" is shown, saved and searched as "Alesha, the Leko on the front truss is flickering". The third is a useful lesson. On a real host it would be marked Not applied, because house of the rising son is made only of ordinary words. See When an entry is "Not applied" below. (The mock host in the picture does not check entries, so it shows no warning.)

As whole words, ignoring capitals. Split or joined spellings count as the same: with mon it or listed, "mon it or", "monit or" and "mon-it-or" all match. A possessive ending is kept: "aleesha's mic" becomes "Alesha's mic". A plain plural "s" is not matched unless you list it. A match never runs across a comma, a full stop or other punctuation that ends a clause. A word that is already the right spelling is never changed. The box will not take a spelling that is the same as the right spelling ("“Alesha” is the right spelling already. Type how it comes out wrong.") or one that is already listed. To remove a word, press its bin. Earshot asks "Remove “Alesha”?" and says "It stops being corrected once you save the glossary. Lines already transcribed keep the text they have."

Listed spellings and conservative known-name matches can be corrected. Distinctive, unambiguous near misses of known names may be corrected automatically. Add an explicit spelling for recurring misses. Names from People are also available to display correction. Numbers are never changed. A correction cannot take part in a number, so text either side of "cue 12" is corrected on its own. Words your automations listen for are kept. A "Sounds like" that would take one of those words away, or change it, is not applied, and its entry says why. Ordinary words are not rewritten. A "Sounds like" that is an ordinary word, or made only of ordinary words, is not applied unless it is just a spelling apart from the right spelling. Drafts can show corrections too. The unfinished last word is left alone until more speech arrives. The corrected text is what is saved, searched, exported and translated. Removing a word later does not touch lines already transcribed. Operators and admins can edit finished lines. Select the incorrect words or use the pencil, enter the correction, and save. Admins can also remember an observed mishearing for future speech. The original remains available; edits never fire automations. Concurrent conflicting edits are rejected rather than overwritten. Production cue abbreviations are expanded for display. For example, LXQ 912 go becomes LX Cue 912 go; cue numbers are preserved. Your words are also passed to the speech engine as hints, on engines that accept them. On a Deepgram channel that means they are sent to Deepgram. See Cloud and audio.

Earshot refuses a correction that could rewrite ordinary speech, touch a number, or change a word an automation listens for. The entry then shows Not applied: and the reason, and the top of the screen says, for example, "2 entries are not being applied. Each one says why below. The rest still work." What you entered Why it is not applied What to do Sounds like light for "Lightwalker" "'light' is an ordinary word; this alias would rewrite normal speech". Every "turn the light on" would become "turn the Lightwalker on". Use a spelling that is not an ordinary word on its own, such as lite walker. Sounds like house of the rising son, or the light for "Theo" It "is made of ordinary words, including a small word like 'of'". "Add a distinctive word to it", or accept that this one cannot be corrected safely. Sounds like down stage for "Downstage Dan" Every word is an ordinary word and it is not a mis-spelling of the right spelling. (clear calm for "Clear-Com" is allowed, because it is only a spelling apart.) Use a sounds-like that is a mis-spelling of the word. Right spelling Cue 12, Twelve or First Electric The word contains something that is read as a number ("'first', which is read as a number"). Numbers are never changed. Rewrite it without that word. Sounds like aleesha 2 The spelling contains a number. Remove the number. Sounds like you go for "Hugo", while an automation listens for go "'you go' would remove 'go' from the text", and an automation listens for that word. The transcript must never hide a cue word that was said, or show one that was not. "Keep 'go' in both the sounds-like and the term", or use a different sounds-like. The same Sounds like on two words, for example lisa for both "Alesha" and "Elisa" Earshot cannot know which you mean, so "it was ignored for both so neither is guessed". Remove it from one of them. A refusal on one spelling does not stop the entry's other spellings, or any other entry. Because the protected words come from your automations, an entry can become "Not applied" when you add or change an automation, and come back when you remove it. Look at this screen after editing automations.

The glossary changes only what people read. An automation is matched against what the recogniser heard, with numbers and show words tidied, and without glossary corrections. Each phrase trigger in the automation editor says so: "Automations hear what was said. Glossary corrections change only what you read." So if a cue depends on a word the recogniser gets wrong, add the mis-hearing to the automation's phrases. Example. You want "alesha go" to fire a cue. The recogniser writes "aleesha go". In the glossary, Alesha with Sounds like aleesha makes the Feed read "Alesha go". Good for readers. It does nothing for the cue. In the automation, set Match mode to Any of and give it two phrases: alesha go and aleesha go. Now the cue fires whichever way it is heard. See Triggers for match modes, and try the phrase on the Test bench.
documents.s: Automations hear what was said, not the corrected text

documents.t: Earshot does not overwrite their work. It says "The glossary was changed on another device." and offers two buttons: Button What happens Load the new version Their glossary replaces what is on your screen. Entries you had not saved are listed under "Your unsaved entries, not in the new version:", each with Add back. Replace it with mine Your version is saved over theirs.
documents.s: If another admin saved while you were editing

documents.t: It cannot fix a word the recogniser hears a different way every time. Only exact listed spellings are replaced. It cannot change a number, on purpose. A wrong number sends the wrong cue. See How Earshot hears numbers. It does not change draft text. A draft line on screen is as heard. The correction lands when the line is final. It will not replace an ordinary word or phrase, even if the recogniser keeps writing one in place of a name. On a channel set to cloud speech, your glossary words leave the building with the audio.
The glossary is part of the show file. Export show file includes it, and an import replaces this computer's glossary with the one in the file. See Show files.
Reading the transcript: the pencil on a changed line. Triggers and Recipes. Troubleshooting: "A name keeps coming out wrong".

Use this when several people talk on one comms channel and you want to see who said what. When Earshot knows a voice, it puts that person's name beside the line. It is a reading aid. Names can be wrong. Measured on computer-made voices only Everything on this page about how often names appear, and how often they are wrong, comes from tests with computer-made voices. It has not been measured on real crew or on a real party line. Real people may do better or worse. Read the numbers below with that in mind. Who can do this Only admins can add people, learn voices and change Names on lines. Everyone else sees the list. Every role sees the names on lines.

Install CAM++ under Models. Enable voice recognition on the channel. In Setup → People, leave Detect new voices automatically on and talk normally. Distinct voices with enough speech appear as Voice 1, Voice 2, and so on. Use a voice's pencil button to give it a name. Its stored identity stays the same, so earlier lines also show the name. Clear subsequent turns refine the profile over several observations. Consecutive speakers can become separate finished lines without a silence between them. Drafts remain an unsplit preview. Roughly 1.5 seconds per speaker is needed for discovery and turn detection; short replies, similar voices and noise can remain unknown or be misidentified. You can still add a person and learn their voice deliberately for a longer, controlled sample. Only admins can change People or the discovery settings.

Install Overlapping voices · MossFormer2 (experimental) under Models (about 245 MB), then enable Separate overlapping voices (experimental) in People. This tries to transcribe two people speaking at once locally. It prepares the model in the background; the Activity log reports when it is ready. While preparing, unavailable or busy, normal transcription continues. Each isolated track is split at pauses using the channel's timing settings, and lines are ordered by onset. Replay audio belongs to the individual line. Names and very quiet speech can still be missed; source separation can also produce extra or incorrect words. This is not yet a low-latency live feature. The synthetic trial on the development M3 Pro took about 8.6 seconds to separate four seconds of audio. It is off by default. More than two simultaneous speakers are not supported, and it has not been tested on real crew or comms feeds. The mock show. Priya, Dan, Ines and Sam are invented, and no real voice has been learned.

Open Setup, Models, find Voice recognition (CAM++) and press Download. It is about 29 MB and you do it once. It is optional and is not marked Recommended. See Models. Until it is installed, the People screen shows a notice that voice recognition is not available, with "Names will not appear on lines, and voices cannot be learned, until this is fixed." and an Open Models button. The Learn voice buttons say "Install the voice model first".

This is optional when automatic discovery is on. To name an already detected voice, edit its existing row instead of creating another person. Open Setup, People, and press Add a person. Type a Name and pick a Colour. The name is shown beside lines in that colour. Press Save person. Two people cannot have the same name ("Someone is already called Priya."). Each person in the list has one of three badges: Badge Meaning No voice yet Earshot has never learned this person's voice. They will never be named. Voice learned Their voice is stored and in use. Voice needs learning again A voice is stored, but its record no longer fits the voice model. Learn it again.

Earshot learns a voice by listening to that person talk on the comms channel they will use. Press Learn voice next to the person (Learn again if they already have one). Under Learn from channel, pick the channel. Under How long to listen, pick 15 seconds, 20 seconds or 30 seconds. Press Start listening. Ask the person to read the displayed passage at a natural pace on that channel. The panel tells you what to say to them, for example: "Ask Sam to talk on Deck Left for about 15 seconds. Anyone else who talks will be learned too, so ask the others to stay quiet." The mock show. Nothing is really being listened to here. While it listens: Underlined passage words have been recognized. Repeat the passage if more speech is needed; highlights survive hiding the panel or leaving Setup and returning. The input meter shows whether audio is arriving. A paused or disconnected input is reported while collection waits. The count is of detected speech, not of time passing. Background voices or noise mistaken for speech can affect collection. The bar reads, for example, "9 of 15 seconds of speech". The panel says "Listening for Sam…", then "Hearing speech", then "More than halfway". If nothing has been heard for a couple of seconds it says "Waiting for Sam to talk…". "On a noisy line, ask for longer: 20 to 30 seconds works better." Only one voice can be learned at a time. Earshot gives up after 3 minutes without enough speech. Cancel stops learning. Hide progress keeps it running in the background; use Show progress or Review result to return. Once enough speech is collected, the host explicitly switches to Processing voice. A full bar alone does not mean the voice is ready. It ends one of four ways: The panel says What happened "Sam's voice is learned." The voice is stored. Sam's badge becomes Voice learned. "Sam's voice was not learned. That did not sound like one person, so nothing was changed. Learn it again with only Sam talking." More than one person was heard. The recording is not kept, and an earlier voice, if Sam had one, is left as it was. "Sam's voice was not learned." followed by a plain message Something else went wrong, and the message says what. "Cancelled. Nothing was changed." You pressed Cancel. After a failure, press Try again.
documents.s: 3. Learn each voice from the channel itself

documents.t: Open Setup, Channels, the channel, and switch on Separate and recognise voices on this channel. It is on for new audio channels; existing channels keep their previous setting. It is set channel by channel. See Channels.
documents.s: 4. Switch it on for the channel

documents.t: On the People screen, under the list, Names on lines has three choices. Pick a card to change it. The card in use carries an In use now badge. Choice The app says Measured on test voices (lines of 1 second or more from voices Earshot had learned) Cautious "Shows a name only when Earshot is very sure. Few lines get a name; a wrong name is unlikely." About 6 in 100 got a name. Lines from people who had not been learned got no name. Balanced (the default) "Names more lines. Sometimes a line gets the wrong name, mostly from someone whose voice was never learned, and more often if they sound like someone whose voice was." About 36 in 100 got a name. About 2 in 100 lines from people who had not been learned also got a name. Eager "Names the most lines, and gets the most wrong." About 62 in 100 got a name. About 5 in 100 lines from people who had not been learned got a name. Read these numbers with care. They describe controlled voice learning, not automatic discovery. They come from 21 computer-made voices (several share one speech engine), not from real people and not from a real party line. Real crew may do better or worse. In the same tests no choice ever gave one learned person's name to another learned person. But when most of the crew was learned, and the person who was not learned sounded like one who was, the unlearned person's lines were named up to 17 in 100 times at Balanced and 33 in 100 at Eager. A voice learned on clean audio and then heard through a simulated comms line got no name at all at Balanced. The default, Balanced, was kept on the condition that this is said plainly. It may need changing after the first recording of a real party line. Two notes sit under the cards: "Automations limited to people always use the most cautious rule, whatever is chosen here." A name you can read on a line does not mean a people-limited automation will fire for it. See Automations limited to people. "If two people are confused, use Learn again to give Earshot a longer, clear sample of each voice."

The mock show. "Priya" beside the Deck Left line is what a recognised name looks like. The name appears in the person's colour, a moment after the line, never before it. It never changes the line's text. Its text alternative, which a screen reader reads, is "Recognised by voice. May be wrong." Short lines get no name. A line needs about a second of real speech. A "go" or a "copy" usually gets none. New comms voices may need several consistent replies before a label appears. Short replies are only combined within the same channel when they sound like the same person; uncertain or stale observations are discarded. Names can be missing while CAM++ is loading or its recognition queue is full. A Behind channel pauses expensive turn and overlap separation, while background voice naming continues. Typed lines carry the name of whoever typed them, which is a different thing: a name someone gave themselves when they joined. Every role sees names, viewers included.
documents.s: What a name on a line means

documents.t: Learned voices are never sent to a browser: not to any role, not to an admin. They are never in an exported show file. A show imported on another computer brings the people's names and colours and no voices. Moving a show to another computer means learning every voice again. See Show files. They are stored on the host, in the show file inside the data folder. See Privacy.

Button Asks What it removes Forget voice "Forget Priya's voice?" "Earshot will stop recognising them until you learn their voice again. Lines already named keep their names." Only the voice. The person stays in the list with No voice yet. Delete (the bin) "Delete Priya?" "Their learned voice is removed too. Automations limited to them will not fire for anyone else." The person and the voice. The pencil edits a person's name and colour without touching their voice.
documents.s: Forgetting a voice, deleting a person

documents.t: Deck Left is a party line shared by Priya, Dan, Ines and Sam. Priya, Dan and Ines show Voice learned. Sam shows No voice yet. Sam is the gap. Until Sam is learned, Sam's lines get no name, or now and then somebody else's. Press Learn voice next to Sam. Choose Deck Left and, because the line is noisy, 30 seconds. Press Start listening. On comms: "Everyone on deck left, quiet please. Sam, talk to me for half a minute: tell me what's on the props table." Wait for "Sam's voice is learned." Check Separate and recognise voices on this channel is on for Deck Left. Watch the Feed. Longer lines from the four of them start to carry names. Short acknowledgements do not. If Priya's lines stop being named next week, press Learn again next to Priya, on the same channel.
documents.s: Example: four people on Deck Left

documents.t: Learn everyone who talks on the channel. Wrong names come from voices Earshot has not learned. Learn them on that channel, not somewhere quiet. The same person learned on clean audio was named far less often on the noisy line. On a noisy line use 20 or 30 seconds, and keep the others quiet. Learn again if a voice stops being recognised. Treat every name as a hint. Do not use a name to decide who gave an instruction that matters.

On a real host, with the real models and three looping recorded channels, two voices were learned through the real screen (about 36 seconds each, 16 to 17 seconds of speech). No voiceprint went to the browser. At Balanced, each channel carrying one voice named every line correctly. On a channel mixing five lines from three voices, the two learned voices were named correctly (13 named lines, none wrong), and the third, never learned, got no name in the first run. Not tried: real people, a real microphone, or comms-quality audio. All the voices were clean and computer-made, and several share a speech engine and so sound more alike than most people do. More in Limits and known behaviour.
documents.s: What has and has not been tried

documents.t: Go down this list: Setup, Models: is Voice recognition (CAM++) installed? Setup, People: does the person show Voice learned? Setup, Channels: is Separate and recognise voices on this channel on for that channel? Is the line very short? Is the channel Behind, or did the model only just start? Was the voice learned on this channel? Is Names on lines on Cautious?

Channels: the Separate and recognise voices on this channel switch. Automations limited to people: experimental, and stricter than names on lines. Privacy: where learned voices are kept. Troubleshooting.

Open Setup, then Show file. The screen says: "The show file holds your channels, groups, automations, destinations and glossary, so you can carry a show to another machine. It does not hold this computer's settings or the transcript." The screen has four parts: Name, Export, Import and Session. Who can do this Only admins. The mock show. Not a real show.
Show name is what appears in the header on every screen, and it becomes the name of the exported file. Type a new one and press Save name. The screen says "Show name saved."

Press Export show file. Your browser downloads a file named after the show and ending .earshot.json. The screen says "Exported. The file has no passwords or API keys in it." In the file Not in the file Channels and their settings The password for joining Groups Cloud keys (Deepgram, DeepL, Anthropic) Automations (triggers, conditions, actions) Link codes of channels from other Earshot computers OSC destinations Learned voices The glossary Webhook addresses, HTTP header values and shell commands (hidden) People's names and colours The path of web addresses in HTTP actions (cut back to the host name) The addresses of linked channels, without their codes The transcript, markers and saved audio The file is not secret-free in every sense It has no passwords or keys, but it does carry your channel names, crew names, glossary and the host names your automations talk to. Treat it like any other show paperwork.

Press Choose a show file… and pick a .earshot.json file. Earshot asks "Import this show file?" before it does anything: Importing the file replaces this show's channels, groups, automations, destinations and glossary with the ones in the file. This computer's settings are kept: access, OSC and MIDI input, cloud keys, start armed and shell commands. Importing never arms the show. Secrets are not stored in show files. Webhook addresses, HTTP header values and shell commands in the file must be entered again, and the automations that use them arrive switched off and marked “Not running”. If the file is rejected, your current show is left as it is. Press Import show to go ahead. Afterwards the screen says "Imported file. This computer's settings were kept and the show is not armed. Any automation that needs a webhook address, header value or shell command is switched off and marked “Not running” until you enter it again."

It replaces show content. This show's channels, groups, automations, destinations and glossary are replaced by the ones in the file. It is not a merge. It keeps every local setting of this computer. Access (who can connect, the password), OSC and MIDI input and their level, allowed devices, cloud keys, Start armed, the shell commands switch, the default speech model and the translation settings all stay as they are. A show file cannot change who is allowed in. It never arms. If the show was Armed when you imported, it goes Safe. Learned voices are never imported. People arrive with their names and colours. Voices already learned on this computer stay for people with the same id. Everything else must be learned again. Secrets must be typed in again. A webhook address, an HTTP header value or an HTTP address hidden in the export arrives empty. Those automations come in switched off, marked "Not running", with a problem saying what to enter. Open each one, fill it in and switch it on. Automations that run shell commands always arrive switched off, whatever this computer's shell setting is. Importing never turns on Allow automations to run shell commands. Switch each automation on yourself after you have read what it does. An imported linked channel with an unusable address is kept, switched off, with its address cleared (it might have held a code). Type the address again. A rejected file changes nothing. Your show is left as it was. An import replaces the show you have There is no undo button. Export the current show first if you might want it back.

A session is one continuous transcript. Earshot starts a new one every time it starts. The screen shows when the current one began. Press New session… to start a fresh one by hand, for example between the matinee and the evening show. Earshot asks "Start a new session?" and says "The live transcript starts again from empty. The current session is kept in the Archive." Press Start new session. Nothing is deleted. The old session is in the Archive, where you can read, search and export it.

You built "Spring Tour at Harbour Hall" on a laptop in the office. The venue has a rack computer that will run it. On the laptop Open Setup, Show file, and press Export show file. Copy the downloaded .earshot.json file to a USB stick, with a note of every secret the show uses: webhook addresses, HTTP header values and full web addresses of HTTP actions, shell commands, link codes, cloud keys. On the venue computer Start Earshot and open it as an admin. Download the speech models while you have internet. See Models. Open Setup, Show file, Choose a show file…, pick the file, read the question, and press Import show. Then put back what a show file does not carry Inputs. The channels arrive pointing at the audio device the laptop used. Open Setup, Channels (or Patch) and point each one at the venue interface's inputs. Check each level meter moves. Automations marked "Not running". Open Automations and press Show it (or Show only these). For each one, type the web address, header value or webhook address again, read it, and switch it on. See When an automation is not running. Shell automations. They arrive switched off. If you use them, turn on Setup, Show control, Allow automations to run shell commands, then read and switch on each automation. OSC destinations. They come across with the show. In the automation editor, under OSC destinations, check each one has the venue console's address, port and protocol. Voices. Every person arrives with a name, a colour and No voice yet. Learn each voice again, on the channel they will use. See People. Linked channels. Type each link code again (and the address, if it arrived cleared). See Showing another Earshot computer's channels. This computer's own settings. An import does not touch them, so they are whatever this computer had.
